#5544. Rising demand puts Locaweb’s data center strategy to the test

Growing demand and hardware shortages are forcing service providers to rethink data center capacity planning. For Locaweb Serviços de Internet S/A, a cloud hosting and digital services provider based in Brasil, keeping up with customer needs means anticipating infrastructure requirements earlier and finding alternatives when equipment isn’t readily available.

That pressure is changing how Locaweb approaches infrastructure decisions. The company is working more closely with technology partners, including Dell Technologies Inc., to assess alternative hardware configurations and manage supply challenges without compromising its services, according to Gustavo Gomes Salviano (pictured, right), chief technology officer of Locaweb.

“I think that [growing demand] brings the infrastructure challenge again to the board,” he said. “Now we need to think more quickly and strategically in the infrastructure than we did before.”

Salviano and Diego Puerta (left), Brasil general manager at Dell Technologies Inc., spoke with theCUBE’s John Furrier for theCUBE + NYSE Wired: AI Factories – Data Centers of the Future interview series, during an exclusive broadcast on theCUBE, SiliconANGLE Media’s livestreaming studio. They discussed capacity planning, supply constraints and the engineering collaboration supporting Locaweb’s growth.

Locaweb began as a hosting and email provider for small businesses before expanding into e-commerce, marketplace and financial solutions. That broader portfolio has increased the range of services its infrastructure must support, according to Salviano.

“First of all is to anticipate the demands,” he said. “We anticipate … more than we’ve done before. But the second thing is … we are working with our engineers and our partners’ engineers, like Dell, to think about how can we solve the problem that we’re facing.”

Memory availability is among the concerns shaping those discussions, alongside costs and delivery schedules. Locaweb and Dell have discussed supply challenges since last year, considering how to secure the right configurations in time to meet demand, Salviano explained.

“Sometimes we are re-engineering our [infrastructure] needs [to] solve the problem of the time and the length of the time of the delivery, the supply chain,” he said. “It’s challenging us to think about our partners and how we can change that without taking any functionality from our products and from our customers.”

Addressing those supply challenges requires more than ordering equipment earlier. Locaweb also needs to consider alternative configurations that can meet its customers’ requirements without compromising performance. The companies’ longstanding relationship helps inform those technical choices. Dell’s familiarity with Locaweb’s environment lets teams assess alternatives against the performance and capacity its services require, according to Salviano.

“When we talk about our needs, our technical needs, they’ll understand our products,” he said. “They know what runs there.”

Those infrastructure decisions are also becoming more important as Locaweb introduces AI capabilities into its business. The company is developing tools that allow nontechnical users to build solutions for their own operational needs. Those tools are helping employees improve business processes, with IT supporting their efforts, Salviano noted.

For Dell, helping customers establish the foundation for enterprise AI begins with understanding their business objectives, according to Puerta.

“It’s not an IT transformation; it’s a business transformation leveraging IT,” Puerta said. “It must come from the leadership. IT is the enabler because what AI is doing is amplifying the possibilities.”

NEW YORK, Nov. 5, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Hyperliquid Strategies Inc (NASDAQ: PURR) ("HSI" or the "Company"), the premier digital asset treasury platform focused on the Hyperliquid ecosystem, today reported its financial and operational results for the quarter ended September 30, 2026.

"We deployed $802 million this quarter and filed an application to become a futures commission merchant," said David Schamis, CEO of Hyperliquid Strategies Inc. "Those two moves are the same bet. Hyperliquid is winning the parts of onchain finance that generate real fees, and nearly all of that value flows back to HYPE holders through programmatic buybacks. Owning HYPE is how we aim to capture economics associated with the Hyperliquid protocol; setting up an FCM is how we intend to help bring markets deployed on Hyperliquid onshore."

Key Highlights (as of or for the Quarter Ended September 30, 2026):

Hyperliquid Ecosystem Momentum1Momentum continues to build around the adoption of the blockchain by the global financial system, with much of that momentum represented within the Hyperliquid ecosystem.

As Hyperliquid pursues its vision of becoming the infrastructure to house all of finance, the Hyperliquid protocol continues to generate an increasingly diversified stream of fees (with about $834 million in value accruing to the Hyperliquid ecosystem for the twelve months ended September 30, 2026), processing billions in daily trading volumes, with much of the value generated by the Hyperliquid ecosystem directly accruing to the HYPE token through programmatic HYPE token buybacks.

Hyperliquid recently announced its intention to add additional deployer functionalities under the name HIP-3*. These optional additional features would allow deployers to build and launch permissioned markets on Hyperliquid's onchain infrastructure. Independent operators would run their own market in a compliant manner, while the chain underneath would stay a neutral infrastructure layer.

Subject to regulatory approval, the FCM would carry US client accounts for permissioned markets deployed on Hyperliquid under HIP-3*, allowing HSI to play a role in bringing perpetual futures to US customers within a regulated framework. There can be no assurance as to the timing or outcome of the application or regulatory approval of permissioned HIP-3* markets.

#5542. RealPRO Select helps lift Realtor.com revenue

Realtor.com reported $160 million in fiscal Q1 2027 revenue, up 5% year over year, extending an eight-quarter growth streak. News Corp cited RealPRO Select expansion and broader RealAssist AI rollout as key drivers.  AI Summary

Move, the parent company of Realtor.com, said the momentum generated by RealPRO Select in fiscal year 2026 has carried over into the first quarter of fiscal year 2027.

During the first quarter of FY 2027, Realtor.com recorded $160 million in revenue, up 5% year over year, marking the segment’s eighth consecutive quarter of growth. These financial results were highlighted during News Corp’s fiscal year 2026 fourth-quarter earnings call on Wednesday evening.

“In a housing market constrained by 7%-plus mortgage rates, Damian [Eales] and the team have exhibited exceptional discipline in their operational focus and AI integration, and that approach has converted revenue growth into meaningful bottom-line expansion,” Robert Thomson, the CEO of News Corp, said during the earnings call.

News Corp executives attributed Realtor.com’s strong revenue performance to the growth of RealPRO Select. The company said it is focused on enhancing the platform with stronger lead generation, branding, productivity tools and training capabilities.

Realtor.com also focused on the expansion of RealAssist AI during Q1, including the launch of a pilot of RealAssist in Rich Communication Services (RCS), integrated directly into Google search and available on iOS and Android.

“The pilot is already attracting new users, driving strong engagement, and helping us capture pre-search intent earlier in the buyer journey before consumers ever enter a browser,” Damian Eales, the CEO of Move, wrote in a blog post about the company’s quarterly performance.

In addition, Realtor.com also launched RealAssist AI for Realtor.com+, which Eales said helps agents onboard their clients faster, build more tailored searches, summarize client activity and draft follow-ups in their own voice.

“The platform is already supporting thousands of successful agent-client connections, and early feedback on these AI tools has been very positive,” Eales wrote.

Eales also highlighted the relaunch of the My Home dashboard, which now includes a collaboration with Opendoor. Eales said this is encouraging sellers to engage a listing agent much earlier in their journey.

In addition, News Corp also noted that Comscore data shows 4.9 visits per unique user to Realtor.com, up 8% annually, and an average of 263 million monthly visits in the quarter, which the company said represents a “substantial” lead over Redfin and Homes.com.

Despite these strong numbers, Realtor.com noted that lead volume was down 11%, which the portal attributed to broader market conditions and its repositioning of customer acquisitions to higher-quality and higher-value leads.

“Despite a constrained housing market, Realtor.com’s strategy is delivering positive results, and we’re well positioned to grow as conditions improve,” Eales wrote. “Our focus remains on investing in our audience and AI tools that enhance a consumer’s experience and augment the role of the professional agent.”

Overall, News Corp’s digital real estate services segment generated $529 million in revenue, up 10% from a year prior. The company as a whole generated $2.28 billion in revenue, a 6% annual increase, and net income of $215 million, up 43% compared to a year prior.

#5540. 20 NHL teams project 2026-27 payrolls above $101 million, 9 of them over the cap

Free daily briefing on global business news.

Projected 2026-27 cap hits for 20 NHL teams, from $101.66 million to $112.97 million, against a $104 million salary cap.

A general manager can scout, draft, and trade with skill, yet one number decides how many of those moves a club can afford to keep. The NHL salary cap sets the outer edge of every roster, and each contract a team signs claims part of the space beneath it. Hockey payroll behaves like a container of fixed size. Every new deal crowds the ones that came before it, and a club with little room left has fewer ways to add a player, retain one, or recover from a misjudged signing. Fans who follow trade rumors and contract talks are watching teams bargain with that ceiling.

The 2026-27 season limits spending at $104 million and sets the floor at $76.9 million, a band of $27.1 million between the least a franchise must lay out and the most it may. Franchises near the bottom of that band have money to deploy on acquisitions and free agents. Those pressed against the top carry obligations, and every dollar such a franchise commits to its current group becomes a dollar unavailable for the next addition. Those commitments reach past a single year. Agreements a front office reaches today shape budgets in seasons that have yet to begin. A crowded ledger in 2026-27 can narrow an organization's options for several summers.

PuckPedia gathers all 32 NHL teams into one table for 2026-27, setting each projected cap hit beside cap space, dead cap, contract count, active roster size, average age, and the cost of forwards, defensemen, and goalies. The site notes that its summary updates in real time, and the page gives no date for its figures. Each total here reflects a moment that could shift with the next transaction. The table offers no ranking of its own. This list sorts 20 of those teams by projected cap hit, from highest to lowest, and each one projects above $101 million. Every position reflects that ordering alone.

Vegas projects a 2026-27 cap hit of $112,974,350, the heaviest payroll on the table and $8,974,350 over the limit. No other club in the league shows a deeper deficit. Within the Pacific Division, Anaheim comes next at $105,144,432, leaving Vegas $7,829,918 clear of its division's second-heaviest payroll. The overage amounts to about 8.6% of the league's cap.

A $41.10 million defense corps sets Vegas apart from every other NHL roster. Pittsburgh comes closest across the league at $37.70 million. Minnesota, at $3.91 million behind, holds the second-largest blue-line bill among these 20 clubs. The Vegas figure runs about 1.9 times Anaheim's, the smallest defense spend in the group. Defensemen absorb 36% of the Golden Knights' total cap hit. Forwards cost $63.45 million, fourth among the 20.

Vegas acquired former Toronto Maple Leafs forward Mitch Marner in a sign-and-trade to play alongside Jack Eichel. The Golden Knights added Nic Dowd ahead of the NHL trade deadline. The Las Vegas Sun describes Dowd as a center who kills penalties and shuts down rival top lines.

Three active roster spots sit open on a team spending beyond the cap. Vegas fills 20 of 23, the thinnest active count in the league, and has 48 of 50 contracts signed. Current space and deadline space both read $2,138,330. Dead space totals $23,958, the smallest nonzero sum among the 20 clubs. Florida, next on that measure, lists $150,000, more than six times as much.

A 29.9 average age ties Minnesota for fifth-oldest among the 20, behind Toronto, Los Angeles, Colorado, and Florida. Vegas carries a 2027 draft value of 6.04, the weakest of all 32 teams and 1.18 below the next-lowest club. The club holds $12,050,834 in 2027-28 tagging room, the fifth-smallest cushion in this group. Stripping out the entire $8.25 million goaltending outlay would leave Vegas about $720,000 above the cap.

Toronto's projected 2026-27 cap hit of $110,791,915 sits $2,182,435 below Vegas and clear of every other club in this group. The Maple Leafs would overshoot the $104 million ceiling by $6,791,915, more than double the $2,975,636 overage Dallas faces. A gap of $3,816,279 separates Toronto from the Stars, which leaves the Leafs and Golden Knights in a tier of their own above the rest of these heavy spenders.

Goaltending claims an outsized portion of Toronto's bill. The Leafs devote $15.18 million to their netminders, and the Rangers, at $16.29 million, are the one team among these 20 with a larger outlay. Forwards account for $62.69 million and defensemen for $32.93 million. Goalies absorb close to 14% of the projected payroll, the second-largest share in the group behind New York. The crease explains how Toronto stays within reach of Vegas. The Leafs put $6.93 million more into goal, while the Golden Knights outspend them by $8.17 million on defense. Up front, the two clubs sit $760,000 apart.

Toronto's $647,618 in 2027-28 tagging room is the smallest figure among all 32 NHL teams. Washington holds the next-thinnest margin among these 20 at $2,400,417, about $1.75 million more. Florida, at $8,597,122, is the one other club in this group below $9 million. Toronto shows $0 in dead space, so none of the overage traces to that category.

The Leafs list 49 of 50 contracts, tied with the Rangers for the highest count in this group, alongside an active roster of 21 of 23. At 30.7, their average age exceeds that of 18 of the other 19 clubs here. Current space and deadline space both stand at $3,325,000, and the 2027 draft value comes in at 21.45. Minnesota and the Rangers are the lone clubs among the nine above the limit to show more current space. No other club among these 20 pairs an overrun this large with a 2027-28 cushion this small.

Dallas projects a $106,975,636 cap hit for 2026-27, the biggest commitment in the Central Division. Minnesota, the closest division rival in this group, trails by $2,434,963. Across the Western Conference, Vegas alone carries a bigger bill. The Stars sit $422,577 above Florida and $3,816,279 below Toronto on the payroll ladder.

Forwards absorb $65.50 million of the Dallas total, or 61.2% of the club's spending. Anaheim's $72.47 million and Florida's $71.00 million exceed that attack budget, but no other club among these 20 spends more on its front lines, Vegas and Columbus included. Among Central rivals, Utah's $64.74 million comes closest, and Colorado follows at $62.23 million. Defensemen cost the Stars $30.31 million. The scoring group commands more than double the blue line's money. Goaltending adds $9.30 million.

Dallas overshoots the cap by $2,975,636, the third-largest overage in the league behind Vegas and Toronto. Its current space stands at $1,274,087, the thinnest cushion among the nine clubs in the red. The deadline figure matches that sum to the dollar. Dead money claims another $2,080,000, the largest such charge in that over-limit group. Florida, one spot lower, carries $150,000 in dead space.

Dallas holds $33,536,419 in 2027-28 tagging room. Among the nine teams above the ceiling, Minnesota's $46,783,126 and the Rangers' $34,023,165 alone exceed it. Toronto, a fellow member of that group, shows $647,618. Columbus, whose current space of $1,354,688 sits closest to Dallas, shows $23,116,666.

The Stars skew older than most peers on this list, with an average age of 29.6 above the mark at 13 of the other 19 teams. The Dallas average sits 3.4 years above Anaheim's 26.2, the youngest mark here. Dallas fills 22 of 23 active roster spots and 45 of 50 contracts. Neither count is full.

Dallas's 2027-28 room runs about 26 times larger than its current margin, which suggests the strain centers on 2026-27.

The Florida Panthers project a $106,553,059 payroll for 2026-27, and forwards claim $71.00 million of it, or 67%. Anaheim alone outspends Florida up front among these 20 clubs. Florida's forward bill tops Vegas's by $7.55 million, even though the Golden Knights carry an overall payroll $6,421,291 larger. Dallas projects a total $422,577 higher than Florida's, yet the Stars pay $5.50 million less for forwards. The lean turns stark against the blue line, where Florida budgets $27.41 million, leaving a $43.59 million gap between the two position groups. Only Anaheim and Chicago devote less to defense in this group. Goaltending takes another $8.00 million, about 7.5% of the total.

Florida landed a division rival's captain. Ottawa traded Brady Tkachuk to the Panthers for a package of draft picks, according to CBC. The deal put Brady alongside his brother Matthew, a Panthers player before Brady arrived. Brady said he requested the move to begin the next chapter of his career.

Florida's commitments overshoot the ceiling by $2,553,059, the fourth-largest overage among the nine teams on this list that sit over it. Vegas, Toronto, and Dallas carry bigger overruns. Florida's current space of $2,285,728 matches its deadline space to the dollar. Florida's 2027-28 tagging room of $8,597,122 looks thin as well. Toronto and Washington hold less among these 20 teams, and Colorado follows at $9,149,975. Dead space amounts to $150,000. Among the nine over-cap clubs, Vegas, Toronto, and Washington report less.

Florida's lineup leans veteran. Its average age of 30.3 trails Toronto, Los Angeles, and Colorado and no other club in this group. Florida's active roster stands at 22/23, and its contract count sits at 47/50. The club's 2027 draft value of 9.15 lands third from the bottom of the 20, with Vegas and Edmonton beneath it. The figures describe an older, attack-heavy payroll with little flexibility left this season or next.

Anaheim commits $72.47 million in projected forward cap hits for 2026-27, the heaviest attacking bill among these 20 clubs and across all 32 teams in the league. Florida comes closest at $71 million and trails by $1.47 million. Vegas, owner of the largest payroll in the group, devotes $9.02 million less to forwards than the Ducks do. Anaheim's defensemen, by contrast, cost $21.93 million, the slimmest blue-line outlay of the 20. Vegas pays $41.10 million for its blue line, $19.17 million more. The attack draws more than three times the defensive total, a gap of $50.54 million.

Forwards absorb about 69% of Anaheim's $105,144,432 payroll. The total sits $1,144,432 above the ceiling, one of nine overages among these clubs. Even so, the Ducks show $2,746,561 in current space, the same amount printed in their deadline column. Dead money comes to $1,025,000. A year ahead, the team holds $15,019,907 in 2027-28 tagging room. Only five rivals in the group report less.

The Ducks ice the youngest lineup across the 20 teams, at an average of 26.2 years, a mark they share with Montreal. Montreal reaches that age on a leaner forward budget. The Canadiens spend $56.20 million on forwards, $16.27 million less than Anaheim. Of the nine clubs over the cap, the next-youngest, the New York Rangers, averages 27.5 years, 1.3 years older. Anaheim fills all 23 active roster spots and uses 45 of its 50 contract slots.

NHL.com reports that forward Troy Terry was expected to miss time after surgery for a hip impingement and a labral tear, with the layoff lasting until at least November. The injury sidelines one member of the league's costliest forward corps. Anaheim's goaltenders account for $9.80 million. Together with the defense, they bring outlays beyond the forward ranks to $31.73 million, less than half of what the Ducks lay out up front.

The New York Rangers pay $16.29 million for goaltending, the largest crease bill among these 20 teams. Toronto comes closest and trails by about $1.11 million. Every other club in the set sits at least $4.59 million behind New York at the position. San Jose budgets $5.00 million for its netminders, the smallest amount among the 20 and less than a third of the Rangers' outlay. Goalies absorb about 15.5% of New York's projected cap hit, enough to make the crease the defining expense on this ledger.

Forwards cost the Rangers $51.95 million, the leanest attacking spend of the 20. Defensemen add $36.28 million, a blue-line bill that only Vegas, Minnesota, and New Jersey exceed here. Blue line and net reach a combined $52.57 million, more than the entire forward corps. Among these 20 clubs, the Rangers stand alone in paying their defense and goaltending more than their forwards. Every other team on this list hands its biggest slice to the scorers, so New York inverts the pattern.

New York's projected hit of $105,091,261 lands $1,091,261 above the ceiling. Current space, by contrast, stands at $3,848,228, the most of any club in this group. #5539. Los Angeles votes all-in on housing, electing YIMBY-backed Raman

Nithya Raman defeated incumbent Karen Bass in Los Angeles as YIMBY groups framed the race around accelerating housing production. City timelines for statewide SB 79 transit oriented housing rules, currently delayed to 2030, are expected to face pressure under the new administration.  AI Summary

City Councilmember Nithya Raman defeated Mayor Karen Bass to become the 44th mayor of Los Angeles, a win for the “yes in my backyard” groups that backed her challenge to the incumbent.

The Associated Press called the race Thursday. Raman, an urban planner and member of the Democratic Socialists of America, led by 4.2 percentage points, 52.1% to 47.9%, with roughly 76% of the expected vote counted.

She is the second DSA member to lead a major U.S. city. New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani won a year ago on an affordability platform that made more housing a focal point. Bass conceded and promised a “smooth and seamless transition.” She is the first Los Angeles mayor in two decades to lose a reelection bid.

Raman won despite long odds. Gov. Gavin Newsom, former Vice President Kamala Harris, retiring former House Speaker Nancy Pelosi and nearly every City Council member backed Bass.

YIMBY Action, YIMBY Los Angeles and California YIMBY were among the housing groups behind Raman. Unions, progressive Democratic organizations, environmental groups and County Supervisor Lindsey Horvath also endorsed her.

Housing and homelessness drove the campaign. Raman pitched expanded medical teams for people in encampments and moving residents out of city-rented hotels into permanent housing. She said she could cut encampments by at least half by 2028.

YIMBY groups cast the race as a test of how fast the city builds. The movement pushes to ease zoning limits and speed approvals to expand supply.

“Her win in California’s largest city is a big moment for the pro-housing movement,” California YIMBY posted on social media.

One early test is how Los Angeles complies with Senate Bill 79, the state law that encourages more housing near transit. City ordinances that took effect June 30 hold off full compliance citywide until 2030. YIMBY advocates will likely press the new mayor and council to move that date up. Raman favored a quicker housing timeline.

Mayor-elect Raman could inherit a $20 million-plus liability if the city doesn’t approve Woodland Hills Country Club’s 398-home plan. The club’s attorney, Dave Rand, a Raman supporter, set a 60-day deadline, and the state housing department wants a response by Nov. 25.

Raman will need the council to do that. Most members backed Bass, so Raman must build a majority from a body that largely opposed her.

She will have allies elsewhere at City Hall. Controller Kenneth Mejia and newly elected City Attorney Marissa Roy, a DSA member, join her in what The Hollywood Reporter called a “triumvirate of progressivism” at the top of city government.

#5538. Humanoid robot maker Agility Robotics debuts on the Nasdaq after SPAC merger

Agility Robotics Inc. debuted on the Nasdaq today after merging with a special-purpose acquisition company.

SPAC deals provide a simpler path to public markets than a traditional listing. In such transactions, a shell company floats its shares and then merges with a privately held business. That business effectively takes the SPAC’s place on the stock exchange where it’s listed.

Agility merged with an investment vehicle called Churchill Capital Corp XI Corp. on Wednesday. The deal and certain “related financings” together pulled in $465 million, a sum that excludes transaction fees. Agility will use the capital to bring its latest Digit 5 robot to market and add manufacturing capacity.

Digit 5 (pictured) is a nearly six-foot-tall humanoid robot with a 20-hour battery life. It moves using custom actuators based on so-called cycloidal drive technology. That’s a motor design that trades off some speed for increased lifting power: Agility says that the Digit 5 can carry up to 50 pounds at a time.

The robot’s batteries are made by a British startup called Nyobolt Ltd. They use niobium, a metal most commonly found in superconductors and jewelry, to speed up charging. Agility says that the Digit 5 can be recharged in just nine minutes, a fraction of the time required by earlier technologies.

The robot runs some of its software on Nvidia’s IGX Thor system-on-chip series. The most advanced chip in the lineup, the T7000, combines a 14-core central processing unit with a computer vision accelerator and two graphics processing units. One is an embedded GPU with 2,560 cores while the other is a standalone chip originally designed for workstations.

Digit 5 also makes use of Nvidia’s HALOS software toolkit. The suite includes algorithms that help robots avoid hazards. Additionally, HALOS provides resources that make it easier to secure the safety certifications required for commercial deployment.

Agility says that it has received more than $300 million worth of pre-orders for Digit 5. Its customers include Toyota Motor Co. and GXO Logistics Inc., a publicly traded transportation company. Agility claims that it also has three other large customers in the manufacturing sector along with a pipeline of more than 30 prospects.

“Digit is doing real work in customer operations today, taking on repetitive, physically demanding tasks,” said Agility Chief Executive Officer Peggy Johnson. “Becoming a public company gives us access to more resources to help accelerate that progress, bring intelligent robots to more workplaces and help build a future where people and robots accomplish more together.”

Agility plans to make Digit 5 available through an early access program in the first half of 2027. General availability is slated for later that year. The company will manufacture Digit 5 at a  70,000-square-foot factory in Salem, Oregon with planned capacity of up to 10,000 robots per year.

#5537. Tucows Reports Third Quarter Results In Line with Expectations with Progress on Balance Sheet Obligations

TORONTO, Nov. 5, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Tucows Inc. (NASDAQ: TCX) (TSX: TC), a global internet services leader, today reported its unaudited financial results for the third quarter ended September 30, 2026. All figures are in U.S. dollars.

"Adjusted EBITDA and gross profit grew year over year, and we remain on track for our 2026 guidance," said David Woroch, President and Chief Executive Officer of Tucows. "We also retired the Ting preferred units valued at $149.3 million, and repaid $6 million on our syndicated loan facility. After quarter end, we agreed to assign Ting's Colorado Springs lease, which is expected to release Tucows' parent guaranty in the spring. Each of these steps makes the business simpler and more flexible than it was a quarter ago."

Consolidated net revenue increased 1.4% year over year to $100.0 million in the third quarter of 2026, driven by revenue growth at Ting.

Gross profit for the third quarter of 2026 increased 20.5% to $29.1 million from the third quarter of 2025, and improved 13% sequentially. Both the year-over-year and sequential expansion was driven primarily by a large, non-recurring re-rate from the renegotiation of our mobile contract within the Corporate segment, as well as year-over-year growth from Ting.

Net Loss for the third quarter was $10.3 million (EPS of $(0.92), compared with a net loss of $23.0 million (EPS of $(2.08)), in Q3 2025. Adjusted net lossÂ¹ was $5.8 million (adjusted EPSÂ¹ of $(0.52)) in Q3 2026 versus an Adjusted net lossÂ¹ of $15.8 million (adjusted EPSÂ¹ of $(1.42)) in Q3 2025.

Adjusted EBITDAÂ¹ for the third quarter of 2026 rose 39.8% to $18.6 million from the third quarter of 2025, and improved 51% sequentially. The Ting segment had strong Adjusted EBITDA performance both year over year and sequentially, but the main driver was the impact in our Corporate segment from our mobile contract re-rate.

We ended the third quarter of 2026 with cash and cash equivalents, and restricted cash and restricted cash equivalents of $41.0 million. This compares with $60.2 million at the end of the second quarter of 2026 and $70.8 million at the end of the third quarter of 2025.

#5536. Bernie Sanders is demanding a national data center moratorium after Democrats' election wins

Free daily briefing on global business news.

Sanders cites local ballot results, while a Color of Change leader says a blanket freeze is contested even among Democrats

Sen. Bernie Sanders called for a national data center moratorium in a post on X $TWTR after Democrats won control of Congress in Tuesday's midterm elections.

Sanders, an independent from Vermont who caucuses with Democrats, said "Americans don't want Big Tech oligarchs wrecking the environment, gutting jobs and threatening humanity's future." He said he and Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez introduced an AI data center moratorium, and that communities voted for local versions of it on Tuesday.

The bill from Sanders and Ocasio-Cortez would freeze the construction of any new data centers across the country until lawmakers set safeguards covering power prices, environmental damage and local consent, according to TechCrunch. Democratic control of Congress may strengthen its prospects, but a presidential veto could still block it.

Rep. Yassamin Ansari, D-Ariz., wrote on X that the top of the Democratic agenda on day 1 should be a pause on advanced AI development, regulation of the industry and a ban on artificial superintelligence. Rep. Greg Casar, D-Texas, who chairs the Congressional Progressive $PGR Caucus, responded "Yes!" to her post, according to CNBC.

Democrats are not united on the issue. Nadine Smith, president and CEO of Color of Change, said some Democrats fear that a ban could hamper the advance of AI and undermine national security, according to TechCrunch. "Even among Democrats, a blanket freeze is contested," she said.

Data centers featured in several winning campaigns. Gina Hinojosa, who defeated Republican Gov. Greg Abbott $ABT in Texas, said in a late-October video that she would halt approval of every data center project until lawmakers enact safeguards for Texans, according to CNBC. Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro put his name to an executive order in August meant to curb the growth of data center projects.

According to CNBC, 56% of voters in its Voter Poll called AI and data centers a crucial or major factor in how they voted. Of those voters, 65% cast ballots for a Democratic candidate for Congress.

Industry is already responding. Meta $META Platforms President Dina Powell McCormick said on Wednesday that launching new U.S. data center projects will grow more difficult, and OpenAI pledged on Thursday to cover all electricity and infrastructure costs at future campuses it owns and operates. Voters in towns and cities across the country backed bans, moratoriums and other curbs on data centers in Tuesday's ballot measures.

Chip and data center stocks fell for a second day on Thursday as investors worried that Democratic gains could slow data center construction. The iShares Semiconductor ETF was down as much as 11%.

#5534. Google Cloud storage moves to the front of the AI stack as enterprises hit the GPU utilization ceiling

ANALYSIS by Paul Nashawaty

For the past two years, enterprise AI investment has been dominated by one conversation: compute. Organizations raced to secure GPU allocations, negotiated infrastructure deals and stood up machine learning platforms at speed. What many discovered only after the fact is that the bottleneck they thought they were solving was not the only one in the room. Storage is now throttling the very accelerators enterprises fought to acquire.

In the latest episode of the AppDevANGLE podcast, I spoke with Ronen Schwartz, vice president of products for Google Cloud Storage at Google LLC, about why storage has quietly become the defining constraint in enterprise AI infrastructure, and what a purpose-built architecture for AI workloads actually looks like. The conversation cuts to a problem that is real, measurable and still largely underacknowledged in most AI strategy discussions.

“Storage just got promoted,” Schwartz said. “Instead of being at the backend as an enabler, it is moving into the front as a critical part of accelerator execution.”

The economics of this problem are direct. Accelerators are, as Schwartz put it, an enterprise’s most expensive line item. Every second they idle waiting for data is money lost — not in some theoretical efficiency calculation, but in immediate, traceable waste. Yet when teams finally get access to their TPUs or GPUs, the data delivery path often hasn’t received the same attention as the compute layer.

“I speak to many customers, and what I’m hearing is the team spent a long time fighting to get their TPUs, their GPUs, to get their hands on accelerators. And once they got them, they’re actually not always able to get the output they needed. Very often it actually goes back to not enough thought put into the data delivery path.”

This is not a fringe scenario. Schwartz described a pattern where organizations identify the storage bottleneck only after it hits them — when GPU utilization metrics fall short of targets and training timelines stretch beyond projections. By then, the cost of underinvesting in storage architecture is already embedded in the project.

One of the clearest insights from the conversation is that AI is not a single workload, and treating it as one creates compounding gaps in storage architecture. Schwartz described training, inference and agentic workloads as having fundamentally different “heartbeats” with distinct data movement patterns that each require targeted design.

Training demands massive sequential reads, but the equally critical pressure point is checkpoint management. Every 15 minutes or so, a training cluster must pause and write a multi-terabyte checkpoint to protect work done against potential failure. “Slow storage in that place freezes the entire GPU cluster,” Schwartz said. Google’s Rapid object storage technology, he noted, can write checkpoints more than three times faster and restore them more than five times faster than standard object storage, and this distinction matters significantly at scale. He pointed to Torin, an autonomous vehicle company, as an example: millions of sensor data points flowing into storage to train vehicle models, where checkpoint performance is not an edge case but a core operational requirement.

Inference introduces a different constraint entirely, that of real-time, latency-sensitive interaction where response time directly affects user experience and token economics. Agentic workloads layer on a third set of demands: shared workspaces, state persistence across agents, low-latency retrieval and the need to support both short-lived and long-running agent processes that may hibernate and reactivate on demand.

“AI is not one workload. Really, the movement of data looks completely different. It’s like different heartbeats depending on where you are in the lifecycle.”

Google’s differentiation argument centers on infrastructure credibility built over years of running hyperscale AI workloads internally before offering the same capabilities externally. Schwartz cited specific performance figures: 15 terabytes per second on Rapid object storage and 10 terabytes per second on Google Cloud managed clusters, which he described as verified industry-leading numbers.

The technical foundation includes zonal colocation, or placing data physically close to GPU and TPU clusters to minimize the time a byte travels to the accelerator. Schwartz described this as a first-to-market capability that required rethinking assumptions baked into traditional storage design, where multi-zone or multi-region distribution was the default goal. For AI workloads, proximity to the accelerator takes priority. Google’s Rapid Bucket technology reduces processing steps in the storage path, enabling a single bucket to deliver more than 15 terabytes per second throughput with support for 20 million queries per second at sub-millisecond latency.

“It is because it is built on the Google infrastructure, which has been used internally longer than anyone else to support accelerators and their performance. But it is also because Google is working with nine out of the ten world-leading AI frontier model companies.” A storage architecture that can demonstrably improve GPU utilization can provide faster iteration through less idle compute and lower effective cost per training run.

The agentic dimension of the conversation revealed an underappreciated wrinkle in enterprise AI readiness. Agents require more than web browsing and database queries; they need access to unstructured data at scale, including images, video, documents and PDFs that represent the bulk of most organizations’ real data assets. Without a way to make that content semantically accessible, agents operate with a restricted and often unrepresentative view of enterprise knowledge.

Google’s response is what Schwartz called a Smart Storage Initiative, anchored by a recently launched Object Enrichment capability. When a file or image lands in a storage bucket, Google AI models automatically extract content and attach structured metadata to the object — in seconds, and at scale. The result is that what was previously unstructured becomes queryable by agents without manual intervention or downstream processing pipelines.

“An agent can now interact with what used to be called unstructured data because there is actually a very good understanding of the content.” The storage layer is also integrated into Google’s broader agentic data cloud and borderless lakehouse architecture, allowing agents to reach data stored outside Google’s environment as well.

For agent infrastructure at scale, Schwartz described dedicated Filestore agent volumes integrated directly into Google Kubernetes Engine and the agent sandbox environment, designed specifically to handle the cost, response speed, and data-sharing requirements of running thousands or millions of agents simultaneously.

The broader market shift here is architectural, not incremental. Enterprise AI infrastructure has been built in layers (compute first, then frameworks, then data) and storage was often treated as a procurement checkbox rather than a performance variable. That sequencing is proving costly. As GPU utilization targets become measurable KPIs and AI operations budgets face tighter scrutiny, the storage layer is being reassessed in a way it hasn’t been in years.

What Google’s position illustrates is that hyperscale operational experience at the storage layer translates directly into enterprise advantage — not as a marketing claim, but as a measurable difference in checkpoint speed, throughput, latency and agent responsiveness. The companies that have been running frontier model training and inference at scale have been forced to solve these problems; enterprise teams are now encountering them for the first time.

For platform engineers, ML infrastructure teams and enterprise architects, the implication is specific: Storage architecture decisions made during initial AI platform buildout will constrain or enable performance for every workload that follows. Revisiting those decisions after the bottleneck appears is significantly more expensive than addressing them in the design phase.

The market is heading toward a point where AI infrastructure conversations routinely include storage as a primary tier, not an afterthought. Organizations that recognize that shift early will extract measurably more value from the accelerator investments they have already made.

To hear the full conversation with Ronen Schwartz, check out the latest episode of the AppDevANGLE podcast. To learn more about how Google Cloud Storage can support the evolving demands of enterprise AI, explore Google’s storage solutions or connect with the Google Cloud team to discuss the right approach for your organization’s workloads.

#5533. 5 things to consider before exercising with a cold

Free daily briefing on global business news.

Mayo Clinic's advice on exercising with a cold turns on where symptoms sit, whether fever is present, and how you feel.

The alarm sounds, your throat feels raw, and your nose has sealed itself shut on the morning you set aside for a long run. Anyone who trains on a schedule knows what comes next. You lie still and weigh a hard-earned streak of early sessions against the pull of the blanket. A cold gives no warning about how far it will spread, and the gym bag by the door offers no verdict either. Fitness habits demand real effort to build, and few people want to surrender one to a sniffle. Many push through out of guilt, or because a race, a class, or a running partner is waiting. The choice feels small in the moment. It returns, though, every time a virus makes the rounds at work or at home, and anyone who keeps a routine will face it again.

Guessing wrong carries a price in both directions. Skip too many workouts, and the worry creeps in that strength, endurance, or pace will slip away along with the momentum that made exercise feel automatic. Push too hard, and a different fear takes over. Can a short break erase the gains? Does an intense session help a person sweat out a bug, or does it drag the misery out? Where does a passing nuisance end and something more serious begin? Habit and hunch answer these questions for many gym-goers, and locker-room wisdom contradicts itself. The cost lands at the exact moment someone feels least equipped to judge.

Mayo Clinic addresses the dilemma in a brief expert-answer page that its staff wrote and dated Nov. 18, 2023. The page poses one question, whether working out with a cold is OK, and answers it with general rules of thumb sorted by where in the body a person feels unwell. It reports no study results, measurements, or statistics. Its guidance draws on a short reference list that includes a chapter on infectious diseases in athletes from a sports medicine textbook, a 2021 paper in BMJ Open Sport & Exercise Medicine on stay-home-when-sick advice, and an AskMayoExpert entry on upper respiratory tract infection. The scope extends past the common cold to COVID-19 and other contagious illnesses. Hedged terms such as "usually" and "may" frame each point as a broad guide for personal judgment. The page names no individual physician as author or reviewer.

An ordinary cold without a fever leaves room for a light or moderate workout, according to the guidance. Two conditions sit inside that allowance. The illness has to be a common cold, and the person cannot be running a fever. Mayo Clinic ties its approval to both at once. A stuffy head with a normal temperature qualifies. The same congestion paired with a fever falls outside the permission.

Modest effort defines the scope of the green light. The page approves gentle or mid-level activity for a cold, and this part of its advice stops short of hard training or a push for a personal best. Someone who feels well enough to move still faces a ceiling on effort. A sniffle grants no license for a punishing session.

Movement brings its own payoff for a blocked nose. Exercise can open the nasal passages and relieve congestion for a short time, Mayo Clinic reports. The page describes a temporary lift. It makes no claim that activity shortens the cold or clears it. Anyone hoping to sweat out the virus finds no support for that idea in this guidance.

The nasal relief arrives through the same low-key effort the page endorses. Opening the airways demands no strenuous training. A person who stays within the allowance collects the benefit without stepping past the guidance. A fever-free person with a blocked nose finds no reason in the advice to cancel a relaxed outing, and the congestion may loosen during one.

Mayo Clinic treats exercise as acceptable in most cases when every symptom sits above the neck. Its examples cover a runny nose, a stuffy nose, sneezing, and a mild sore throat. Each of those complaints stays in the head and throat, the region the guidance marks as compatible with training.

Location drives the whole test. Applying it means taking stock of where the discomfort settles before heading out the door. The permission covers people whose ailments all stay above the neck. A single problem that reaches lower moves a person out of this category. The four named complaints work as a quick checklist for sorting a borderline morning.

The sore throat on the list carries a qualifier. Mayo Clinic names a mild one. A throat that hurts more than that falls outside the cases the guide describes. The word "mild" folds severity into the test. A person with a scratchy throat has to weigh how much it hurts in addition to where it sits.

Mayo Clinic attaches a condition to the green light. People in this situation should cut the session short and dial down the effort. The page illustrates the point by swapping a run for a walk. Its advice pulls two separate levers, how long a person keeps going and how much strain the body absorbs. The recommendation lowers both at once.

The walk-for-run swap keeps the same basic movement and softens the impact. A person with a head cold can hold on to the habit of moving by choosing a gentler version of the usual activity. A runner who switches to walking covers ground, keeps the shoes laced, and preserves the rhythm of a scheduled outing. The change trims the load and keeps the streak unbroken. Under Mayo Clinic's framework, an above-the-neck cold reshapes a workout's length and intensity and leaves the decision to stay active intact.

Chest congestion, a hacking cough, or an upset stomach means the workout should wait, according to Mayo Clinic's guidance on exercising with a cold. The page names these three complaints as examples of trouble below the neck and attaches one instruction to them. Skip the session.

The neck draws the boundary in this framework. Complaints that settle in the chest or the gut fall beneath it, and Mayo Clinic files them among the reasons to stay home. Any one of the three signs puts a person on the resting list. The guidance asks for no tally and sets no threshold beyond the presence of the sign itself.

The examples span more than one body system. A congested chest and a hacking cough affect the airways below the throat, and an upset stomach points to digestion. The instruction reaches past breathing trouble to discomfort anywhere in the trunk.

Mayo Clinic pairs these signs with a full break and keeps its shorter, easier option for milder cases higher up. A person coughing from the chest has no lighter version of the run or the class to fall back on under this guidance. The choice narrows to two outcomes, a pared-down outing or rest, and the location of the discomfort settles which one applies.

The dividing line shifts with the illness. Congestion that starts in the nose and later reaches the chest moves the same person from conditions that permit training to conditions that demand a pause. A morning check of where the misery sits, repeated each day until recovery, keeps the decision current.

Mayo Clinic tells anyone running a fever, feeling worn out, or aching in muscles across the whole body to skip exercise. These three signs share a trait the above-the-neck complaints lack. None of them stays in the nose or throat. Each signals an ailment that has moved past the head, and the clinic treats any one of the three as reason enough to sit out a planned session.

Fever draws the sharpest line in the advice. The clinic's approval of light or moderate activity with an ordinary cold hinges on the absence of a fever. A rising temperature cancels that approval. A person who managed a gentle walk with a stuffy nose yesterday loses the option once the thermometer climbs, even if the congestion has not changed.

Fatigue and widespread aches stand as independent triggers. The clinic lists them beside fever and does not require all three to show up together. Exhaustion on its own justifies a rest day, and so does an all-over ache. A person with a normal temperature and a clear chest who feels drained has grounds to shelve the workout.

Anyone carrying COVID-19 or another illness that passes to others should stay away from group training, according to Mayo Clinic. Here the concern shifts from the patient to everyone nearby. A fitness class or team practice brings other people within range of an infection, and keeping away protects them. The rule singles out the group setting, which places classmates, teammates, and gym partners at the center of the choice.

Fever and fatigue test whether a person can handle exertion, and contagion tests whether a room full of people can share space with that person without risk. A contagious person who feels fit enough to train can pass the first check and fail the second. Feeling strong earns no exemption from the group rule. Under this guidance, bowing out of the gathering becomes a duty to fellow participants as much as a choice about personal health.

Feeling terrible is reason enough to stop, and the guidance leaves the final call on training while unwell to your own body. Mayo Clinic treats an honest read of how you feel as the starting point for each choice. The page offers no checklist that defines feeling terrible. Judgment sits with the person who carries the symptoms. Misery needs no further test to justify time off.

A few days on the sidelines while sick should not hurt fitness or performance. The reassurance answers anyone who fears sliding backward after a short pause. Its hedged phrasing stops short of a guarantee. The page names no exact number of days, and it offers nothing to anyone facing a longer layoff.

Training at your usual intensity during an ailment beyond a simple cold invites injury or a more serious illness. The warning pairs two separate harms. One is physical injury, and the other is a sickness that grows worse. The danger lives in a mismatch, with an illness bigger than a cold meeting an unchanged effort. People who decide to work out while sick should trim both how hard the session runs and how long it lasts.

Recovery signals the moment to ease back toward the usual routine in gradual steps. The return hinges on how the body mends. The page attaches no calendar date to it, which matches its silence on how long a harmless break can run. A doctor can settle the question whenever you cannot tell whether activity is safe. The advice keeps that fallback for moments when self-judgment runs out.

Every hazard the advice names comes from doing too much, and none comes from resting. The page links injury and deeper illness to full effort, and it links no harm to a few days away. Doubt, by that logic, points toward the couch.

#5532. Bitcoin Bounces Back From 6-Week Low Despite $1B ETF Exodus

The CryptoNews editorial team is composed of seasoned writers specializing in cryptocurrency and blockchain technology. Their expertise ensures comprehensive, accurate, and insightful content for...

Bitcoin bounced back above $78,000 just now after hitting a six-week low, even as U.S. spot Bitcoin ETF sheds $1.16 billion across three trading sessions. The recovery came as daily withdrawals slowed sharply, giving BTC buyers room to push back after a steep selloff following the expected Democrats’ congressional win.

BTC climbed to $78,500, recovering from its overnight plunge as crypto markets rallied alongside U.S. stock futures. The rebound followed a difficult stretch for Bitcoin, with security concerns and political uncertainty weighing on investor sentiment.

The latest Bitcoin ETF figures show selling pressure easing, but institutional investors have yet to return in force. Withdrawals dropped from $643.2 million on October 30 to $115.6 million on November 3, while Bitcoin recovered from its six-week low.

U.S. spot Bitcoin ETF recorded three consecutive sessions of net withdrawals, totaling approximately $1.16 billion. The fund lost $643.2 million on October 30, followed by $398.6 million on November 2 and another $115.6 million on November 3.

BlackRock’s iShares Bitcoin Trust (IBIT) led Tuesday’s withdrawals with $95 million in outflows. Grayscale’s Bitcoin Mini Trust lost another $52.6 million, adding to the pressure on the funds.

Several products still attracted fresh capital. Bitwise’s BITB recorded $21.9 million in inflows, while Fidelity’s FBTC added $6.8 million. Morgan Stanley’s MSBT also attracted $3.3 million.

The latest Bitcoin ETF data shows daily withdrawals falling by more than 80% from Friday’s peak. October also ended with roughly $515 million in net outflows, while November’s first three reported sessions added another $1.16 billion in withdrawals.

The slowdown offers a more encouraging signal for Bitcoin bulls, although the funds remain firmly in net-outflow territory. Institutional investors are still reducing exposure rather than rebuilding positions.

Discover: The Crypto Presales This Q4 2026

Bitcoin’s recovery comes after a sharp selloff that pushed it to its lowest level in six weeks. The market has faced several pressures simultaneously, including the recent Binance security breach and uncertainty surrounding U.S. crypto legislation.

Democrats winning control of both congressional chambers raised questions about the industry’s legislative agenda. However, Bitcoin recovered alongside stock markets just now as the initial reaction gave way to renewed buying.

$80,000 is now the focus, with the next resistance zone sitting between $79,500 and $80,000. A break above that range could open the door toward $82,000, particularly if ETF outflows continue shrinking. The sharp decline in daily withdrawals shows institutional selling is losing some momentum, giving BTC a chance to extend its recovery.

However, Bitcoin needs to reclaim $80,000 to turn the bounce into a stronger bullish move. Failure to clear that level could leave BTC vulnerable to another rejection, especially with ETF investors still pulling capital. A return below $77,000 would expose the recent $75,600 low, where buyers previously stepped in.

The immediate outlook hinges on whether Bitcoin can turn $78,000 into support and challenge $80,000 with stronger buying volume. Slowing ETF withdrawals offer an encouraging backdrop, but a sustained move higher would require renewed spot demand rather than another short-lived relief rally.
