#5518. Data centers are learning to be flexible

Free daily briefing on global business news.

Data centers are driving up electricity demand, but flexible power use could ease grid congestion and speed up connections

Jim West/UCG/Universal Images Group via Getty Images

A version of this article originally appeared in Quartz’s AI & Tech newsletter. Sign up here to get the latest AI & tech news, analysis and insights straight to your inbox.

Picture a soccer club that bought a passenger van for its tournaments a few times a year. The van sits in a driveway the rest of the year. Buying it was the right call, because a van that wasn’t there on tournament weekend would have stranded the team.

The American power grid works the same way, and now we have numbers to show just how little of it gets used. This month, under a new state law, Virginia’s utilities reported theirs. Over the year ending in July, the distribution grid run by Dominion $D Energy, the utility behind the northern Virginia data center boom, was being used at 41% of its capacity on average.

Even in its busiest hours, the system averaged 80%, with some pockets running higher and others lower. In the state’s rural southwest, where demand has been falling, Appalachian Power reported 14% for the year and 54% at peak.

Grids are sized for the few hours a year when everyone runs the air conditioner at once, and building for those few hours is expensive. A data center that pulls full power around the clock raises that peak, and raising the peak means buying another van that mostly sits in the driveway, costing money while it gathers dust.

Researchers argued there might be a cheaper route than building, and it required something we prize in people: Flexibility. Duke $DUK researchers calculated that the existing grid could absorb nearly 100 gigawatts of new demand if the newcomers agreed to cut back its power use for roughly half a percent of the year.

The study caused a stir in energy circles, and Google $GOOGL hired its lead author. The idea came down to a trade. A customer accepts being throttled in the few hours when the local grid is stretched, and in return connects in months instead of years.

The clearest track record of this working belongs to California’s PG&E. EV charging companies, which draw heavily on the grid, saw the wait for power fall to four to eight months from one to three years before its Flex Connect pilot.

In the pilot’s first two years, the power participants asked for was there nine hours out of ten. In the hours it wasn’t, the limits cut into operations less than 1% of the time.

Batteries offered another way to ease the pressure at peak. In 2025, a data center company in Oregon secured a faster hookup from Portland General Electric $GE by agreeing to add a 31-megawatt battery, enough to run about 25,000 homes for two hours, that it could switch to if needed.

Others flexed the computing itself. Google started by putting off work that could wait whenever grids in Belgium and Taiwan ran tight. In 2024, it dialed back machine learning jobs three times when the grid around Omaha was under strain. This year it promised five utilities it would hold back as much as a gigawatt of data center demand when the grid was stretched.

Startups are selling software that slow, pause or relocate AI jobs when the grid is tight. There were plenty of ways to do it, and more kept coming.

Flexibility is already becoming required in some regions. A 2025 Texas law requires new large data centers to install equipment that lets the grid operator cut their power remotely in emergencies. Late last year, FERC, the federal agency that regulates the grid, directed the operator PJM to create interruptible transmission options for data centers built next to power plants. The Southwest Power Pool, which runs the grid across much of the Great Plains, made a similar move.

Of course, waiting is expensive, and data center queues in popular markets can run for years. Take an Nvidia $NVDA chip that costs $30,000 and is depreciated over three to five years, or $6,000 to $10,000 a year. Picture 100,000 of them in one cluster, waiting for power the way Microsoft $MSFT’s chief executive, Satya Nadella, said some of his company’s chips were last year. A year of waiting represents $600 million to $1 billion in potential computing value that goes unused.

The trade cost something on the other side too, although it was much less. For companies racing each other to build more powerful AI, even a few curtailed hours counted. If those 100,000 chips sat idle for the equivalent of 44 hours a year, the lost computing time would be worth $3 million to $5 million.

Flexibility will not fully replace the building the aging grid needs, because old equipment has to go regardless. But utilities planned to spend at least $1.4 trillion through 2030, with data centers and load growth among their top reasons, and a large transformer could take more than two years to arrive. Flexibility could shrink that bill, and that wait.

#5517. Andy Jassy’s prediction: Amazon could have two $1 trillion businesses within a decade

by Todd Bishop on Oct 29, 2026 at 6:08 pmOctober 31, 2026 at 8:51 am

No company has ever had a business with $1 trillion in annual revenue. Andy Jassy says Amazon is on a path to have two.

Amazon Web Services and the company’s stores business could both reach that milestone in the next five to 10 years, the Amazon CEO said Thursday in the company’s third-quarter earnings release and on its call with analysts.

It’s “pretty rare” for Jassy to make a projection that far out, Morgan Stanley analyst Brian Nowak observed on the call, asking how he gets there.

Jassy’s answer started with AWS, which is at a $184 billion annual revenue run rate after growing 39% in the third quarter. He expects growth of more than 40% in both 2027 and 2028, and pointed to a $578 billion backlog of contracted AWS revenue.

The largest customers reserve capacity in huge blocks, sometimes as much as a gigawatt at a time, giving Amazon “very good visibility” into 2027, 2028 and part of 2029, he said.

Beyond that, he said, businesses are still early in using AI, the cost of running AI models keeps falling, and new uses keep emerging, such as AI models finding and fixing security flaws.

“You can’t predict with any certainty five to 10 years from now, especially at these types of growth rates,” Jassy said of AWS. “But it’s not a stretch for us to imagine that this could be over a trillion dollar business.”

Jassy’s forecast is a big jump from seven months ago. In March, Jassy told employees that AWS had a chance to reach at least $600 billion in annual revenue within about a decade, double his earlier expectation, according to Reuters.

Amazon’s stores business is bigger than AWS. Sales from Amazon’s online and physical stores totaled $309 billion over the past 12 months, or about $575 billion if Jassy is including third-party seller services and advertising in his trillion-dollar projection. We’ve asked Amazon to clarify.

For comparison, Walmart, the world’s largest retailer, had $713 billion in revenue in its most recent fiscal year.

Whichever numbers he’s using, Jassy said “some folks are sleeping a bit” on how much progress the stores business has made.

Jassy argued that Amazon’s stores business is gaining ground on competitors. Amazon added more than $90 billion in gross sales over the past 12 months, he said, and is adding about twice as much per quarter as its next-largest U.S. competitor.

Units sold are up nearly 15% so far this year, Jassy said. He noted that nearly 80% of retail sales still happen in physical stores, which he expects to shift online over time.

The bold prediction came on a rough day for the company. Amazon shares fell more than 7% in after-hours trading after its profit fell short of Wall Street’s expectations.

It’s not going to be cheap to get there. Amazon expects to spend about $220 billion on capital projects this year, mostly for AWS, and Jassy said the company will spend “meaningfully more” in 2027. He said Amazon has “a clear line of sight to attractive financial returns” and is earning back its capital spending faster than before.

The impact is showing up in Amazon’s finances. Its free cash flow, the cash left over after capital spending, was negative $42.4 billion over the past 12 months, compared with positive $14.8 billion a year earlier.

With its spending running ahead of the cash its businesses bring in, Amazon has raised $115 billion through long-term debt this year. Its interest expense more than tripled in the third quarter to $1.7 billion, cutting into its profit.

“We’re in the very early days of this inflection,” Jassy said. “Our strategy is working, and I expect it will for the foreseeable future.”

#5516. 10 sectors where 2026 tech layoffs landed, from Oracle to Nike

Free daily briefing on global business news.

Tech has logged more than 200,000 layoffs in 2026. Here are 10 sectors, from cloud software to streaming, where cuts landed.

Picture opening your inbox before sunrise to learn that today is your last day at the company. Across the technology business in 2026, thousands of people have lived some version of that morning, and the pink slips have reached beyond the engineers who write code. Recruiters, lawyers, product managers, and human resources staff have joined the casualties. Many reports place the U.S. at the center of the downsizing. Anyone who works in tech, hires tech talent, or relies on a company that does has reason to watch where the next round falls.

Spending priorities explain much of the upheaval. Several companies have tied job reductions to heavier AI investment, and payroll has become the place where they find the money. Pushback has come from government and from workers. California Gov. Gavin Newsom unveiled a tool in June to follow how AI affects the labor force, pitching it as a way to ready the state through governance and policy. More than 4,500 Google $GOOGL staffers signed a petition seeking protections, including buyouts ahead of any mandatory layoffs and guaranteed severance. The calendar adds urgency. TrueUp counts more than 200,000 tech layoffs in 2026 with a couple of months to go, against more than 245,000 across all of 2025. By TrueUp's reading, this year's tally appears to be outpacing last year's.

Yahoo Tech maintains a rolling tracker of 2026 tech job losses, logging them company by company and month by month from March through its Nov. 4 update. Writers Katie Teague and Valentina Palladino assemble each entry from company statements, executive memos, social media posts, and outside news reports. Many entries describe announced plans or moves that other outlets reported, and several companies did not disclose how many people they let go. The tracker does not total or rank industries. This article sorts its company entries into 10 sectors, an editorial selection running from enterprise software to telecom and consumer brands. The order makes no claim about which sector shed the most jobs.

Oracle $ORCL shed 21,000 jobs over the past year, about 13% of its workforce, according to a June 23 filing. Another round followed in September, and the company never disclosed how many people it hit. Recipients reportedly opened early-morning emails on Monday, Sept. 14, telling them the day would be their last. Reports tie the September round to Oracle's effort to offset the money pouring into AI chips and data centers.

Intuit $INTU plans to lay off 3,000 employees, about 17% of its headcount. CEO Sasan Goodarzi wrote in a memo that the reductions would help the company concentrate on weaving AI throughout its services. Atlassian $TEAM dismissed some 1,600 people on March 16, around 10% of its workers. CEO Mike Cannon-Brookes told the team the cuts would let Atlassian pay for more investment in AI and enterprise sales out of its own savings while shoring up its finances. His framing casts payroll savings as the bankroll for AI, the clearest statement of the trade in this group.

Cloudflare is eliminating more than 1,100 positions in a restructuring tied to AI. Rackspace, a cloud computing services provider, let go of 750 workers, around 15% of its employees, as it pivoted toward AI. Cisco $CSCO is cutting just under 4,000 jobs, including 471 in the Bay Area.

Monday.com is dropping 20% of its people, about 630 in all, as it works to make its AI platform a core offering. Earlier in the year, the company built its main product around the idea that business customers want their teams working alongside AI agents. ClickUp CEO Zeb Evans announced a 22% cut as the company leans on AI to raise productivity. Evans insisted the move "wasn't about cutting costs" and pledged the savings would flow "directly back into the people who stay." ClickUp introduced million-dollar salary bands for employees who "create outsized impact using AI."

Salesforce $CRM axed at least 86 jobs in California. Workday $WDAY is laying off around 140 Bay Area employees to slim its tech team, part of a broader plan to pare its worldwide ranks by 2.5%. Seven of the 10 companies here tied their job losses to AI, through executive statements or press reports. In this corner of tech, AI spending competes with salaries for the same dollars.

Canva is eliminating 22% of its staff, just over 1,200 employees, as the design software company merges its product, growth, and platform teams. Reports place the overhaul in November and describe a push to reduce "subspecialisation," the habit of carving work into narrow roles. Fewer niche jobs could leave the employees who stay with a wider spread of duties.

Wix set a parallel course in May. Cofounder and CEO Avishai Abrahami announced on X $TWTR that the website builder would trim around 20% of its workforce, a reduction that should reach about 1,000 roles based on headcount. Abrahami pointed to the changes AI has set in motion and said the company needs to "become a faster, leaner, and flatter organization." He pinned part of the pressure on the exchange rate between the Israeli shekel and the U.S. dollar. Wix has its headquarters in Israel, which explains why the currency entered his reasoning.

Canva and Wix are each shedding about a fifth of their people, and both describe the goal in structural terms. Canva wants to thin out narrow specialties, while Wix wants a shallower hierarchy. Each plan redraws how the remaining staff split their work.

Webflow's reduction comes with no public headcount, though one employee called the round "a bloodbath." The word conveys how severe the layoffs felt to at least one person inside the company. A move toward AI appears to sit behind the cuts. CEO Linda Tong has said AI is rewriting how marketing teams build, test, and fine-tune digital experiences, which is the work Webflow's tools exist to support. Among the four companies here, Webflow's account alone comes from a rank-and-file worker.

Airtable let go of an undisclosed number of workers under its owner, Bending Spoons, the company that acquired Vimeo. Federico Simionato, a product leader at Bending Spoons, laid out the thinking on X as a "deep belief that small teams ship more and better." His wording lines up with Abrahami's call for a leaner company and with Canva's merger of separate teams.

Wix and Webflow both point to AI in this group, and Wix's CEO paired it with a currency squeeze. Canva and Airtable explain their cuts through team structure alone, with no mention of the technology. Half of these companies tie their layoffs to AI, and the other half treat compact teams as the goal in itself.

Epic Games announced on March 24 that it was laying off more than 1,000 workers, and CEO Tim Sweeney traced the move to a "downturn in Fortnite engagement" for its free-to-play shooter. His note to staff framed the problem as plain arithmetic. Epic was "spending significantly more than we're making," Sweeney wrote, and needed major reductions to keep the company funded. He added that AI played no part in the decision. One fading hit can destabilize a payroll built around it.

Electronic Arts $EA plans to eliminate 400 jobs, about 3% of its workforce, and the move includes closing BioWare, the studio behind the Mass Effect games. Shuttering BioWare will also cancel the next Mass Effect title. Earlier in the year, EA told investors it would rein in research and development spending as part of a push to save upwards of $700 million. A modest headcount trim can carry a franchise's next chapter out the door.

Xbox is shedding 3,200 roles through fiscal year 2027, Xbox chief Asha Sharma wrote in a post on X $TWTR. The first 1,600 people left on July 6, and the company said at the time that another 1,600 terminations would follow. In September, Xbox announced 268 more eliminations across Halo Studios, other first-party studios, and additional corners of Xbox Game Studios, all under a "reset" unveiled over the summer. The July and September rounds account for 1,868 roles, which leaves 1,332 of Sharma's total still to come. Soon after the July departures, Sharma joined a U.S. Federal Reserve task force advising on "productivity and jobs."

Sony $SONY Interactive Entertainment said in June that it is removing "a significant number of employees" from Bungie, but it gave no count. The losses reach most of the Destiny team, some members of the Marathon $MPC team, and SIE groups that support Bungie. Stripping out most of Destiny's developers leaves open how the series continues.

Ubisoft dismissed 105 employees at Red Storm Entertainment to reduce costs. Development has ended at the studio, which makes the downsizing permanent. Red Storm employed 180 people in 2022 and has weathered several earlier waves of job losses. The latest round alone equals more than half of that 2022 headcount.

Eidos-Montréal announced on March 30 that it would let go of 124 people, and studio head David Anfossi chose to depart. The studio's LinkedIn post pointed to "changing project needs" across production and support teams and said talent and performance played no role.

None of the six game companies in the tracker names AI as the trigger. The reasons they do give run to player engagement, spending, shifting projects, and a corporate reset, which ties the industry's losses to its own business pressures.

Meta $META began removing 10% of its workforce in May, about 8,000 employees, and it plans to shut 6,000 open roles to free up money for AI. The planned vacancy closures equal three-quarters of the dismissals. Meta is shrinking the payroll it carries today and the one it once meant to build.

Smaller rounds at Meta preceded the big one. The company cut about 700 people starting March 25 across Reality Labs, social media, and recruiting teams, according to reports. Reality Labs operates Horizon Worlds for the Quest VR headset, and Meta is stepping back from metaverse creation. Meta also reportedly set the end of May as the exit date for roughly 200 Bay Area workers, 124 in Burlingame and 74 in Sunnyvale. Trimming recruiters fits the move to close open positions. Both steps point to slower hiring ahead.

Microsoft $MSFT's July round hit 4,800 jobs, around 2.1% of its staff, with most of the losses in its gaming division. Buyouts form the other half of its approach. In April, the company extended its first-ever buyout to as many as 7% of employees. The one-time retirement program covered workers at the senior director level and below whose age and years of employment add up to 70 or more. A later reported offer reached 60,000 employees. Buyouts let the company lower headcount while leaving each worker to decide whether to go.

Amazon $AMZN's reductions arrived in scattered pieces. Reports put white-collar losses in its stores business at fewer than 1,000, with about 250 more in devices and an undisclosed number in its AGI group. A warehouse in Homestead, Florida, shed more than 600 positions. Amazon also eliminated roughly 30,000 people in rounds spanning October and January. The entries stretch from retail and devices to AI research and a warehouse floor, reaching corporate offices and frontline operations alike.

Apple $AAPL laid off at least 60 people in August in its Vision Group, the team behind the Vision Pro headset, and estimates put the companywide total above 200. The Intelligent Systems Experience group, which handles some AI features on Apple devices, also lost employees, reportedly because of architecture changes for the company's AI-infused Siri. An undisclosed number of Fitness+ workers departed too. The Vision Pro launched in 2024 at a starting price of $3,699, and incoming CEO John Ternus would reportedly put the category "on ice." Whether Apple exits AR and VR for good remains an open question.

Headset and metaverse teams surface in the rounds at both Meta and Apple, a sign that the two companies are cooling on mixed reality in the same year.

Visa $V is cutting about 2,600 jobs, around 7% of its workforce, and technology and product teams bear most of the losses. Efficiency drives part of the effort. In a memo, CEO Ryan McInerney wrote that Visa must "continue evolving how we work" and that "AI is also helping to accelerate this evolution and shape the way work gets done at Visa." Reports indicate that AI was one factor among several.

The card network intends to reinvest in consumer payments and value-added services such as stablecoin, according to reports. Visa is trimming technical staff while steering money toward newer payment products. The move shifts resources inside the company as much as it lowers expenses.

Coinbase is laying off 700 employees, about 14% of its headcount. CEO Brian Armstrong pointed to two pressures: the current market and AI's effect on how the company works. Coinbase stands as the lone firm in this group to name market conditions, which ties its downsizing to outside forces as well as internal strategy.

Visa's plan removes almost four times as many people as Coinbase's, yet Coinbase's share runs twice as high. The percentages put Coinbase near 5,000 people and Visa at about 37,000. At Coinbase, the cut reaches about one in seven workers.

Robinhood plans to trim its ranks by 10%, around 290 positions, as part of a restructuring it announced through the Robinhood Comms account on X $TWTR. The announcement leaves open whether AI shaped the decision. CEO Vlad Tenev said the company will turn to frontier technologies to drive its execution further. His phrasing points toward new tools without naming any.

The three companies acted in consecutive months, with Coinbase in May, Robinhood in June, and Visa in July. AI runs through the explanations from Visa and Coinbase, yet each executive paired the technology with a second motive, efficiency at Visa and the market at Coinbase. Payments companies appear to fold AI into cost calculations that predate it.

Uber $UBER announced 3,300 job cuts, about 10% of its workforce, and pointed the steepest reductions at the distance between employees and the top of the company. The plan trims staff sitting seven or more layers below the CEO by 20% and shrinks micro-teams by close to 50%. Together, the two targets describe an org chart losing its middle rungs and its smallest units at once. CEO Dara Khosrowshahi's memo on the changes made no mention of AI. Uber also reportedly cut 10% of its customer service staff in July.

Etsy followed a similar path with about 220 layoffs, 12% of its employees, to simplify its setup. Product and engineering teams took most of the losses. CEO Kruti Patel Goyal said the changes would help build "the organization we believe Etsy needs for the future." A company spokesperson said AI adoption did not drive the decision. At 12%, Etsy's reduction ran two percentage points deeper than Uber's.

Patreon let go of 93 people, 20% of its headcount, and tied the move to "changing our organizational structure and how we work." Its email to creators and team members stated that the company was "not making the above changes because we believe AI replaces humans." The same message conceded that AI has reshaped the tech industry and Patreon's own working methods. The email held both positions at once, crediting AI with changing daily work while denying it any role in who lost a job.

Groupon planned the deepest proportional downsizing among these companies, roughly 25% of its people or 400 positions, with the cuts expected by the end of the third quarter. The company set out to rebuild itself as an AI-native business. Of the six employers here, Groupon stands alone in making AI the stated purpose of its overhaul.

eBay is trimming 9% of its workforce, following a February round that eliminated about 800 positions. A company spokesperson described the move as a way to line up eBay's teams and resources behind its top strategic priorities. Zillow is laying off just over 500 people, and its CEO pointed to "a disciplined cost structure and getting more efficient" as the goal.

All six of these companies gave reasons for their cuts, and several, including Uber, Etsy, Patreon, and eBay, pinned them on how they arrange their teams while leaving AI aside. Across consumer marketplaces, reshaping the org chart drove more of the downsizing than automation did.

Netflix $NFLX plans to shed about 1,000 people, around 6% of its global workforce, in its largest round of job losses since 2022. Product, tech, legal, and human-resources teams will carry the bulk of the reduction, according to reports. The streamer has struggled to raise customer engagement and broader growth, and the downsizing lands amid that struggle. Legal and human-resources staff work far from the screen, so the reductions reach past the engineers who build the service.

Disney $DIS started its retrenchment in April, when Josh D'Amaro announced 1,000 layoffs two months after becoming CEO. Marvel followed by releasing 8% of its employees. In his memo, D'Amaro described the cuts as part of a search for ways to streamline operations across parts of the company. He argued that the fast pace of change in Disney's industries forces it to keep reassessing how to build a nimbler workforce that leans more heavily on technology.

Disney's next move could reach thousands of jobs, according to November reports describing a plan to lower annual costs by 20%. The company has not confirmed the plan. People familiar with the matter say the savings could pair staff departures with other spending trims. If Disney carries out the plan, the April layoffs would mark the first stage of a broader contraction.

NPR offered voluntary buyouts to 300 newsroom employees after losing federal funding, yet it will accept 30 of them, one in 10 of those offered. The news organization plans targeted dismissals if volunteers fall short of the target. Its approach resembles the buyouts Microsoft $MSFT extended this year. How many staffers step forward will decide whether NPR moves to forced exits.

Vimeo parted with more than 120 people, about 25% of its city staff, in its third wave of exits since Bending Spoons acquired it. Bending Spoons also owns Airtable, so one parent has pared headcount at two separate tech brands this year. Three waves under the same owner show the shrinking did not stop once the purchase closed.

LinkedIn plans to drop about 875 roles, or 5% of its personnel, to reorganize teams and steer attention toward growing areas, an anonymous person told reporters. A source said the move was "not for artificial intelligence to replace jobs at LinkedIn."

None of the five employers here named AI as the main reason for shrinking, and LinkedIn's source ruled it out. The reasons on record at Netflix, Disney, NPR, and LinkedIn run to engagement and growth struggles, cost targets, lost public money, and team reorganizations. Across streaming and media, audience and funding pressures account for the losses more than automation does.

General Motors $GM is letting go of around 500 to 600 employees in information technology, with reports describing the goal as a way to "trim costs and clear the way to bring in staff with skills in other technology areas." The automaker's rationale pairs savings with a change in expertise. GM wants room on its payroll for people who know different technical fields. The cutback shrinks the current IT group while it opens seats for new hires, making the move a swap of skills as much as a cut in headcount.

Redwood Materials, a battery recycling company, laid off 10% of its employees, or 135 people, in April, a month before the GM news broke. The two figures imply a staff of about 1,350 before the cuts. Redwood's chief HR officer wrote in an email that the company acted "to sharpen our focus, our work and the size of our teams to support the direction Redwood is going in the future." The message names no new direction and sets no savings target. It puts its weight on team size and focus, casting the layoffs as a reset of priorities.

Lucid $LCID, an EV automaker, belonged to a June wave of job losses that reached 14,000 positions across companies such as game developer Bungie and trading platform Robinhood. Lucid tied its own downsizing to an effort to "boost profitability amid growing competition." The phrase points to pressure on earnings, a different motive from GM's skills swap or Redwood's tighter priorities. No count of Lucid's departures accompanies the report. Lucid's slice of the June total remains unknown.

Each explanation in this group turns on cost, profit, or team size, and none of the three mentions AI. The timing runs in sequence, with Redwood in April, GM in May, and Lucid in June. Vehicle and battery companies kept shedding staff across three straight months without citing the AI spending that pushed cuts at several other firms.

Samsung is eliminating 179 jobs as it moves its New Jersey headquarters to Texas later this year, and estimates put the number of affected workers at around 1,000. The gap between those two figures shows how an office move spreads beyond the people it puts out of work. Many more employees face disruption than face dismissal. The plan surfaced in July, as Samsung joined the companies that cut staff after Microsoft $MSFT's round that month.

Reuters put the New Jersey count at 739 roles affected in some way. A portion of those employees received relocation offers, and others lost their jobs. Another 100 roles disappeared in Texas, most of them in the mobile division. The destination office, in other words, shed people of its own. The move falls short of a clean transfer of headcount from one state to another. The three counts track different groups, and no single total ties them together.

Intel $INTC is shrinking its Data Center Group and has disclosed no tally of the positions involved. The company described the overhaul as a way to become more focused and efficient, and it said it remained committed to its product roadmap. The roadmap pledge signals that Intel intends to keep its product plans on course while the group gets smaller. Without a number, outsiders cannot gauge how deep the unit's cuts run.

The Wall Street Journal reported in April that GoPro, the wearable camera maker, will lay off 145 employees this year under a cost-cutting restructuring plan. The reductions continue through the end of the year, which spreads the job losses across months instead of a single day. Among the three firms, GoPro states the plainest motive. Its plan aims to lower expenses.

None of the three hardware entries links its staffing moves to AI. The reasons on record are a headquarters move, a leaner data center operation, and budget control. The pattern sets this corner of tech apart from the companies that trimmed payroll to make room for AI spending.

Nike $NKE is cutting about 1,400 roles in its global operations, and most of those positions sit in technology, according to Chief Operating Officer Venkatesh Alagirisamy.

Technology staff carry the larger share of this reduction at a consumer brand. Nike's appearance in a tracker of tech job losses shows the pullback spreading past companies whose business is software. Alagirisamy's account does not say how many of the roughly 1,400 positions fall outside technology. It does establish that tech jobs make up the majority.

T-Mobile $TMUS is reportedly shedding more IT roles after a January round of layoffs. No firm count has surfaced, and reports suggest the total could run into the hundreds. The size of this second round remains an open question. Its target is not. The newer reductions land on the same function Nike singled out.

Both companies aimed their cuts at technology work. Together, they suggest internal IT teams have become a target even at telecom and consumer firms, far from the software makers that fill most of this list.

#5515. Power outage takes down KEXP streaming for Seattle radio station’s worldwide audience

by Kurt Schlosser on Oct 30, 2026 at 10:23 amNovember 2, 2026 at 8:22 am

KEXP’s website and online streaming were down Friday morning after a power outage hit the Seattle radio station, though its over-the-air broadcast was back and running.

The outage started around midnight, and the station was on and off for a while before it was “knocked offline by a major power outage” between 2 and 3 a.m., said Dashel Schueler, KEXP’s director of marketing and communications. Schueler didn’t know the cause of the outage.

The station’s backup power system, known as an uninterruptible power supply (UPS), also failed.

“There’s no power to the server room infrastructure because the UPS that is supposed to protect all of that gear has failed,” Schueler said. Staff are trying to power critical devices to restore services while they wait for the UPS to be repaired or for a workaround that bypasses it.

There’s no estimate yet for when streaming will return.

Listeners in the Seattle area can tune in at 90.3 FM. The outage affects the KEXP.org stream and the station’s mobile app. KEXP estimates about 175,000 people stream its live broadcast each week, and another 85,000 listen to its shows on-demand.

The outage also took down 92.7 KREV, the station KEXP now owns in the San Francisco Bay Area, which relies on KEXP’s Seattle-based digital infrastructure. Because KEXP’s DJs pick songs live rather than playing a preset playlist, underwriting breaks vary in timing and length, Schueler said. DJs fire the separate Seattle and Bay Area spots manually and at the same time.

KREV was back by around 8:30 to 8:45 a.m., running on a barebones setup KEXP typically uses for remote broadcasts, Schueler said. Listeners may notice some issues while the station gets everything put back together.

Around 7:30 a.m., KEXP DJ John Richards read messages on air from listeners across Seattle who were happy to have the station back — terrestrially at least.

A few posts from listeners on X and Bluesky referenced the streaming outage.

Update: Late Friday afternoon KEXP said it was still working to restore services, but it did manage to put up a temporary livestream on its site.

Update: KEXP CEO Ethan Raup details what went wrong and how it was fixed in this post on LinkedIn.

#5513. Pump.fun Perps on Hyperliquid: How the 0.10% Builder Fee Works

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

On a $10,000 Bitcoin perpetual order placed through Pump.fun, Pump.fun can charge up to $10.

Hyperliquid, the exchange that actually matches and settles the trade, charges a standard taker $4.50. Only one of those fees has a written rule sending it toward a token burn, and it's Hyperliquid's.

Most launch coverage focused on whether to buy HYPE or SOL. The more useful question for PUMP holders is where each dollar of perps fees goes. When you compare Pump.fun's fee schedule, its buyback methodology and Hyperliquid's fee documentation, then, you'll see they don't connect the way many people assume.

Pump.fun didn't build a derivatives exchange. Its perps run on Hyperliquid's order books through builder codes, a feature that lets outside apps send user orders to Hyperliquid and add their own fee on top. Hyperliquid's engine handles matching, margin and liquidations.

The product first appeared in Pump.fun's API around October 9, when Wu Blockchain spotted a /coins/perps endpoint showing prices, funding rates, open interest and maximum leverage, all pulled from Hyperliquid's mainnet. The same endpoint also listed SOL, Nvidia, Tesla, gold and crude oil contracts. Trading launched around October 16 and 17, with up to 40x leverage on BTC and 25x on ETH reported at launch.

Pump.fun updated its terms and conditions on October 17. The perps feature is blocked for users in the United States and Ontario, along with sanctioned parties.

Pump.fun's official fee schedule splits the cost of a perp trade into separate parts.

Here's the math on a $10,000 market order at entry-tier rates, assuming Pump.fun charges its full maximum:

For a maker order, the gap is wider: $1.50 to Hyperliquid and up to $10 to Pump.fun. At full rate, the app routing the trade earns more per order than the exchange that runs it. Note that 0.10% is the published maximum, not a confirmed rate for every trade.

This side of the trade has the clearest documentation. Hyperliquid says its fees are "entirely directed to the community," meaning its HLP vault, the assistance fund and market deployers.

The assistance fund converts trading fees into HYPE automatically as part of the chain's execution.

According to Hyperliquid's documentation,

So every Pump.fun perp trade feeds part of Hyperliquid's own token-burn mechanism through standard protocol rules. That share never touches Pump.fun's treasury.

There's one more possible layer. Some of the markets in Pump.fun's API, such as stocks and commodities, are the kind of contracts that third-party HIP-3 deployers usually run on Hyperliquid. Those deployers can set their own fee share. If Pump.fun lists them, another party joins the split.

Under Hyperliquid's builder code rules, the builder fee goes to the builder's address on Hyperliquid. Builders claim it through the standard referral-reward process. The fee is charged in the collateral asset, so for these markets it builds up in USDC on Hyperliquid, not in SOL on Solana.

That matters once you check Pump.fun's PUMP buyback methodology. The program puts 50% of revenue toward buying and burning PUMP. It defines revenue as income from:

Perps builder fees and bridge fees aren't on that list. The page also says buybacks aren't a commitment to future purchases, except as "deterministically programmed prior to April 29, 2026." Perps launched in October, so they weren't covered by that commitment.

To be fair to Pump.fun, the absence of a rule isn't proof that the money stays out of buybacks. Pump.fun could add perps to its revenue definition at any time. But as of today, no published Pump.fun document links a perps fee to a PUMP burn. Any connection would also need USDC moved off Hyperliquid and converted, because the buyback table records purchases in SOL.

This also changes how to read the buyback numbers I've covered before. The PUMP page shows $490.65 million in cumulative buybacks on its dashboard and $465 million in Newsletter #14. It also says the fee dashboard has misreported revenue and buyback amounts since Custom Pairs launched and that this "will be fixed soon." If perps revenue grows, Pump.fun's total income and the share that actually reaches PUMP burns could move further apart.

Hyperliquid makes the builder side of this traceable. It publishes daily fill files for each builder at:

[https://stats-data.hyperliquid.xyz/Mainnet/builder_fills/](https://stats-data.hyperliquid.xyz/Mainnet/builder_fills/){builder_address}/{YYYYMMDD}.csv.lz4

The builder address must be entirely lowercase. A builder's total collected fees also appear in Hyperliquid's referral info query.

Without Pump.fun's builder address in its fee schedule, terms or announcements, nobody outside the company can add up the actual perps revenue, which is the number that would show whether this product is a side feature or a real revenue line. Once that address is public, the next step is to check whether a matching amount ever shows up in the PUMP buyback table.

Until then, the honest answer is this: Hyperliquid's share has a documented path to a HYPE burn, while Pump.fun's share has a documented path into Pump.fun's own wallet.

#5512. Canva, Block and Meta layoffs in 2026 came with different severance terms

Free daily briefing on global business news.

Tech layoff severance packages from Canva, Block and Meta show how far some employers go beyond base pay, from equity and laptops to extended healthcare

Sixteen weeks of base pay is a common reference point for severance at major tech companies. Outplacement figures from Challenger, Gray & Christmas and tracking by Simple Severance both put typical tech severance pay at around that level. Several layoffs in 2026 produced terms that differed from that baseline in the amount of pay, in what came with the pay, or in both.

A severance offer is rarely a single number. The packages in this list combine several parts: base pay, extra weeks tied to tenure, continued healthcare coverage, treatment of unvested equity, cash stipends or grants, company equipment and career support. Each employer assembled those parts differently.

Layoffs at Canva, Block $SQ and Meta $META in 2026 show that range. One company let departing staff keep their company-issued laptops. Another extended healthcare to employees' families. Block cut jobs twice in the same year, and the terms of its second round differed from the first.

Comparing tech layoff severance packages means looking past the headline count of weeks. Tenure formulas raise the total for long-serving staff. One company in this list adds two weeks for each continuous year of service, while Block adds one. Healthcare terms vary in length and in who is covered. Equity rules can decide whether a recent hire keeps shares or forfeits them. Some packages also include money aimed at what comes next, such as a transition stipend or a grant to start a venture.

The five entries that follow are a selection, not a ranking. Four describe individual layoff rounds: Canva in November, Block in February and November, and Meta in May. The fifth looks at the 16-week baseline and how the reported terms sit beside it. Each entry sets out the terms as reported. Where reporting on a round left out a detail, such as a headcount, the entry says so.

Reporting on these rounds does not say whether the base pay was delivered as a lump sum or as continued salary. The entries describe pay in weeks or months only, without assuming either method.

Canva promised every employee affected by its November 2026 layoffs at least six months of base pay, wherever in the world they worked. The cuts reached 22% of the company's workforce, which HR Brew puts at 1,271 employees.

The six-month figure is a floor, not a fixed amount. Each departing worker was promised no less than that much base pay.

Canva also changed how it treated equity for its newest employees. Vesting is the process by which granted stock becomes the employee's to keep. Many tech stock grants vest on a schedule that starts with a cliff. Under a one-year cliff, an employee earns no shares at all until the first anniversary of their start date. After that date, the remaining shares usually vest in smaller portions over the rest of the schedule. Someone laid off before reaching the cliff would normally walk away with nothing from the grant.

Canva removed that one-year vesting cliff for affected employees. Recent hires who had not yet reached their first anniversary keep their shares instead of forfeiting them.

The package extended to hardware. Departing employees could keep their company-issued MacBooks rather than return them.

Canva also put money toward what departing staff do next. It offered $10,000 grants to employees starting either a business or a community venture.

Healthcare was part of the offer. Canva provided one year of coverage "where applicable," a qualifier the reporting does not define further.

Job-search support rounded out the package. Affected workers received 12 months of LinkedIn Premium, along with career coaching and help with their résumés. LinkedIn Premium is the paid subscription tier of the professional networking site. It adds tools such as direct messages to members outside a user's network.

Canva announced other changes alongside the cuts. The company said Sydney would become the main base for more of its product teams. It also said some employees would be asked to move to centralized hubs.

Block $SQ's February 2026 layoffs came with 20 weeks of salary for departing employees, plus one additional week for every year of tenure. The package also included six months of healthcare coverage and a $5,000 transition stipend.

The salary portion has two parts. The 20 weeks act as a floor that applied to departing staff whatever their length of service.

The tenure component sits on top of that floor. Each year at Block added one more week of salary. A longer-serving employee therefore left with more weeks of pay than a recent hire.

Healthcare coverage ran for six months as part of the package. Reporting on the round does not say whether that coverage extended to employees' families. It also does not name the program or mechanism used to provide it.

The $5,000 transition stipend is a separate element. It was reported as a single cash amount, not as a figure calculated from salary or tenure.

Reporting on this round covers three elements: pay, healthcare and the stipend. It does not describe how unvested equity was treated. It also does not say whether staff kept company equipment or received career coaching or similar support. That limits any comparison of this severance package with others to the three elements that were reported.

Reporting on this round gives no headcount and no share of Block's workforce.

Block $SQ's November 2026 layoff package started at seven weeks of base pay. Affected employees also received one more week of pay for each year they had worked at Block.

The package had a fixed starting amount and a variable one. Every departing employee began from the same seven weeks. The tenure weeks then added to that figure. A worker with longer service at Block received more than a recent hire.

Block also gave departing staff a 30-day pay-without-working period. During that window, employees remained on pay without being expected to do their jobs. With the 30 days added, the November package had three separate pay elements: the seven-week base, the tenure weeks and the 30-day period.

Reporting on the round does not give a combined total that reconciles with these parts. This entry lists each element separately for that reason.

Healthcare for the November round ran through COBRA. COBRA is a U.S. federal law that allows eligible workers to keep their employer's group health coverage for a limited time after leaving a job. The reported terms name COBRA but do not say how long coverage lasted under Block's package. They also do not say whether Block paid any part of the premiums. That gap matters for departing staff. COBRA premiums are generally paid by the former employee unless an employer agrees to cover part of them.

The November terms differ from those of Block's February 2026 round. February's package started at 20 weeks of salary. November's started at seven weeks of base pay. Both rounds added one week for each year of service. With a smaller starting amount, the tenure weeks made up a larger part of a long-serving employee's package in November than in February.

The reported November terms do not mention a transition stipend.

No headcount or share of the workforce has been reported for Block's November cuts.

Meta $META's May 2026 layoff round affected roughly 10% of its workforce. Departing employees received 16 weeks of base pay, plus two additional weeks for each continuous year of service.

Reporting on the round gives the cut only as a share of staff. It does not say how many people lost their jobs.

The 16-week base equals four months of pay before any tenure is counted. Every employee in the round started from that same floor. The tenure weeks then build on it for each continuous year an employee spent at the company.

The formula ties those extra weeks to continuous service. That makes the length of an unbroken stretch at Meta the deciding factor in the final payment. A longer uninterrupted run brings more weeks of pay. A shorter one brings fewer. Reporting on the round does not explain how Meta treated a break in service.

Healthcare continuation came alongside the pay. Meta continued health coverage for 18 months. That coverage reached employees' families as well as the employees themselves.

HR Brew reports that the 18-month term tripled the healthcare coverage Meta offered in previous layoff cycles. The publication does not give the length of that earlier coverage.

The 18-month period runs longer than the stated healthcare terms in two other 2026 packages. Canva offered one year of coverage where applicable. Block $SQ's February round included six months. Block's November round named COBRA but gave no duration. Its length cannot be set beside Meta's.

Severance at major tech companies has typically landed around a 16-week baseline, according to outplacement figures from Challenger, Gray & Christmas and tracking by Simple Severance. HR Brew draws on both sources to set recent packages against that common reference point. It does not name a specific report or date from either source.

A baseline describes what is typical, not what is required. Each employer still sets its own formula for base pay, tenure credit and benefits. That makes the 16-week mark a yardstick for reading individual offers.

Against that yardstick, HR Brew treats three parts of Canva's November 2026 package as outliers. The first is the floor of at least six months of base pay for every affected employee worldwide. The others are the decision to let staff keep their company-issued MacBooks and the $10,000 grants for startup or community ventures.

Block $SQ's February 2026 round started above the benchmark. It paid 20 weeks of salary before any tenure credit. It then added one week for each year an employee had worked at the company.

Meta $META's May 2026 round started at the benchmark itself. Its formula paid 16 weeks of base pay. It then added two weeks for each continuous year of service. That formula lifts the total above the 16-week mark for anyone with at least one continuous year.

Block's November 2026 round set its base pay starting point below the benchmark. That package opened with seven weeks of base pay plus one week per year of tenure. It also included a separate 30-day pay-without-working period.

Weeks of pay are only one part of a layoff severance package. Comparing offers on that measure alone leaves out other terms. Healthcare terms vary by company. Meta continued coverage for 18 months for employees and their families. Block's February round gave six months of healthcare, and its November round named COBRA without a stated duration. Canva offered one year of coverage "where applicable." Block's February round also added a $5,000 transition stipend.

#5511. Metal fabricator NIC Global to cut 103 jobs near Seattle, move production to Eastern Washington

by Lisa Stiffler on Oct 30, 2026 at 10:24 amOctober 30, 2026 at 10:25 am

Metal fabricator NIC Global plans to close its Woodinville, Wash., plant, eliminating 103 jobs. Declining business from local customers is prompting the company to shift production primarily to Eastern Washington to meet data center-related growth.

The layoffs are scheduled to begin Jan. 18, 2027, with final departures Aug. 31, 2028, according to a notice filed with the Washington Employment Security Department. Affected jobs include assembly, engineering, quality assurance, metal fabrication specialists, and forklift positions.

The building will be returned to its landlord when the lease ends in September 2028.

“This is a sad day for our company. Woodinville is where NIC was formed — three Seattle-area sheet-metal shops brought together under one roof in 2001 — and the people in that building built the foundation of everything NIC is today,” Troy Wood, company president and CEO, said via email.

The 100,000-square-foot site mostly served energy and medical device customers. Wood said the volume of work at the plant has declined while demand has increased in Eastern Washington for customers building power distribution technology needed by data centers.

“NIC is a supplier of sheet-metal fabrications and assemblies, and in our business, being close to our customers is what keeps us competitive,” Wood said.

While most of the work from Woodinville will go to Spokane, and a smaller portion will go to NIC’s Gallatin, Tenn., facility. The company also has manufacturing in Pullman; Chillicothe, Ohio; and Denton, Texas. The work outside of Washington is focused on the heavy truck sector. The company’s headcount is nearly 600.

Laid-off workers will be encouraged to apply for openings at other plants.

There are smaller fabricators remaining in the Seattle area, including JEMCO Components & Fabrications, which provides precision machining and sheet-metal fabrication for customers in medical, aerospace and defense sectors, and QUAL-FAB serving medical and dental customers.

NIC’s legal and financial headquarters will stay in the Woodinville area, where the company plans a new office for its finance, IT, sales and West Coast support teams.

Wood praised the quality and reliability of the Woodinville employees’ work.

“I am grateful to every one of them,” he said, “and especially to those who chose to stay with us through two and a half years of uncertainty and kept doing their jobs with integrity.”
