#5510. 25% to 10%: how 18 tech companies cut their 2026 workforces

Free daily briefing on global business news.

Groupon, Canva, Oracle, Meta, and 14 more: a selection of 2026 tech layoffs sorted by the share of staff each company cut.

Picture opening an early-morning email and reading that today is your last working day. Tech workers across the industry have absorbed news like that throughout 2026 as companies reorganize to keep up with the swelling capabilities of artificial intelligence. Chief executives write memos about flatter structures, fewer management layers, and freeing cash for AI investment. Each of those decisions lands on people who depend on a paycheck to cover their bills. Nothing in the record suggests the wave has crested, and more reductions look likely before the year ends.

TrueUp finds that this year's job cuts appear to be arriving faster than last year's. Its count tops 200,000 tech layoffs so far in 2026, within reach of the more than 245,000 it tallied across all of 2025. Many reports place the U.S. at the center of the losses. Workers have started to push back. More than 4,500 Google $GOOGL employees signed a petition demanding buyouts before any mandatory layoffs, along with guaranteed severance. State government has taken notice too. In June, California Gov. Gavin Newsom unveiled a tool to track how AI affects the workforce and said the state was preparing for AI's advance through governance and fresh policy. Layoffs on this scale have turned private staffing decisions into a public concern.

Yahoo Tech keeps a running tracker of 2026 tech layoffs that moves month by month from March through November, with its latest update on Nov. 4. Its entries draw on news reports, company statements, and filings, and they cover far more companies than this list includes. The tracker itself does not sort companies by the share of staff they cut. This list pulls 18 entries that state a company-wide percentage and orders them from highest to lowest, giving the edge to the larger stated headcount when two companies post the same figure. Several of those percentages carry hedges such as "about" or "roughly," and some describe plans that will unfold over months or years. A share of workforce measures how far a cut reaches into a company, something a raw job count can obscure. A small firm and a global giant can report the same percentage while shedding headcounts that differ by thousands.

Groupon announced plans in May to eliminate roughly 25% of its workforce, about 400 jobs, the deepest proportional cut in this selection of 2026 layoffs. The company expects most of those positions to disappear by the end of the third quarter, based on a Securities and Exchange Commission filing, according to the Tribune. The schedule spreads the exits over several months instead of a single day of departures. Anyone staying through that window would work beside colleagues whose positions were about to vanish.

Financial filings put Groupon's worldwide headcount at 1,734 at the end of 2025, according to the Tribune. Measured against that base, the planned exits come to about 23% of staff, or nearly one in four employees. Many employers on the tracker have disclosed larger headcount losses, yet few have proposed removing so large a slice of their own payroll. The company has been shrinking for years. Earlier rounds of downsizing took it from more than 11,000 employees to fewer than 2,000 over the past decade, the Tribune reports. Cutting this deep into an already slimmed-down company reshapes the whole organization, unlike trims confined to one division or a thin layer of management.

Groupon tied the restructuring to one goal, rebuilding the business as an AI-native company. Its stated aim names AI as the destination, a direct connection that several other firms in the tracker sidestepped. Money figures in the plan as well. The Tribune reports that Groupon projects annualized savings of about $25 million and intends to put as much as half of this year's projected savings into AI infrastructure. The company also argued that the margins of scaling local commerce cannot support a "human-bandwidth solution." Read together, those statements make the layoffs both a cost cut and a funding source for the AI buildout Groupon now treats as its growth engine. The word "rebuild" signals an intent to remake Groupon from its foundations.

Canva is eliminating 22% of its staff, a reduction of just over 1,200 employees at the design software company. A cut of that size implies a starting headcount of roughly 5,500. The November announcement makes Canva one of the most recent names in a year crowded with tech job losses. A reduction this deep forces a company to decide which work continues and which stops, and Canva has signaled its answer through how it is reshaping those who remain.

Canva is folding its product, growth, and platform teams into one another as part of the same restructuring, according to reports. The merger redraws the company's internal map while Canva trims payroll. Three teams that once operated as separate units will run as a combined organization. Pairing that consolidation with the layoffs means employees confront new team boundaries and a thinner bench at the same moment.

Canva also aims to pare back "subspecialisation," the same coverage indicates. Fewer narrow specialties could hand those who stay a heavier load of responsibilities. Each worker left may cover ground that a bigger, more specialized roster once divided. The shift favors breadth over depth, so someone who once owned a single niche may end up juggling several.

No AI rationale surfaces in the descriptions of Canva's downsizing, which sets it apart from several 2026 entries that pin the exits on artificial intelligence or on rising AI spending. Canva's example shows that one of the steepest proportional downsizings in this selection came with no AI explanation attached. The changes described so far concern how Canva arranges the work itself. Combined divisions and broader roles point to a company that expects to run leaner, relying on generalists after this round. The accounts leave open which roles Canva will keep, but the direction tilts toward wider job descriptions spread across fewer hands.

ClickUp eliminated 22% of its workforce in May 2026 as the company turned toward AI to raise productivity. CEO Zeb Evans announced the layoffs himself, in a post on X $TWTR.

Evans denied that savings drove the decision. He said the layoff "wasn't about cutting costs," and he described the money it frees as flowing "directly back into the people who stay." His account treats the job losses as a reallocation, with payroll leaving one group of employees and landing with another. Read that way, ClickUp's total spending on people need not fall at all. The same dollars change hands.

Million-dollar salary bands give the remaining staff a concrete target. ClickUp introduced the bands for employees who "create outsized impact using AI," a standard that ties the company's highest pay to a single kind of contribution. Workers who stay now have a stated reason to measure their output against what AI lets them accomplish. The structure turns skill with AI tools from a useful asset into the clearest path toward the top of ClickUp's pay scale. It signals to job seekers what the company prizes before they apply.

Evans' reported remarks center on the people who remain and put no number on the departures. The 22% share stands as the sole gauge of how deep the reduction reached. More than one in five positions disappeared. Without a headcount, outsiders cannot tell how many people lost their jobs or how large a pool of money now flows toward the workers left behind. The gap leaves Evans' reinvestment pledge without a figure anyone can check against later results.

The disavowal of cost motives and the new compensation tier point to a company betting that a smaller staff, rewarded for what each person achieves with AI, can deliver more than the larger one it replaced.

PayPal $PYPL intends to eliminate around 20% of its staff, or nearly 4,800 employees, under a plan the Wall Street Journal reported in May. The reductions will roll out over the next few years. PayPal is the only company in this selection whose reported timeline stretches that far, a schedule that treats downsizing as a long project.

CEO Enrique Lores laid out the strategy for investors in two steps. The first strips duplication and extra layers from PayPal's organizational structure. The second speeds up the adoption of AI and automation across the company's operations.

Lores' ordering puts the cleanup ahead of the technology push. Several companies in this selection name AI as the main force behind their layoffs. PayPal's chief executive began with redundant roles and stacked hierarchy and turned to automation in his second step. His remarks cast AI as a tool to apply after the company sheds its excess management.

The multiyear horizon turns the 4,800 figure into a target. No milestones accompany it. Nothing in the reporting reveals how many positions disappear in any given year or which divisions absorb the first rounds.

Among the four companies in this selection trimming about one-fifth of their workforce, PayPal's number dwarfs the rest. Wix, Monday.com, and Patreon account for fewer than 1,800 roles combined, and PayPal's total runs nearly triple that sum. A cut of nearly 4,800 at around 20% implies a payroll of roughly 24,000 people, the largest base in that group.

Oracle $ORCL and Meta $META are the lone companies in this selection with larger job totals, and both are shedding a smaller slice of their staff. Oracle has carried out its cuts and Meta has begun its round, while PayPal's exits lie ahead. PayPal pairs a roughly 20% share with the third-largest headcount here, a match no other company in the selection can claim.

Wix, the website builder, is cutting around 20% of its staff, a reduction expected to touch roughly 1,000 roles. The 1,000 figure is an estimate based on the company's headcount. Working backward from those two numbers puts Wix's workforce near 5,000 people. The plan surfaced in May 2026, a month that also brought layoffs at Groupon, ClickUp, Intuit $INTU, Meta $META, PayPal $PYPL, and Coinbase.

Avishai Abrahami, Wix's chief executive, laid out the goal in a post on X $TWTR and boiled it down to three adjectives: "we need to become a faster, leaner, and flatter organization." Each word aims at a different target. Speed governs the pace of work, leanness governs size, and flatness points to fewer management tiers between employees and leadership. The job losses themselves deliver leanness, and the push for flatness suggests management layers will thin as well.

Wix also blames part of the decision on a force outside its software business. The company, based in Israel, points to the exchange rate between the Israeli shekel and the U.S. dollar. No other company among the 18 in this list names currency as a reason to downsize. The other companies' explanations range across AI, team structure, profitability, and market conditions.

Webflow, another company that builds and hosts websites, let people go in May in a round of unclear size. A developer told the San Francisco Chronicle the round outstripped Webflow's last major one, a 2024 reduction that affected 8% of its staff. One worker called the cuts "a bloodbath" in comments to the same paper. The tracker points to a shift toward AI as the likely cause. Webflow CEO Linda Tong argued that AI is redrawing the rules for how marketing teams build, test, and refine digital experiences. She added that "the companies that move decisively through moments like this are the ones that come out ahead."

Two website builders moved to shed staff in the same month, a pattern that hints at strain across the category. Wix carries a burden Webflow's chief did not cite, a home currency working against it.

Monday.com is laying off 20% of its workforce, about 630 people, as it pushes to turn its AI platform into a core offering. The two figures put the company's headcount before the July cuts near 3,150, with roughly 2,520 employees staying on. The reduction extends a product bet Monday.com placed several months earlier.

Monday.com built its main product earlier in 2026 around the belief that a growing number of business customers want their employees working alongside AI agents. The July round carries that belief past the software and into the organization that builds it. A company that sells agent-assisted work to clients will operate with a staff one-fifth smaller once the layoffs take effect.

Company leaders sounded confident about AI competition roughly five months before the job cuts. CNBC reported in February that co-CEO and co-founder Eran Zinman said Monday.com had felt no effect from AI companies. Zinman added that the company had reoriented its marketing and advertising around AI. On an earnings call, management told analysts that Monday.com held a strong market position. Executives cited new AI features, among them agents and a vibe feature, built to raise conversion and engagement.

Monday.com's 20% matches the share at PayPal $PYPL, Wix, and Patreon, yet its pace diverges from PayPal's. PayPal plans to spread nearly 4,800 job cuts across the next few years, per the Wall Street Journal. Monday.com's July layoffs come with no comparable multiyear timeline. In raw numbers, PayPal's plan reaches more than seven times as many jobs as Monday.com's. Wix's estimated 1,000 roles and Patreon's 93 jobs fall on either side of Monday.com's total.

By midyear, the AI push had reached Monday.com's marketing, its flagship software, and its payroll. Whatever pressure AI companies did or did not apply, Monday.com has chosen to compete on their ground, staking both its software and its staffing on AI.

Patreon cut 20% of its workforce in July, eliminating 93 jobs as it reworked what the company called "our organizational structure and how we work." Ninety-three positions at that share imply a staff of roughly 465 before the cuts. No other company in this selection that disclosed both a share and a headcount comes out smaller. Patreon shares the 20% tier with three far larger employers on this list, yet its job count amounts to a sliver of theirs. A layoff of fewer than 100 people still removed one worker in five at a company of that size.

Patreon's email announcing the cuts rejected AI as the motive, stating that "we are not making the above changes because we believe AI replaces humans." The same message conceded ground with a second line: "AI has fundamentally transformed the tech industry, though, including how we work." Side by side, the two statements deny that AI can stand in for people while admitting it has changed how the company functions day to day.

Jack Conte laid out the practical shape of the overhaul. He described a flatter hierarchy, with teams refocused on the company's top priorities. Conte also wrote that AI has altered how Patreon builds products and communicates, and that this change bears on how the business operates and arranges itself.

The disclaimer and the concession clash on the surface alone. Patreon rejected the notion that software could take over the work its people did. It named AI as a force behind the way it works, and Conte's account links that force to the company's internal design. The leaner hierarchy he described leaves surviving teams with fewer managerial layers above them and a narrower set of goals in front of them.

Patreon's explanation keeps AI in the background and the reshaped hierarchy in the foreground. The record suggests the technology changed how Patreon works first, and the 93 exits followed from the slimmer structure that emerged.

Squarespace is cutting 19% of its workforce, about 300 people, in a November move that the website-building company frames as a reset of how it operates.

Jeff Seedman, a Squarespace representative, told TechCrunch the changes aim to simplify the company's operations, sharpen its priorities, and let it move faster. He presented the overhaul as a way to ready Squarespace for the next stage of its growth. His explanation emphasizes speed and focus. It specifies no teams, offices, or product lines, and it never refers to AI.

AI-driven "vibe-coding" site builders have shaken Squarespace's industry as they gain popularity, according to the tracker. Seedman offered no such link himself. The connection between that new competition and the job cuts reflects the tracker's view of the market, and no company statement confirms it.

Webflow, a rival that builds and hosts websites, ran its own layoff round in May without disclosing the size. A developer told the San Francisco Chronicle the round outstripped Webflow's last major reduction, which hit 8% of its staff in 2024. An employee called the cuts "a bloodbath" in comments to the paper. The tracker identifies a shift toward AI as the apparent cause.

Webflow CEO Linda Tong argued that AI is rewriting how marketing teams build, test, and refine digital experiences. She added that companies that seize such moments come out ahead. Her framing puts AI at the center, a contrast with Squarespace's statement, which leaves the technology unmentioned.

Squarespace's 19% cutback runs more than twice as deep as Webflow's 2024 cut. Six months separate the Webflow round from Squarespace's November announcement. Across that stretch, two companies selling tools for building websites both shrank, yet only Webflow's chief executive pointed to AI as a force reshaping the work. In this record, Squarespace's silence on AI leaves the tracker's market reading as the only link between its cuts and AI-powered rivals.

Lucid $LCID, the electric vehicle maker, is cutting about 18% of its workforce in a June round that extends to the assembly line. Full-time employees, contract workers, and hourly manufacturing staff all fall within its scope. Including contract workers carries the impact past Lucid's own employees. Lucid is the lone automaker among the companies on this list, so its reduction affects people who build cars as well as those who work at desks.

Lucid's production side absorbs a concrete share of the loss. IBTimes UK reports that the company eliminated the second production shift at its Casa Grande, Arizona, factory. Dropping a shift removes a whole rotation of plant labor, which matches the hourly roles the layoffs include. An operation that runs one shift in place of two has less room to raise output if demand climbs.

Chief Operating Officer Marc Winterhoff is leaving the company alongside the layoffs. His departure takes away the executive whose title covers operations at the moment the company pares its factory staff. Leadership turnover and a shrinking payroll converge on the same part of the business.

Lucid ties the layoffs to money and markets, saying they aim to "boost profitability amid growing competition." The explanation centers on earnings and rivals and leaves AI out. Groupon, Monday.com, Intuit $INTU, and other companies on this list linked their job losses to AI, which sets the carmaker's rationale apart. Lucid's case shows that a company can arrive at a cut this steep through competitive and financial pressure, with technology absent from its stated motives.

Lucid's round landed in a June that brought 14,000 job cuts across companies such as game developer Bungie and trading platform Robinhood. A vanished shift and a departing COO point to a carmaker surrendering capacity and labor costs to secure the gains its statement seeks.

Intuit $INTU plans to lay off 3,000 employees, about 17% of its workforce, Reuters reported in May. No later report confirms the cuts as complete, and the figure still describes an intention.

CEO Sasan Goodarzi told employees in a memo that the layoffs would help the company focus on infusing AI across its services. His explanation links the job losses to the products Intuit offers its customers, with AI woven through them. The reduction becomes a way to redirect the company toward that goal.

Read together, the headcount and the percentage imply a company of roughly 18,000 employees before the reduction. A cut at this depth would remove about one in every six jobs at Intuit.

Intuit's planned total outstrips the raw job counts at several companies that sit higher in this list. Groupon, Wix, Monday.com, and Squarespace each post a steeper share while shedding fewer people. Groupon and Monday.com also framed their layoffs around AI, yet their combined 1,030 jobs amount to about a third of Intuit's plan.

The tracker's entry names no teams, offices, or regions, and it gives no completion date. Employees in every Intuit division face the same uncertainty until the company specifies where the cuts will land. Goodarzi's memo points to the destination, AI across Intuit's services, but leaves open which jobs the company will trade to get there.

Snap $SNAP is eliminating 1,000 workers, or 16% of its staff, according to Variety, and the company presents the smaller workforce as a bet on compact teams equipped with AI. The April 2026 announcement removes roughly one in six positions at Snap.

Investor pressure shaped the timing. Snap announced the layoffs weeks after Irenic Capital Management called on the company to make changes that would lift its performance and revenue. The short gap between Irenic's request and Snap's decision places the job losses inside a larger argument over how the company should improve its results. An outside shareholder's demand and an internal technology strategy point in the same direction, toward fewer people producing more.

CEO Evan Spiegel grounded his case in what he had observed inside Snap. "We have already witnessed small squads leveraging AI tools to drive meaningful progress across several important initiatives," he said. His remark treats existing teams as proof that the approach works. In his telling, the gains came before the cuts, which recasts the downsizing as an expansion of a method he believes Snap has tested. The quote names none of those initiatives and offers no measure of the progress. Outsiders have only his word for how much the squads achieved.

Snap is using AI to streamline its operations and to support the employees who remain. The math reveals the load they carry. A 1,000-person reduction equal to 16% implies a pre-layoff headcount near 6,250, leaving roughly 5,250 employees to absorb the duties of departed colleagues.

Snap's leadership is wagering that a staff that lean, armed with AI tools, can deliver the turnaround Irenic Capital sought. The bet ties an investor's financial demand to an AI thesis Snap has never proven at its new size. Snap controls its payroll. It cannot dictate revenue, which hinges on whether Spiegel's squads keep up the pace he described.

Rackspace cut 750 workers in June, around 15% of its staff, as the cloud computing services company turned its attention toward AI. Read together, the headcount and the percentage imply a workforce of roughly 5,000 before the layoffs. About one in seven employees lost a job.

Rackspace's filing names a strategic decision to give less weight to some older service delivery operations as the chief driver of the restructuring. Most of those operations belong to its Public Cloud unit. The filing describes steering the freed resources into building out the company's enterprise AI offerings.

The company frames the layoffs as a decision about where to spend. Rackspace chose which work to downgrade and which to grow, and the restructuring centers on older public cloud delivery. The jobs it eliminated and the products it wants to build sit in different corners of the business. Staff whose roles supported legacy operations carry the cost of a bet on a newer line of work.

Roughly 4,250 employees remain to carry out the shift. Rackspace now relies on a smaller workforce to keep the operations it retained running while it builds an enterprise AI business that its own filing presents as unfinished.

The cryptocurrency platform Coinbase is laying off 700 employees in a May round that removes around 14% of its staff. A reduction of 700 at that proportion implies a pre-layoff headcount of roughly 5,000. About one worker in seven is leaving the company.

CEO Brian Armstrong pinned the decision on two forces, the current market and AI changing the way Coinbase works. His account pairs an outside pressure with an internal one. Market conditions sit beyond the reach of any single firm. A shift in how work gets done reflects a choice about the shape Armstrong wants his organization to take.

The dual explanation separates the crypto firm from employers in this selection that tied their layoffs to AI alone. Armstrong did not present AI as the sole driver. By naming external conditions alongside it, he linked Coinbase's payroll to forces the company cannot steer. His framing leaves room for two readings: some lost roles track how the market behaves, and others disappear because the work itself has changed. Armstrong's public statement does not say how many positions each force claims.

Robinhood, another trading platform, said through its communications account on X $TWTR in June that it planned to let go of 10% of its workers, around 290 jobs. Whether AI shaped that move remains unclear. CEO Vlad Tenev said the company would be "utilizing frontier technologies to push our execution even further." His language points toward technology without any reference to external pressure. Two companies in adjacent corners of finance reached for different vocabulary to explain shrinking payrolls.

Coinbase's cut runs 4 percentage points deeper than Robinhood's and reaches more than twice as many people. Armstrong also offered the fuller public rationale. Of the two, the company asking more of its workforce is the one that named more reasons for doing so.

Oracle $ORCL eliminated 21,000 jobs over the past year, roughly 13% of its workforce, according to the filing it submitted June 23. The tracker credits Oracle with the heaviest layoff impact of 2026 so far. The filing's one-year window reaches back into 2025, so the figure does not line up with the calendar year. Even so, the headcount sits in a different category from most companies here, several of which shed a few hundred people or fewer.

Artificial intelligence appears in the document as a cause. Oracle wrote that adopting and deploying AI across its operations has already led to reductions in its workforce and may keep doing so. The second half of that admission carries the warning. By putting that possibility on the record, the company signaled that 21,000 might not be the final tally.

Spending on AI infrastructure drove the downsizing, according to reports that describe the goal as stopping a cash drain from Oracle's buildout. The company has reportedly sought to offset the money flowing into AI chips and data centers. In that trade-off, payroll gave way to hardware.

The purge began in March, when early projections put the coming cuts in the thousands without settling on a total. On the last day of the month, more than a dozen employees announced on LinkedIn that they had lost their jobs, according to Business Insider. The notices those workers received pointed to Oracle's current business needs and told them, "we have made the decision to eliminate your role as part of a broader organizational change." The wording framed each departure as one piece of a larger reorganization.

Another round followed in September, and its size remains unknown. Employees reportedly received early-morning emails on Monday, Sept. 14, telling them the day was their last on the job. The September round arrived less than three months after the June filing raised the prospect of further reductions. Oracle's cuts now run past the 21,000 it disclosed, by a margin no one outside the company has counted.

Etsy laid off about 220 people, or 12% of its workforce, in August to simplify its organizational structure. Most of the losses fell on product and engineering teams. Staff in those groups design and build the company's technology, and the layoffs struck that technical core harder than any other part of Etsy.

CEO Kruti Patel Goyal called the layoffs necessary to build "the organization we believe Etsy needs for the future." Her rationale looks ahead and treats the move as a redesign of how Etsy arranges its people. The reported reasoning names no revenue shortfall, cost target, or investor demand. The overhaul itself serves as the stated motive. Several other tech employers tied their 2026 reductions to freeing money for AI, among them Meta $META and Atlassian $TEAM.

An Etsy spokesperson told CNBC that AI adoption did not drive the cuts. A handful of other companies have issued similar denials this year. Epic Games said its March dismissal of more than 1,000 people had no connection to AI. LinkedIn's plan to let go around 875 employees drew a comparable disclaimer from one source, who said the decision was "not for artificial intelligence to replace jobs at LinkedIn." Etsy's denial carries the company's own voice, which gives it more weight than a single source's account.

Dropbox's October layoff of roughly 200 workers, about 9% of its staff, targeted many of the same functions, with engineering, product, design, and general and administrative teams bearing the bulk. Etsy removed a similar number of people at a higher share, a sign that Etsy started from a smaller headcount. Dropbox co-CEO Ashraf Alkarmi tied his company's layoffs to choices about where to invest and how to organize, a rationale close to Goyal's focus on structure. Engineers and product staff carried the heaviest load at both companies. Etsy's case shows that a double-digit cut to those ranks can proceed while the company itself rejects AI as the cause.

Meta $META began cutting 10% of its workforce in May, around 8,000 employees, and plans to close 6,000 open roles on top of those exits. The company tied the reduction to one goal: freeing more room for AI spending. Eliminating vacancies trims tomorrow's payroll in the same way dismissals shrink today's. Combined, the two moves would remove roughly 14,000 positions from Meta's staffing plans, counting openings never filled alongside people already on the job.

A far smaller March round came first. Meta started letting go of about 700 people on March 25, The New York Times reported, and the losses landed on Reality Labs, social media, and recruiting teams. The May layoffs reached more than 11 times that headcount. Shedding recruiters in March and scrapping thousands of openings two months later point the same way, toward a company that intends to hire less.

Reality Labs, the unit that runs Horizon Worlds for the Quest VR headset, absorbed part of the March blow as Meta steps back from building the metaverse. Thinning that division signals a company redirecting its people away from virtual worlds. The same wave reached social media teams too, which carried the reductions beyond the metaverse effort.

A Reuters report in March raised the prospect of a much deeper reduction, suggesting Meta could cut 20% of its staff because of rising AI investment. The March round fell well short of that estimate. The May layoffs reached half of it. Even at the lower share, Meta's stated reason for the spring cuts, making space for AI outlays, matched the motive the news service had described in March. The Reuters report overshot on scale but identified the same cause.

Between March and May, Meta moved staff away from its metaverse projects and toward AI, and closed vacancies would make up more than 40% of the positions it is removing from its books.

Uber $UBER announced in September that it would eliminate 3,300 jobs, about 10% of its workforce, in a restructuring built around the distance between rank-and-file staff and the top of the company. CEO Dara Khosrowshahi cast the overhaul as an effort to strip out management tiers and steer resources toward growth. "We are removing layers, simplifying team structures, refining our global location strategy, and focusing our people and investments against the biggest opportunities ahead of us," he said.

Uber pinned numeric targets to the reorganization. The company said it would shrink the number of employees who sit seven or more levels below the CEO by 20%. It intends to cut its count of micro-teams by almost 50%. The two goals measure the plan by organizational depth and fragmentation, and the job losses serve those aims.

The cuts reach managers and regular employees alike. Each management tier adds a rung between the CEO and the people doing the work. Sparing supervisors would leave the ladder as tall as before. By including both groups, Uber matched its layoffs to its stated goal of a flatter chain of command.

Khosrowshahi's memo left AI off its list of reasons, which sets Uber apart from several companies in this selection that blamed rising AI spending for their cuts. The memo instead invoked "the autonomous future" as the horizon Uber is working toward.

Uber's July round, a narrower cut, carried a different message. Bloomberg reported that month that Uber laid off 10% of its customer service division as it sought to "embrace artificial intelligence" and streamline its staffing. In May, the company had said it would slow hiring as it leaned more on AI inside its own operations. The two rounds point to a split in how Uber explains its cuts. Bloomberg's account tied the support-staff trims to AI, while the September memo grounds the companywide reset in management depth.

Atlassian $TEAM let go of roughly 1,600 employees on March 16, around 10% of its workers, and CEO Mike Cannon-Brookes presented the move as a way to bankroll the company's next bets. He said the reductions would "self-fund further investment in AI and enterprise sales, while strengthening our financial profile."

Cannon-Brookes's wording ties each eliminated job to spending that comes after it. He named two destinations for the freed money, AI and enterprise sales, and attached no dollar figure to either. His reference to the company's financial profile adds a third aim. Atlassian wanted the savings to firm up its books as well as pay for new work.

Cannon-Brookes made no attempt to separate the layoffs from money. His statement names savings, new investment, and the balance sheet in a single line, a plain admission that cost discipline drove the decision alongside strategy. Other chief executives in this selection have distanced their job losses from budget pressure, but Atlassian's leader built his explanation on it.

A new internal blueprint accompanied the layoffs. Cannon-Brookes said Atlassian is "changing the way we work and reorganising around our System of Work to move faster." His remark pairs a structural overhaul with a push for speed. The headcount cut arrived bundled with a redesign of how the remaining teams operate. Fewer people have to deliver faster results inside a reworked system, which raises the stakes for every employee who stayed.

Atlassian moved early in the year. Its mid-March round landed about two months ahead of the May wave that brought cuts at seven other companies on this list, from Groupon and ClickUp to Meta $META and PayPal $PYPL. Atlassian also matched the share of staff cut at Meta and Uber $UBER while losing fewer people than either. Under the self-funding approach, Atlassian's AI budget grows out of its payroll savings. Its technology push and its headcount move in opposite directions.

#5509. Filing: Chip startup Powerlattice raises $86M to ease AI’s power crunch

Chronicling the Seattle and Pacific Northwest startup scene. SEE MORE

by Kurt Schlosser on Oct 30, 2026 at 11:30 amOctober 30, 2026 at 3:35 pm

Powerlattice, a Vancouver, Wash.-based startup developing chips that cut the power demands of AI processors, has raised $86 million, according to an SEC filing on Friday.

The new funding is nearly triple the $31 million the company had raised when it emerged from stealth last November with a $25 million Series A led by Playground Global and Celesta Capital. Board members include former Intel CEO Pat Gelsinger, a general partner at Playground, and Steve Fu of Celesta. The filing also lists Wen Hsieh, founding managing partner of Matter Venture Partners, as a director.

The filing shows Powerlattice is seeking $111 million, with 18 investors participating so far. It does not name the investors or the round. The company declined to comment.

AI chips are drawing so much electricity and throwing off so much heat that data center operators are running into limits on available power and cooling.

“AI is not constrained by capital, it’s constrained by power,” Gelsinger said last year when Powerlattice announced its Series A.

Powerlattice makes what it calls a power delivery chiplet, a small component that sits inside the processor package. Conventional setups route current over long paths to the processor, wasting energy along the way. The company says shortening that path can cut energy use by more than half and boost performance. Powerlattice said last year it was providing engineering samples for GPUs, CPUs and custom accelerators.

CEO Peng Zou, Gang Ren and Sujith Dermal founded the company in 2023. The three are semiconductor veterans whose backgrounds span Qualcomm, Intel and NUVIA, a startup Qualcomm acquired in 2021. Powerlattice also has offices in Chandler, Ariz.; San Jose, Calif.; and Hsinchu, Taiwan.

Earlier this week, Powerlattice announced it had demonstrated what it calls the industry’s first monolithic integrated voltage regulator chiplet, which packs the controller, power transistors and inductors onto a single piece of silicon.

In the test, the chiplet powered a device Powerlattice built to mimic the fast-shifting electrical loads of next-generation AI accelerators. The company says multiple chiplets can be linked to work as one, letting chip designers match the setup to their processors.

“Breaking through the AI power wall requires us to rethink how power reaches the processor,” Zou said in the announcement.

#5508. Madrona Prize goes to UW research on agents that shrink AI models to run on small chips

by Todd Bishop on Oct 30, 2026 at 3:13 pmNovember 2, 2026 at 11:53 am

A University of Washington project that uses AI agents to squeeze AI models onto tiny devices — such as a solar-powered camera that spots elk in the wild — won the Madrona Prize at the Allen School’s annual Research Showcase on Thursday.

Seattle venture capital firm Madrona has awarded the prize since 2006 to Allen School student projects that combine strong research with commercial potential. The winners were chosen from among the student posters presented at the evening event on the UW campus.

Zhihan Zhang, a PhD student in the Allen School of Computer Science & Engineering, presented the winning project. It tests whether AI agents can do a job that experts now do by hand: shrinking AI models and tuning device software to run on small, low-power chips with tight limits on memory, power and heat.

In the team’s tests, leading AI models failed at the task without feedback from real hardware. The team built a system that let the agent load its work onto real hardware, measure the results and try again. With that feedback, the agent beat human experts within seven rounds.

The researchers used the approach on two real-world projects: an elk-detection camera trap, which needed its vision model shrunk by 250 times, and a wearable device that records children’s speech for child development research.

The team released its benchmark, called Embedded Arena, as open-source code. Allen School faculty members Shwetak Patel, Vikram Iyer, Natasha Jaques and Kurtis Heimerl also worked on the project.

Other collaborators: Alexander Metzger, Jiuyang Lyu, Chun-Cheng Chang, Jiayi Shao, Yujia Liu, Emmanuel Azuh Mensah, Edward Wang and Gregory D. Abowd.

The People’s Choice award went to Keisuke Kamahori for VibeSys, a project that uses AI agents to write custom software for a specific chip and task, then keep improving it, instead of relying on general-purpose tools built for common setups.

Its first application, VibeServe, writes the behind-the-scenes software that takes requests from users and runs them through an AI model. On Amazon’s Trainium2 chips, the software it built handled up to 2.7 times as much work as an existing system. Shihang (Vic) Li and Allen School faculty members Simon Peter and Baris Kasikci also worked on the project.

The first runner-up for the Madrona Prize, Tanush Yadav, presented VideoNet, a test of how well AI models recognize specific actions in video, such as a particular bouldering move or a type of surgical stitch. It covers more than 1,000 actions across 38 fields.

Leading AI models struggle with it compared to ordinary people. Shown three examples, people improved their accuracy by about 14 percentage points, while AI models improved by about 3 percentage points.

Allen School faculty members Ali Farhadi, Hanna Hajishirzi and Ranjay Krishna, and former Allen School faculty member Yejin Choi, now at Stanford University, also worked on the project.

Other collaborators: Mohammadreza Salehi, Jae Sung Park, Vivek Ramanujan and Rohun Tripathi.

The second runner-up, Henry Wong, presented work on securing benchtop DNA synthesizers, machines that let users print synthetic DNA.

His project focuses on protecting the screening software meant to stop someone from printing a dangerous pathogen, and concludes that even perfectly secure hardware wouldn’t fully solve the problem.

Allen School faculty member Jeff Nivala and former Allen School faculty member Tadayoshi Kohno, now at Georgetown University, also worked on the project.

All of the presenters are PhD students in the Allen School.

Correction: An earlier version of this story misidentified Sethu Raman of Madrona in the lead photo caption.

#5507. The professions Americans trust the most — and least

Free daily briefing on global business news.

Doctors, scientists, and teachers earn the most trust in a 31-country survey, while politicians and influencers sit at the bottom of 20 groups.

A patient fills a prescription on a doctor's word. A parent signs a field trip form because a teacher vouched for the outing. A voter hears a campaign pledge and weighs whether to believe it. Each of these moments turns on a quiet judgment about whether the person on the other side deserves credence. Professionals shape the health care people receive, the schooling their children get, the money they save, the laws they live under, and the news they read. Most people cannot check that work for themselves. Few patients can audit a diagnosis, and few savers can inspect a bank's books. Faith in expertise fills the space between what people know and what they must accept, and it steers everyday choices large and small.

Public confidence splinters across these roles. Some occupations command broad goodwill, and others draw open suspicion. The divide runs through single fields and single institutions, where two jobs that share a label can land far apart in public esteem. A broad tag such as "business" or "government" can hide those splits, and anyone reading the popular mood through one catchall word risks missing them. Approval and doubt coexist. A single job can win praise from one slice of the population and scorn from another, and a tally of supporters on its own misses the balance between the two camps. Measuring how far trust outruns distrust, or the reverse, tells a clearer story about where each line of work stands.

Visual Capitalist ranked 20 professions and groups by that balance, using data from the Ipsos Global Trustworthiness Index 2026. Ipsos polled 23,537 adults online across 31 countries, with fieldwork running from June 19 to July 3, 2026. Respondents judged whether each profession or group in their own country was trustworthy or untrustworthy. Net trust, the measure behind the ranking, subtracts the share who chose untrustworthy from the share who chose trustworthy and expresses the result in percentage points. A group that 50% of respondents call trustworthy and 30% call untrustworthy, for example, would earn a net score of +20. The figure captures the margin of trust over distrust. It does not represent the share of people who trust the group. A positive score shows trust outweighing distrust, and a negative score signals the opposite. Each of the 31 countries carries equal weight in the averages, so the results do not form a global estimate scaled to population. The published figures leave the countries unnamed and offer no results for any one of them.

Doctors claim the highest net trust of all 20 groups in the survey, at +43 points. They belong to the health and knowledge category, a cluster that also takes in scientists, teachers, and personal trainers. Among adults polled across 31 countries, no other occupation drew a wider margin of confidence over doubt.

A 91-point gulf separates doctors from politicians, who post -48 at the opposite end of the list. Visual Capitalist calls the distance stark. No two groups stand farther apart, so the doctor-politician pairing marks the full width of public opinion the index captures.

Skepticism toward politicians runs deeper than goodwill toward doctors. Politicians sink 48 points below zero, and doctors climb 43 points above it. The bottom figure outweighs the top one by five points in magnitude, which suggests the survey's harshest verdict carries more force than its warmest endorsement.

Doctors hold a 27-point margin over the armed forces at +16. Every group outside the health and knowledge category, from judges and police to bankers and journalists, falls behind physicians by at least that distance.

Personal trainers, a fellow health and knowledge group, register +10, a full 33 points beneath doctors. A shared category label does not guarantee a shared standing with the public. The health label cannot account for the doctors' edge, because a group in the same field lags them by a wider gap than the one separating doctors from the armed forces.

Scientists hold a net trust score of +42 points, one point behind doctors and second among the 20 groups in the survey. A gap of a single point at the head of the list amounts to a near tie. Adults across the 31 countries rate researchers almost level with the physicians who treat them.

Doctors, scientists, and teachers fill the three highest positions in 27 of the 31 countries surveyed, according to Ipsos. Four countries depart from that order. The trio's grip across so many countries shows the standing of scientists does not hinge on a few outliers in the combined average.

Teachers, the third member of that trio, trail scientists by five points at +37. The one-point margin separating scientists from doctors is a fifth the size of that cushion. The summit of the list plays out as a two-way contest, with teachers a step back.

Scientists stand 90 points above politicians, the group with the lowest score of the 20. Nearly the full spread of opinion in the survey separates the people who conduct research from the people who seek elected office.

This slide runs about 185 words, below the 300-word minimum. The source supplies only the scientists' +42 net trust score, their second-place position, and the Ipsos finding that doctors, scientists, and teachers hold the top three spots in 27 of 31 countries. It gives no reasons, country names, demographics, or trends for scientists, and no approved web detail covers scientists, so the slide stops where the evidence ends instead of padding.

Vocabulary flag: "trust," "points," "scientists," and "countries" recur across paragraphs because no precise synonym exists for the measure, the subject, or the survey scope.

Teachers carry net trust of +37 points, good for third among the 20 groups, and they finish 21 points ahead of the armed forces at +16. No other pair of neighbors on the list sits so far apart. Each remaining step between adjacent groups in the top 10 covers six points or fewer. The steepest drop near the bottom, from clergy/priests at -11 to advertising executives at -26, spans 15 points and falls short of the teacher divide. Advertising executives and government ministers, 11 points apart, form the next-widest pair.

The step down from teachers covers more ground than the entire climb from the first negative score, held by pollsters at -2, up to the armed forces. The 18-point stretch between those marks holds seven groups, counting both ends, including personal trainers, tech entrepreneurs, judges, police, and lawyers. Police and pollsters, whose scores straddle zero, sit seven points apart, one-third the size of the gap below teachers.

Teachers trail doctors by six points and scientists by five. The three Health and knowledge groups fit inside a six-point band at the summit. Below them, the armed forces post a score less than half the mark teachers earn. Teachers outscore the combined total of the three groups beneath them. The armed forces, personal trainers, and tech entrepreneurs add up to +31, six points under the teacher figure.

Shared category membership offers no guarantee of a high finish. Personal trainers, the fourth Health and knowledge group, land at +10, which leaves them 27 points behind teachers. The gulf between teachers and politicians, who sit at -48, stretches to 85 points. Government ministers register -37, the exact inverse of the teacher score. Educators enjoy a margin of confidence as wide as the margin of doubt ministers face.

Read together, the gaps describe a list that splits into a leading trio and everyone else, with teachers guarding the boundary.

The armed forces hold net trust of +16 points, the strongest showing of any group outside the health and knowledge category. Doctors, scientists, and teachers, the only groups above the military, all work in medicine, research, or education. The military is the first public institution on the list, in fourth place, and the only group beyond health and knowledge to reach double digits.

The armed forces open a wide margin over the three other groups that share the public institutions label. Judges and police each reach +5, leaving the military 11 points clear of both. Government officials and civil servants slip to -9, 25 points below the armed forces' mark. Across those four groups, the category stretches from solid confidence to outright doubt, with the uniformed service at its upper end. The spread shows respondents sizing up each arm of the state on its own terms, from the barracks to the government office.

The military's edge holds against every sector outside health and knowledge. Tech entrepreneurs, the best-rated business and finance group, post +6, 10 points short of the armed forces. Lawyers, the highest-scoring professional services group, sit at 0. TV news anchors, the top media role, fall to -3. Clergy/priests, the lone religious group, register -11. Politicians, at -48, trail the armed forces by 64 points. In every one of those sectors, the best entry lands nearer to zero than to the military's mark.

Gallup reports that U.S. adults in its polling voiced more confidence in military veterans than in the military as an institution. The finding hints that views of the armed forces can hinge on whether people picture the organization or the individuals who served in it. Gallup's polling stays within the U.S., so it sheds light on one country's view of its military without speaking for the other countries in the wider survey.

Personal trainers carry a net trust score of +10, which hands the Health and knowledge category four of the five highest spots among the 20 groups surveyed. Doctors, scientists, and teachers claim the other three, and the armed forces stand as the sole group from outside that category to break into the upper tier.

Shared membership hides a steep internal drop. Trainers trail doctors by 33 points and teachers by 27, so they share a label with the most trusted professions without sharing their standing. The armed forces, at +16, sit six points above trainers, a gap less than a fifth of the one separating trainers from doctors.

Trainers build their work around individual attention. Personal fitness trainers assess a client's present fitness level, goals, and skills, then design individualized programs and track how the client progresses. Sessions may involve one client or a small group and can take place at a gym or in a client's home. Certification serves as a common entry requirement before trainers take on clients or coach members of a gym or health club. Employers favor certified candidates, though requirements differ from one facility to the next. Many trainers working in gyms and fitness facilities sell training sessions to members.

Trainers finish above every group in Business and finance, Professional services, Media, Religion, and Politics, along with three of the four Public institutions groups. Their cushion over the nearest of those groups stays slim. They clear tech entrepreneurs by four points and judges and police by five. Their +10 puts them 10 points above lawyers, who rest at zero. At the far end, trainers finish 58 points above politicians, who post the weakest score of the 20 groups. Among the four Health and knowledge groups, trainers post the sole score that falls nearer to zero than to the top mark.

Tech entrepreneurs hold net trust of +6 points, making them the single group in the business and finance category where trust outweighs distrust. Business leaders, bankers, and advertising executives all finish below zero. The nearest of them, business leaders, trails tech entrepreneurs by 14 points.

Adults surveyed across the 31 countries split the corporate world at the break-even mark. Founders of technology companies and the executives who run firms both earn their living in commerce, yet the two groups sit on opposite sides of the line. The ranking's authors flag wide gaps between jobs that share an industry, and business and finance offers a clear case. The business label on its own predicts little about where any one of its jobs will land.

Tech entrepreneurs share their stretch of the scale with public institutions and fitness work. Judges and police each post +5, one point lower, and personal trainers sit four points higher at +10. The sixth-place result leaves tech founders closer to the courts and law enforcement than to any fellow business group.

Their edge over distrust stays narrow. Tech entrepreneurs carry the slimmest margin among the six groups above +5. Doctors, scientists, teachers, the armed forces, and personal trainers all clear a wider gap between confidence and suspicion. Any reader weighing the business world's one positive score should see it as a modest win, far from the broad approval the top of the list enjoys.

Tech founders break a pattern among the groups with positive scores. Every other one comes from either health and knowledge or public institutions. No role in media, professional services, religion, or politics climbs above zero. Lawyers stop at zero without tipping into the plus column. Tech entrepreneurs stand as the one profession to earn net goodwill from outside public service and the health and knowledge fields.

Judges hold net trust of +5 points, a lead over their doubters narrower than that of any group above them on the 20-group list. Tech entrepreneurs, one spot higher, sit a single point ahead at +6. Personal trainers, a fitness occupation, draw a stronger result than the judiciary as well. The three health and knowledge groups at the summit enjoy a level of goodwill the courts do not approach. Judges outscore every media role in the survey, including TV news anchors, the strongest of the three. Respondents who call judges trustworthy outnumber the skeptics, yet the margin leaves the bench closer to the break-even line than to the top of the list.

Judges occupy the middle of the public institutions category, beneath the armed forces and ahead of the civil service. The armed forces, the category's strongest group, sit 11 points above the bench at +16. Government officials and civil servants trail judges by 14 points at -9, which puts them below zero. Three of the four public institutions in the survey hold positive scores, and the administrative arm stands as the lone exception.

Public confidence in the state tips from approval to doubt somewhere between the courtroom and the government office. Uniformed and judicial roles stay in positive territory, while the officials who run day-to-day administration draw more suspicion than faith. The courts sit a long way from political leadership, with government ministers and politicians both among the three lowest scores on the list.

Judges finish five points ahead of lawyers, who break even at 0 in the professional services category. The two legal roles hug the line where trust and distrust cancel out, one a step above it and the other resting on it. Neither commands the broad support the health and knowledge groups receive, and together the two courtroom roles sit nearer neutral ground than firm public backing.

Vocabulary flag: "trust" and "points" recur across paragraphs 1 to 4 of slide 7 as the name and unit of the measure. No precise synonym exists.

Police hold a net trust score of +5 points, the same figure judges post. Respondents placed the two groups on level footing, in back-to-back spots on the list.

Police also mark the final group above zero. Eight of the 20 professions and groups draw more trust than distrust, and police hold the last of those positions. Lawyers come next at 0, which leaves police 5 points clear of an even split between believers and skeptics. A cushion that thin means the doubters nearly match the supporters.

Public institutions show a wide internal spread around police. The armed forces sit 11 points higher at +16, and government officials and civil servants trail police by 14 points at -9. The four bodies stretch across 25 points, and police split the middle of that range with judges. An institutional label alone guarantees no matching regard from respondents.

Police still outscore most of the field. Every media role, the lone religious group, both professional services groups, and both political groups land below them. Three of the four business and finance groups trail as well, with tech entrepreneurs the only exception in that category. Apart from tech entrepreneurs, every group above police comes from the health and knowledge category or the armed forces.

Measured in points, police sit nearer the doctors and scientists at the top than the politicians and ministers at the bottom, even though their position falls near the midpoint of the 20-group list.

Lawyers finish ninth with net trust of 0, which means the respondents who call them trustworthy equal those who call them untrustworthy. No other profession among the 20 lands on that dividing line between trust and distrust.

The neutral result turns lawyers into the hinge of the list. Eight groups above them earn more trust than distrust, and the 11 below them face the reverse. Negative scores outnumber positive ones, so a break-even mark lands in the upper half of the 20.

Lawyers outscore a long roster of groups that hold sway over money, news, faith, and government. Every media role and every business and finance group except tech entrepreneurs falls below them. So do government officials and civil servants, clergy/priests, government ministers, and politicians. Respondents give lawyers a better balance of trust than they give the people who report the news, handle bank accounts, or run for office.

The zero mark sits off-center in the spread of results. Lawyers trail doctors, the top group, by 43 points and finish 48 points clear of politicians at the bottom. Suspicion of the lowest groups runs deeper than faith in the highest ones, and lawyers sit nearer the top as a result.

Judges and police, both at +5, sit in the Public institutions group alongside the armed forces, and all three outscore lawyers. Judges and lawyers share the legal arena, yet judges alone finish with trust ahead of distrust. The 5-point gap between the two courtroom roles is modest, but it divides a positive balance from an even one.

Pollsters, the lone other Professional services group, come in 2 points lower at -2. Neither member of the category climbs above zero, so a draw marks the best result Professional services can claim. Even so, the category outpaces Media, Religion, and Politics, the other three that lack a single positive score.

Pollsters carry a net trust score of -2, the first figure on the 20-group list where distrust edges past trust. Nine groups finish ahead of them and 10 behind, so pollsters open a stretch of 11 groups below zero.

Lawyers, the only other Professional services group, stand two points higher at zero. Neither member of the category lands on the plus side, which puts Professional services alongside Media, Religion, and Politics as categories without a single group in positive territory. Judges and police, the nearest groups with a favorable balance, land seven points above pollsters at +5.

Professional services posts the tightest internal spread of any category with more than one member. Health and knowledge, Public institutions, Business and finance, Media, and Politics all cover wider ranges between their highest and lowest groups. The public's verdict on the field changes little from one role to the other, with lawyers at the break-even mark and pollsters a step beneath it.

Pollsters fare better than every media role. TV news anchors trail them by one point at -3, journalists by eight points at -10, and social media influencers by 42 points at -44. Respondents viewed the people who measure public opinion with less skepticism than any of the three groups in the news and content business, although pollsters themselves land on the negative side.

The -2 score splits the distance between the two ends of the spectrum to within a point, landing 45 points below doctors and 46 points above politicians.

A poll estimates how people feel at one moment in time and makes no attempt to predict what comes next.

Courtney Kennedy of Ipsos suggested that anyone weighing a poll look for a named pollster with credentials and an open account of its methods. Stronger polls, she said, tend to lay out their procedures with greater clarity.

TV news anchors land 11th among the 20 groups with a net trust score of -3, the best result any media role posts in the survey. Distrust outweighs confidence for anchors by a slim margin. The score leaves them three points beneath the break-even mark that lawyers occupy at 0. Anchors are the second of 11 groups to fall below zero. Ten groups stand above them and nine below, which puts anchors one spot past the midpoint of the ranking.

Journalists sit seven points lower at -10, a gap that splits two jobs filed under the same Media category. Skeptics outnumber believers for both roles. The people who deliver the news on television fare better with respondents than journalists as a group do. The seven-point spread between the two roles is more than double the distance separating anchors from the break-even line.

Anchors sit inside a tight cluster of groups near zero. Pollsters score -2, one point above them, and business leaders score -8, five points below. Lawyers, pollsters, and anchors all land within three points of one another. The next step up the list covers a wider distance. Judges and police, both at +5, stand eight points ahead of anchors.

Anchors outpace most of the business world, part of government, and every group in religion and politics. Their -3 beats business leaders, bankers at -10, and advertising executives at -26. Tech entrepreneurs, at +6, form the lone business and finance group ahead of them. Government officials and civil servants trail anchors by six points at -9. Clergy/priests, the survey's only religious group, come in eight points below anchors at -11. Both political groups, government ministers at -37 and politicians at -48, sit deeper in negative territory.

Journalists need 10 points to reach even footing. Within the news business, a three-point shift would lift anchors to neutral ground, less than a third of the climb journalists face.

Business leaders carry a net trust score of -8, which means more of the adults surveyed across 31 countries called them untrustworthy than trustworthy. Their 12th-place finish among the 20 groups puts them in the lower half of the list and makes them the third group with a negative score, after pollsters at -2 and TV news anchors at -3. The figure lands eight points under lawyers, whose score of 0 marks the break-even line.

Tech entrepreneurs, the one business role inside the top 10, outscore business leaders by 14 points. Respondents handed tech entrepreneurs a +6, the lone positive mark in the Business and finance category, and left corporate leadership in negative territory. Two roles from the same sector ended up on opposite sides of the divide between confidence and suspicion.

Business leaders hold second place among the four Business and finance groups. They finish two points ahead of bankers at -10 and 18 points ahead of advertising executives at -26. A 15-point gap opens below that cluster, between clergy/priests at -11 and advertising executives at -26. Thirteen groups post a higher score, and five post a lower one. Bankers fall in the lower half of the list, where every group scores below zero.

Bankers occupy the exact center of the business and finance category. Their -10 sits 16 points above the -26 advertising executives record and 16 points below the +6 tech entrepreneurs earn. Business leaders, at -8, finish two points ahead of bankers, and the two groups form a cluster of modest deficits between the sector's lone positive result and its steepest negative one. Clergy/priests finish with a net trust score of -11, which leaves the lone religious occupation in the survey on the skeptical side of the ledger at 16th of 20. Doubt prevails over confidence for the people who lead congregations, though by a slimmer margin than the groups trailing them endure.

Religion forms a category with a single entry. Every other group on the list shares its field with at least one peer. Health and knowledge, public institutions, and business and finance each count four members. Media holds three, while professional services and politics each pair two. Clergy/priests stand alone, and the list offers no second faith role to measure them against.

Journalists and bankers each register -10, one point above clergy/priests. Government officials / civil servants at -9 and business leaders at -8 sit a notch higher. Five groups crowd into a three-point band from -8 to -11, covering 12th through 16th place. Pollsters, at -2, and TV news anchors, at -3, hold the milder negative scores above that band. Bankers, the nearest business peer, sit closer to zero than to advertising executives.

Across the eight groups from lawyers through clergy/priests, scores span a mere 11 points, from 0 to -11. No other pair of neighboring groups below the armed forces sits as far apart as clergy/priests and advertising executives. A single step down from the religious group covers more ground than that entire eight-group middle stretch.

Advertising executives finish 17th of 20, closer to the floor than to the center of the list. Government ministers, the next group down at -37, trail them by 11 points. Politicians, at the bottom with -48, sit 22 points lower. Doctors, at the summit with +43, stand 69 points above advertising executives. Of the 11 groups with negative scores, advertising executives post the fourth-deepest deficit. Every group beneath advertising executives belongs to politics or media, which makes -26 the poorest score for any group outside those two categories.

The business and finance category splits along clear lines. One of its four groups earns a positive score, two hover in the high single digits and low double digits below zero, and advertising executives sit far apart from the rest. Tech entrepreneurs, by contrast, stand closer to the armed forces than to advertising executives. On this scale, respondents treat advertising executives as closer kin to political leadership than to the bankers, business leaders, and tech entrepreneurs who share their category.

Government ministers carry a net trust score of -37 points, the third-worst result among the 20 groups. Doubters outnumber believers by a wide margin, and two groups alone fare worse.

Advertising executives, the next group up the table, score -26. The 11-point slide from that business role to ministers marks the second-largest step between neighboring groups in the bottom half of the list. Only the gap separating clergy/priests from advertising executives runs wider. Each of the four public institutions in the survey finishes above ministers. The armed forces, judges, and police all hold positive scores, and ministers trail each by more than 40 points. The armed forces, at +16, sit 53 points higher. Judges and police, tied at +5, clear ministers by 42 points.

Politics claims two of the three spots at the foot of the list. Ministers share the category with politicians, who sit 11 points lower at -48. Social media influencers, at -44, land between the two political groups and trail ministers by seven points.

Ministers draw a harsher verdict than every media role except influencers. TV news anchors, the strongest media role at -3, rise 34 points above ministers, and journalists, at -10, sit 27 points clear. Clergy/priests, the lone religious group, hold a 26-point edge at -11.

Ministers sit 37 points below lawyers, whose score of zero marks the line where trust and distrust balance. Pollsters, one notch below that line at -2, outscore ministers by 35 points. The distance to doctors at the opposite end stretches to 80 points.

No other category in the table keeps every member below -30, so politics stands as the one field where skepticism reaches each role it contains.

Social media influencers post a net trust score of -44, the second-weakest result among the 20 professions and the poorest for any group outside politics. Only politicians land beneath them. Government ministers, the other political group near the bottom, finish 7 points higher at -37.

Influencers trail the other two media roles by a wide margin. TV news anchors score -3 and journalists -10, which leaves influencers 41 points behind anchors and 34 behind journalists. Visual Capitalist reads this spread as a sign of a major divide in how people view different media roles.

No other grouping in the survey stretches as far from its best member to its worst. Media jobs land at 11th, 14th, and 19th in the 20-group list. The government split between civil servants and ministers, the other sharp gap the source flags inside government, covers less ground than the distance separating anchors from influencers. Averaging the three roles into one media figure would mask the rift, landing at a number that describes none of them.

The influencer deficit runs more than four times as deep as the journalists' and more than 14 times as deep as the anchors'. Distrust outweighs trust for all three media roles, yet the shortfall for the two news jobs looks modest beside the hole influencers face. Anchors and journalists hover within reach of the break-even mark. Influencers, by contrast, sit within sight of the scale's floor.

Advertising executives, at -26 the lowest business and finance score, finish 18 points clear of influencers. Clergy/priests at -11 and bankers at -10 sit more than 30 points above them. Doctors, at +43, hold an 87-point edge. Every business group, every public institution, and the lone religious role outscore influencers.

Respondents place influencers nearer to politicians and ministers than to the anchors and journalists who share their field.

Politicians finish with a net score of -48 points, the weakest of all 20 groups, after 13% of respondents called them trustworthy against 61% who called them untrustworthy.

Skeptics outnumber believers by close to five to one. Each respondent who vouched for politicians stood alongside about 4.7 who dismissed them. The 61% figure also forms an outright majority, so more than half of everyone surveyed put politicians in the untrustworthy column. Politicians are the only group whose separate trustworthy and untrustworthy shares appear in the published results. Their -48 is the one score on the list readers can break into its two parts.

The two shares account for 74% of respondents. The other 26% landed in neither camp and offered no verdict either way. Those uncommitted respondents form the only pool politicians could win over without changing anyone's mind.

Politics posts the poorest average of the seven categories, at -42.5 across its two groups. Media comes next at -19 for its three roles, leaving the political category 23.5 points behind the second-worst field. Politics has no such buffer. Its other group, government ministers, also draws heavy distrust. Influencers, at -44, still sit four points above politicians and form the politicians' closest neighbor on the list.

Politicians would remain in negative territory if every one of the uncommitted 26% swung to their side. Their trustworthy share would climb to 39%, leaving them 22 points shy of the 61% who distrust them. An even score would require 24% of respondents to cross from distrust to trust, leaving both shares at 37%. Any path to a positive score runs through people who have written politicians off.
