#5506. Washington governor rips Microsoft over TV ad in leaked audio

by Todd Bishop on Oct 30, 2026 at 5:21 pmNovember 2, 2026 at 6:29 am

Washington Gov. Bob Ferguson called out Microsoft for bankrolling a political action committee responsible for a TV ad describing state government as broken, according to newly leaked audio from a Seattle Chamber leadership conference last week.

Remarks at the Seattle Metropolitan Chamber of Commerce’s Regional Leadership Conference, held at the Suncadia resort near Cle Elum, Wash., are supposed to be off the record. But The Washington Observer, an independent newsletter on state politics, published the audio Friday, saying it was obtained from an unnamed source.

In the audio, Ferguson zeroed in on a line near the start of the ad — that in Washington, “it used to be all you needed was an idea, a dream and the guts to chase it.”

The governor repeated the words “it used to be” for emphasis, in a tone of disbelief.

“What’s up with that?” Ferguson asked the crowd of business and government leaders. “First, does anyone else in this room believe that? I sure as hell don’t.”

“I talk to people every day who have that idea, that dream. They’re chasing it and they’re getting it,” he said. He cited the record $3.5 billion that Seattle-area startups raised in the third quarter, more than triple the same period a year ago, according to PitchBook data.

The Microsoft relationship: Ferguson, who noted that he had worked as a lawyer for Microsoft, said he loves the company and respects what it does. But he seemed especially peeved that the ad ran during the Seattle Seahawks game, where it reached people across the state and those from elsewhere who might want to come here and start a company.

“If we’re partners, partners should treat partners like partners, right?” he said.

He asked the room to imagine him running a multimillion-dollar ad criticizing Microsoft. “You guys would think I lost my mind if I did that,” he said.

Ferguson called Microsoft a key partner and a member of his economic roundtable, and said he works well with the company. “But it works both ways,” he said.

Ferguson acknowledged that the state has problems. “Are there challenges? Sure,” he said. But he said he didn’t think the ad was “helpful for where we all want to go.”

He told the crowd he welcomes constructive feedback, but asked business leaders to think about how they communicate, and to talk up the state’s workforce, economy and startup funding along with its challenges.

“What we have here is so bloody special,” he said.

Ferguson, who took office in January 2025, also reminded the room that he isn’t going anywhere. “I plan on being governor for a long time,” he said, adding that he works with all of them, “Microsoft included.”

The Observer noted that $10 million, roughly what the group has left to spend, would be a good start on a campaign to run someone else for governor in 2028.

The newsletter said it stripped the audio from a video of Ferguson’s remarks, to protect its source. Among those in the audience was Michael Mattmiller, who represents Microsoft in Olympia. He and Ferguson “kinda-sorta hugged it out afterward,” the Observer reported.

Who’s behind the ad: The campaign comes from Washington Needs to Compete, a PAC funded in large part by Microsoft and its current and former executives. The group has raised about $13.8 million, according to state campaign finance records, including more than $5 million directly from Microsoft.

Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella and former CEO Steve Ballmer each gave $250,000, and Vice Chair and President Brad Smith gave more than $500,000. Other backers include T-Mobile, F5, Alaska Airlines and Weyerhaeuser.

Washington Needs to Compete has spent about $3 million so far, according to state records. Most of it has gone to state legislative races, the Observer reported, including more than $700,000 backing Rep. Amy Walen, D-Kirkland, in the 48th District, home to Microsoft’s Redmond headquarters.

The group spent $97,000 to air the ad during the Seahawks’ Oct. 15 Thursday night loss to the Denver Broncos on Prime Video and $130,000 during their Oct. 25 Sunday night win over the Kansas City Chiefs on NBC, according to the Observer.

Microsoft referred GeekWire’s inquiry to the group, which the company described as a growing coalition of more than 60 funders that want to keep the state competitive.

A press representative for the group sent a statement from Nick Streuli, an officer of Washington Needs to Compete. Streuli runs the government relations firm Sundial Advocacy and was previously policy and outreach director for former Gov. Jay Inslee.

“Washington Needs to Compete is committed to our state and wants to see it succeed,” Streuli said in the statement. “Rising costs are making it harder for businesses to invest and grow here. We are starting a conversation about our economic challenges and how to solve them.”

What the ad says: The spot opens with a nod to “inventors in garages,” “mom-and-pop shops down Main Street” and farmers “feeding the world,” before declaring, “In Washington, it used to be all you needed was an idea, a dream and the guts to chase it.”

Then it turns: “But today, Olympia is broken, spending more while you get less.” Jobs are leaving, the ad says, and “it’s harder than ever to afford a home and raise a family.”

It doesn’t name Ferguson or any legislation. It ends by saying Olympia needs to “quit wasting money, fix what’s broken and put Washington families first.”

Taxes and the business climate: Ferguson this year signed a 9.9% tax on household income above $1 million, known as the millionaires tax, which takes effect in 2028 and is projected to raise about $3 billion a year. Initiative 645, which would repeal it, is on the Nov. 3 ballot.

In September, Smith joined former Gov. Chris Gregoire and dozens of regional officials to launch a partnership aimed at reversing the Seattle area’s economic slide. “The warning signs are flashing on our economy,” Smith said at the time.

The region lost nearly 7,000 jobs in 2025, according to the group, and Washington has fallen from 32nd to 47th in CNBC’s ranking of states by cost of doing business since 2017.

In the same CNBC study, Washington ranks 11th overall, up from 14th last year, and fifth for its economy. WalletHub ranks Washington’s economy second in the nation, behind Massachusetts.

Washington’s gross domestic product grew faster than any other state’s in the first quarter of 2026, driven largely by its tech sector, according to federal data released in June.

Long-term plans: On its website, Washington Needs to Compete describes itself as businesses and residents building “a modern, permanent political organization” to support leaders and ideas that “strengthen our economy, improve affordability and expand opportunity,” through elections and public education.

The site lists its top five contributors as Microsoft, T-Mobile, the Washington Coalition for Responsible Taxes and Spending, F5 and Smith.

The group is saving most of its money for future campaigns, the Observer reported.

Updated Nov. 2 with comment from Washington Needs to Compete.

#5505. I Dropped Out of Harvard to Start a Company That Lets You Copy Successful Investors. It’s Powered $2B in Trades.

You're viewing the US website. Looking for the Site edition?

Steven Wang wants everyday investors to learn from the best and grow their wealth.

This as-told-to story is based on a conversation with Steven Wang, founder and CEO of Dub, a social investing platform that allows everyday investors to follow verified Wall Street professionals and wealth managers and automatically mirror their strategies. Wang left high school to build, fund and sell a VR startup called Realism. By age 18, Apple had hired him as an engineering product manager. He went on to attend Harvard before dropping out to focus on Dub, which has powered $2 billion in trades. The piece has been edited for length and clarity.

My parents immigrated here from China. We didn’t have a lot of money growing up, so money was always a big topic in the family. I started hustling on the playground: just doing business here and there, selling Pokémon cards, etc. That got me interested in financial markets. I read a couple of the early books from Ben Graham and Warren Buffett. Then I asked my parents to open me a custodial trading account in second grade. They loaned me $200.

I remember losing a lot of money in those early days. It was still $7 a trade before Robinhood. But it was so cool, this concept of ownership in a company, no matter how small it was. In many ways, it was the first time I really realized the American dream. That was super inspiring for me as a kid, and I continued to invest.

Early on, I got into technology too, through robotics. I ended up starting my first company, in virtual reality, during my sophomore year of high school. It was my first time leaving home, raising venture capital. We actually sold the business, and that was the first time I made some real money as a kid. So that led me to go work for Apple. I was the youngest person on our team. Then I decided to go to college.

I started at Harvard in the fall of 2020. Not a great time to start school. The pandemic had just hit. Classes were on Zoom. And the markets were starting to get really frothy. Crypto was taking off, all the SPACs (special purpose acquisition companies). Everything was happening. Robinhood and Coinbase were IPO-ing in the middle of 2021. I was trading all day long because there was just so much time.

Trading in 2021 was very different from when I started. The rise of social media, the influencer economy. People and their ideas drove investments — the biggest example of that was GameStop. People believed in one guy with a random username so much that they really changed the financial industry as we knew it.

So I was inspired to think about, How do we productize that? How do we make it simple to follow someone’s trades or investments that you believe in? And that led to the birth of Dub, the platform that makes it simple to copy someone else’s portfolio. That was five years ago. I left school and moved to New York City, and I’ve been working on Dub since.

When it came to fundraising for Dub, I feel like the Harvard dropout piece helped. And I’d sold a company before in high school. The investors from my first company didn’t even know what I was doing but offered to back the venture. So I definitely had a fundraising advantage many people starting out don’t necessarily have. And Dub was lucky to attract some of the best investors in the world — a lot of people that I’d idolized, like the CEOs and founders of Uber, Airbnb, Robinhood, Kalshi. Today, they remain some of my closest mentors.

We did our Series A last year, more than $30 million. As we’ve grown, the money’s been more a function of validation of the business and less that original vision and pitch, because we’re just a much larger and scaled company now. So I would say the fundraising was harder in a sense because it was based on the proof of the business.

It took about two and a half years to build Dub into a product people could use. No one had ever done what we’re doing with copy trading in the U.S. And to be a brokerage like Robinhood or Schwab, you have to get regulated by FINRA, the SEC. So it took us a long time to get that regulatory structure together, and then a long time to get it approved by the regulators. But that gave us a moat because we’re the first ones to do something that no one had really tried before. So that was exciting. Also, this is pre-AI, so building a whole brokerage from the ground up is a lot of work.

You can think of Dub like eBay or Airbnb. Anyone can become a seller. So if they think they have a good strategy or good skill at investing, they can open an account just like a regular user, and they can choose then to publish their portfolio that they build. And a portfolio is like a fund, a basket of stocks they can trade in and out. Once these are launched, any user on Dub can see it, and they can decide to copy that portfolio. Whenever that portfolio trades, it automatically mirrors those trades in any customer account. Now, we have 400 to 500 of these people who have built these portfolios and launched them. It’s a minimum bar of $10,000 to invest in your own portfolio to launch it. So we have some quality filters. And there’s a very diverse range of investing strategies.

We also have 20 premium creators, and it’s a very high bar to become one. You need to have an extended track record. Any creator on Dub has the chance to get “promoted” from a regular creator to a premium creator. They need to meet a minimum time on platform, show that they can beat the market in performance and pass a series of interviews with our investments team so that we know they are real investors worth following and also not just lucky.

Only premium creators get a cut. Premium creators can charge a percentage of assets management fee, similar to ETFs or mutual funds.

Dub makes money through our subscription, which is $89.99 per year, and we also take a cut of the management fees that premium creators make.

We just launched Arlo, one of the industry’s first AI investing assistants that uses algorithms to mirror how financial advisors make decisions. Usually, to hire an investment advisor or put your money at Goldman Sachs, you need to be worth millions, if not tens of millions of dollars. With AI, for the very first time, it’s going to be like when Robinhood made trading free. There’s going to be a democratization event where probably 90% to 95% of the advice that you get from a real-life investment advisor can now be provided by AI.

So we decided to embark on this journey about a year ago, and it’s a lot harder than it looks. It’s not just like talking to ChatGPT or Claude. There’s a lot of work to make sure it gives accurate, regulated advice, no hallucination, but also has the right math and algorithms to figure out accurate mathematical advice to give someone. And it needs to give the same response every time.

I think this will be a really cool moment in history where we look back upon this maybe five to 10 years later, like, Wow, now anyone with a phone can much better manage their money and not go into investing blind. The AI advisor will automatically build you a portfolio: These are the five people that you copy, this is what percentage you should do in each person, etc. And that’s how you build the most optimized, diversified portfolio that is aligned with how you want to invest and your risk tolerance.

We are clearly undergoing one of the most drastic moments in human history. Intelligence in many ways is getting rewritten by a potentially uncontrollable entity. So yes, there’s doom-ism, but on the flip side, optimistically, people at a younger age have never been able to build more with less. I would have loved to have AI when I started Dub. It would have been a whole different company-building experience. So to any young person, I’d say, if you have a dream, go pursue it. It’s one of the most beautiful things in life. Don’t hesitate. You may not have this chance again in a long time.

#5504. Zebec ZBCN Buyback: 40.5M Tokens Held, Not Burned, as Supply Stays Unchanged

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

Zebec says it bought back 40.5 million ZBCN in the third quarter and is keeping them "out of circulation."

On-chain, those tokens didn't reach Zebec's buyback treasury wallet during the quarter. They arrived on October 21, three weeks after Q3 ended, the same day Zebec announced the buyback, sent from what Solscan labels a Crypto.com hot wallet.

The amount matches Zebec's claim almost to the token. But the wallet's history also shows something "out of circulation" doesn't usually suggest: it has moved 59 million ZBCN out before. Let's go through the wallet to check what Zebec's buyback claim actually covers.

Zebec Network announced on October 21, in an X post, that it repurchased 40,536,539 ZBCN in Q3 for about $100,000. That implies an average price of roughly $0.00247. The money came from Zebec Cards and payroll fees across Zebec Enterprise and the SuperApp.

Zebec's explainer, Inside the ZBCN Buyback Program, says buybacks are "funded by operating revenue" from payroll, payments, cards and related services, not from treasury reserves. That's a real point in Zebec's favor.

The scale is small. ZBCN has a 100 billion maximum supply, so 40.5 million tokens is about 0.04% of it.

Zebec says the repurchased tokens "will not re-enter circulation." They weren't burned. ZBCN's total supply is exactly the same as it was before the buyback.

That's a deliberate policy. The program began in 2023 under the old ZBC token and originally included burns. In early 2024, the Zebec DAO approved ZIP-4, which paused burns while keeping recurring buybacks. Zebec says the DAO expects to decide by the end of 2026 whether to propose bringing burns back. Governance happens through the Zebec DAO portal.

The practical difference matters. A burn permanently destroys tokens. "Out of circulation" depends on Zebec continuing to hold them and on data providers leaving them out of circulating supply. The blockchain doesn't enforce either one.

Zebec's blog says repurchased tokens are held "in the designated on-chain Buyback Treasury Wallet and with Uphold Institutional," but doesn't give the address. The account linked with the announcement is EkXEg6de172aoLvr7w86YzQ2rf5oEFD3iUt8uQsLQuQW. ZBCN's Solana mint address is ZBCNpuD7YMXzTHB2fhGkGi78MNsHGLRXUhRewNRm9RU.

As of October 22, Solscan shows the wallet holding 108,256,701.48 ZBCN, worth about $246,157 at $0.002273.

The Q3 check passes. On October 21 at about 14:11 UTC, the wallet received two ZBCN transfers from an address Solscan labels "Crypto.com Hot Wallet":

Together, that's 40,535,224.09 ZBCN, just 1,315 ZBCN (about $3) short of Zebec's figure. That's a 99.997% match. The small difference is likely due to fees or rounding.

One detail stands out: the account is off-curve. Solscan shows "isOnCurve: FALSE," which means the address is derived by a program and has no private key of its own. Accounts like this are usually controlled by a program such as a multisig, so moving tokens requires that program's approval. That's a better setup than a single person's wallet, but it isn't a lock.

The timing shows how the program works. The wallet's transfer history suggests a repeating pattern, with each batch arriving after its quarter has ended:

Those three batches add up to the wallet's current balance within 0.01 ZBCN. So the "buyback treasury" holds the last three quarters of deliveries and nothing else.

This means that during each quarter, the purchased tokens weren't in the on-chain treasury. The pattern points to buying on an exchange, with tokens sitting in an exchange account until they're withdrawn to the treasury around announcement time. The chain doesn't show when the Q3 purchases actually happened, so for July 1 to September 30, the "$100,000 Q3 buyback" can't be checked on-chain. Only the October 21 delivery can.

That's common practice and not a sign of wrongdoing. But it means the on-chain record confirms delivery, not the purchases themselves.

If the balance only covers the last three batches, what happened to earlier buybacks? The transfer history answers that, too. The wallet has sent ZBCN out twice, both times to the same address, shown on Solscan as 9Sq2nZ...4TEine:

That's about 58.97 million ZBCN moved out of a wallet described as holding tokens that "will not re-enter circulation."To be fair, Zebec says tokens are "periodically consolidated with Uphold Institutional for custody," and these outflows may be exactly that. There's no confirmation that 9Sq2nZ...4TEine belongs to Uphold. Once tokens leave this wallet, readers can't follow them using Zebec's disclosures. These transfers also show what a burn would prevent: tokens in this wallet can, and do, move.

The Q3 claim holds up better than I expected. The wallet received almost exactly 40.5 million ZBCN, and the balance reconciles to the token. What the chain can't show is when the tokens were bought, or where earlier buybacks are now.

Three disclosures would close those gaps:

For now, Zebec did buy and deliver its Q3 tokens, and the supply is the same as it was before.

#5502. Elon Musk spent at least $225 million in Texas. The governor-elect who sued for Abbott emails and vowed a data center freeze won anyway

Elon Musk directed at least $225 million of his midterm spending to Texas, according to OpenSecrets data NPR reported. Texas is home to the headquarters of Tesla and SpaceX, and on Tuesday its voters handed Democrats the governor’s office, a U.S. Senate seat, and the state House anyway.

Democrat Gina Hinojosa unseated three-term Gov. Greg Abbott, becoming the state’s first Latina governor and ending a Republican hold on the office that began in 1995. James Talarico defeated Republican Ken Paxton, the first Democratic U.S. Senate win in Texas since 1988. Democrats also won control of the Texas House for the first time since Republicans took it in 2002.

For Musk, the result replaces a governor who championed his Texas expansion with one who sued to see Abbott’s communications with him and has promised to freeze data center approvals. Tesla, SpaceX, and Terafab, the $16.8 billion chip plant they are building in Grimes County, all depend on state cooperation for their next phase in Texas.

Musk gave more than $445 million to Republican candidates, PACs, and outside groups this cycle, making him the top donor of the midterms, according to OpenSecrets; other tallies run higher. Since May 2025, he has given more to federal political groups than George Soros has personally given in his lifetime, a Fortune analysis found.

Texas hosts Tesla’s Austin headquarters and Gigafactory, SpaceX’s Starbase launch site, and X, which became part of SpaceX when SpaceX merged with xAI in February. Tesla, a Fortune 500 company, is unlikely to see immediate manufacturing disruptions.

It could face more scrutiny of its Autopilot and Full Self-Driving technology and its planned Cybercab robotaxi rollout, especially with Democrats also winning both chambers of Congress. Democratic lawmakers could also push for a closer look at Musk’s companies and their government relationships.

SpaceX’s Texas expansion and its AI infrastructure ambitions could meet tougher environmental reviews and more contentious debates over electricity, water, and data center development. Hinojosa has made that fight central. “I will issue a moratorium — a ban — on all data center approvals,” she said in an Oct. 22 video, pledging to keep it in place until the Legislature passes new protections, the Texas Tribune reported.

Abbott himself paused new data center permits in September pending a grid audit. The open question for Musk is how long, and how broadly, a Hinojosa freeze would apply.

Terafab’s first phase represents a capital investment of more than $16.8 billion and is expected to create 3,000 jobs, according to Abbott’s office. The full project could be built in up to four phases at a total cost of $55 billion to $119 billion, Manufacturing Dive reported.

The state has extended a $30 million Texas Enterprise Fund grant, and the plant qualifies for the Jobs, Energy, Technology, and Innovation (JETI) program, which reduces school property taxes for large projects. The election doesn’t automatically cancel those commitments, but closer scrutiny of incentives and environmental requirements could raise costs or slow later phases.

Terafab is a chip plant, not a conventional data center. Its energy and infrastructure demands could still draw attention from officials concerned about industrial expansion, and Musk has said the facility will produce AI chips at scale.

Hinojosa challenged Abbott’s relationship with Musk before she won. On Oct. 19, the first day of early voting, she sued for access to unredacted communications between Abbott’s office and Musk and his companies. Her lawsuit says the governor’s office described some of those records as “intimate and embarrassing.”

She pointed to a $1.66 billion JETI tax break tied to Terafab, more than $54 million in state grants to SpaceX, and Abbott’s push for the state broadband office to award Starlink $110 million upfront from federal funds, a move that triggered an audit of the office. Abbott’s office called the suit “a baseless stunt.”

State District Judge Catherine Mauzy ordered Abbott’s office on Oct. 26 to let Hinojosa inspect the records, and the 15th Court of Appeals stayed that order the next day. Bloomberg Government separately reported that Mauzy had donated $500 to Hinojosa’s campaign in June.

Starting in January, Hinojosa will control state appointments, the veto, and the governor’s office that administers the Texas Enterprise Fund. Republicans kept their 19-12 majority in the Texas Senate, but Democrat Vikki Goodwin’s win in the lieutenant governor’s race gives the party the chamber’s presiding officer.

Shares of Musk’s two public companies fell the day after the election while the broader market rose. Tesla closed down 3.3% and SpaceX down 3.8% on Nov. 4, according to Yahoo Finance.

The timing doesn’t prove investors were reacting to Texas. But Wells Fargo’s chief equity strategist, Ohsung Kwon, had warned that a Democratic win in the governor’s race could be a “left-tail event” for the AI trade, CNBC reported.

Musk is also weighing a merger of Tesla and SpaceX, a deal that Democratic majorities in Congress could now scrutinize. Fortune has reported on what the merger talks reveal about his power.

Hinojosa takes office in January, the same month lawmakers return to Austin. The next tests are how far her data center freeze reaches, whether Terafab’s JETI agreements draw legislative review, and whether the fight over Abbott’s Musk records outlasts his administration.

#5500. OpenAI debuts new cybersecurity-focused AI model amid growing alarm about AI-driven cyber attacks

OpenAI has debuted a new AI model geared towards helping cybersecurity professionals.The company says that the new model, called GPT-6 Cyber, outperforms its general-purpose GPT-6 Astra model on most cyber tasks. Because of the risk that the model could be used to conduct cyberattacks if it fell into the wrong hands, OpenAI is current making the model available only to a small handful approved security customers. Fortune first reported that OpenAI was planning to release a specialized cyber model based on GPT-6 in September.

As AI models have become better at finding software flaws and turning them into working attacks, businesses have come under increasing pressure to strengthen their cyber defenses. Gartner forecast in September that worldwide AI cybersecurity spending would reach $51.3 billion this year, nearly double last year’s $25.9 billion.OpenAI is increasingly leaning into this market, seeing it as an important path to growing its enterprise sales. This is OpenAI’s fourth cybersecurity-focused model this year, following versions released in April, June and August. The company also hired a chief revenue officer, Dali Rajic, who comes from a cybersecurity software background.

Google and Anthropic are also competing for security customers. Anthropic’s Glasswing program gives vetted users access to capabilities that its public models might block. Google, which previously emphasized a lightweight, low-cost model for repeatedly scanning large codebases, has also begun offering vetted defenders access to its frontier Gemini 4 Argon model without cyber guardrails through its Fairwind Program.OpenAI’s GPT-6 Cyber focuses on advanced vulnerability research and exploit development. To test a server’s defenses, researchers may try breaking into it to see what an attacker could do with a flaw. The same methods can be used in malicious attacks, so general-purpose AI models impose restrictions that can also block legitimate security work. OpenAI has said it trains its Cyber models both to improve specialized cybersecurity skills and reduce refusals for certain tasks that can serve attackers and defenders.

OpenAI tested GPT-6 Cyber on Firefox, Mozilla’s web browser, and the Linux kernel, the core software underlying many servers. Firefox must handle potentially malicious webpages without exposing users’ data, while the Linux kernel controls access to a machine’s resources. Both are open-source projects whose code has been inspected, tested, and hardened by developers and security researchers for years. And yet AI models are still able to find novel vulnerabilities.

OpenAI says researchers used GPT-6 Cyber to find 81 previously unknown, high-severity Firefox vulnerabilities and develop working exploits for 948 Linux kernel vulnerabilities, including 588 previously unknown flaws. The Linux exploits could let an attacker with ordinary local access gain root privileges, the highest level of control over the system. Researchers developed working exploits for more than five times as many Linux vulnerabilities as in a July study using GPT-5.6 Sol, which was considered a state-of-the-art model for cyber tasks when it was released that month.

OpenAI currently offers two levels of access to trusted cybersecurity professionals through its Daybreak program: Daybreak Red supports advanced work such as simulating attacks and building tools that allow for red-teaming, while Daybreak Blue focuses on defensive tasks such as reviewing code, analyzing malware and investigating incidents.GPT-6 Cyber will initially be available to a select group of approved Daybreak Red customers only, with access expanding to all Red customers over the coming weeks, the company said. Separately, OpenAI said it is expanding early testing of Astra for defensive security work to more organizations and individual security researchers. through Daybreak Blue.

Wen Shao is a reporting fellow at Fortune covering AI, with a focus on the companies, economics, and infrastructure shaping the industry.

#5499. Here’s What Makes the CEO of a $15 Billion Company Stop Reading a Document: ‘I Can Tell Pretty Quickly’

You're viewing the US website. Looking for the Site edition?

This leader has little patience for this kind of writing, tossing reports away as soon as he detects it.

Writing and editing are the most common uses of AI among U.S. workers. In Gallup’s May 2026 survey, 51% of workplace AI users said they used the technology for those purposes.

Now the CEO of $15 billion GoDaddy, the world’s largest domain name provider, is pushing back against those popular use cases. In a new interview with Business Insider, GoDaddy CEO Aman Bhutani said he won’t outsource his writing to AI, and he has little patience for employees who send him AI-written work.

“If somebody sends me a document and I can tell pretty quickly it was written by AI, I don’t read it,” Bhutani said in the interview. “Because if the person couldn’t take the time to write it, then I definitely shouldn’t take the time to read it.”

Bhutani said there is a difference between using AI for clarification and letting it completely take over the writing. Workers can turn to the technology to better understand an unfamiliar word or phrase, but they must be able to turn their own ideas into a clear narrative, he said.

Turning ideas into compelling narratives is a critical skill, Bhutani added. Employees who write documents on their own are continuously practicing “the art of iteration,” or refining their written work and improving over time.

“What I’m really looking for is: What was the original observation? What was the original hypothesis, and what got you interested in this idea? Why do you think it matters? Right?” he said. “Because AI only knows what the internet already knows. It doesn’t know what we know deep inside us, and there are ideas coming from us all the time.”

Bhutani looks for a few tells when reading someone’s work. He notes that many of his colleagues speak English as a second language, so he is suspicious if they submit unusually polished prose.

Length can also raise a red flag. Some pieces run too long, while others are short but written in a recognizable “punchy and clear” tone that marks AI.

Researchers at Florida State University have found that common words such as “delve,” “intricate,” “realm” and “underscore” can be signs that AI wrote a block of text, especially when these keywords appear repeatedly.

AI also has some common stylistic habits. For example, it offers repeated contrast formulas: “It’s not just X — it’s Y.” It also relies on flowery metaphors, such as describing a subject as an “intricate tapestry.”

AI additionally yields perfect grammar and a plethora of em dashes. It provides an overly uniform structure, with similarly sized sections, repeated lists and conclusions that restate the introduction. It also generates inflated language, with grand claims and elaborate wording.

However, those clues alone aren’t proof that AI wrote a piece of text. AI detection tools like Turnitin can misidentify human writing. Turnitin advises against using its results alone to take action against a writer.

#5498. Pope Leo XIV on AI

by Oren Etzioni on Nov 1, 2026 at 10:11 amNovember 1, 2026 at 10:57 am

On Friday, 17 days after his surgery for lung cancer, Pope Leo XIV stood before a room of AI luminaries at the Vatican and delivered a speech on AI. No pope has engaged with AI as seriously, or as deeply, as Leo XIV. The timing shows how much AI matters to him. His remarks were important, on target, and blessedly short: about 740 words, compared with roughly 42,000 in Magnifica Humanitas, the AI encyclical, which I wrote about in May.

“The future of artificial intelligence is not pre-determined.”

I agree with four of his five points. The fifth, a call for international institutions to govern AI, is where we part ways.

First, “the future of artificial intelligence is not pre-determined.” He wants us to ask of AI, “What purpose should it serve?”

Second, “machines are tools, not persons.” Granting AI legal personhood, he warns, risks “leaving those who suffer harm to confront a faceless entity.”

Third, “certain decisions must never be delegated.” Decisions over life, freedom and the use of force have to stay with people, and he urged the states meeting in Geneva in November to “take concrete steps toward banning lethal autonomous weapons.”

Fourth, intelligent technologies “must never become ends in themselves or serve merely the interests of a privileged few.”

Fifth, “What we currently need are institutions capable of putting these principles into practice, particularly effective international institutions that can safeguard the global common good.”

I disagree with the fifth for two reasons.

The first is that the UN, the obvious candidate, has shown a remarkable inability to act. When Russia invaded Ukraine in 2022, the Security Council couldn’t even pass a resolution calling for its withdrawal, because Russia holds a veto. Days later, the General Assembly demanded the same withdrawal by a vote of 141-5, and Russia ignored it.

The second is that international institutions are poorly suited to governing a technology that changes every few months. The pope’s own example makes the case. States have discussed autonomous weapons under a UN weapons convention in Geneva since 2014, with a formal expert group since 2016. After 12 years, the review conference that meets Nov. 16-20 will decide whether to begin negotiating a treaty.

“Take concrete steps toward banning lethal autonomous weapons.”

Thousands of AI researchers, me among them, have called for a ban since 2015. There still isn’t one, and I don’t expect Geneva to deliver it. In those same 12 years, AI went from labeling photos to writing software. I suspect real international cooperation on AI won’t come until the major powers face something like the mutually assured destruction that drove nuclear arms control.

Several AI thinkers spoke at the meeting before the pope did.

Max Tegmark of MIT warned against handing decisions to machines, citing tech executives’ predictions that “AI will be in charge, not humans.”

I agree that people have to stay in charge. When AI causes harm, a person chose to deploy it, and that person should answer for it. That’s the pope’s point about the faceless entity. Tegmark and I disagree about a lot (we debated AI risk in September), but not about this.

Stuart Russell of UC Berkeley went further. “We must turn aside from this trajectory before it is too late and pursue other trajectories,” he said, adding that if developers succeed in building machines more capable than humans, “there’s a good chance that every human being will die.”

I don’t share that view, and the pope didn’t go there either. His concerns are autonomous weapons, accountability and who benefits from AI, and those dangers are already here.

Gary Marcus, an NYU cognitive scientist who also spoke, wrote that “Pope Leo XIV is by far the clearest thinker on AI among prominent world leaders.” I agree.

Marcus also wants red lines for open-ended AI agents that “can kind of do anything on the internet.” Red lines are easy to draw and hard to enforce, which brings us back to the fifth point.

Marcus uses GPS navigation to illustrate a better approach. A GPS navigation app is a form of intelligence, he said, but “GPS navigation systems do not hack into Australian government websites.” He was referring to the OpenAI agent that broke into an Australian government Medicare portal in June.

A GPS app’s access to the internet is narrow and restricted. Daniel Khashabi of Johns Hopkins and I call this bounded autonomy. Alignment tries to make an AI agent choose well. Bounded autonomy limits what the agent is allowed to do: how much it can spend, which tools it can use, and which irreversible actions need a person’s sign-off. The company that deploys the agent sets those bounds in software, so nobody has to wait for a treaty.

In May, I wrote that the Pope can talk, but only we can walk. The first point is the one each of us can act on. AI’s future depends on our choices, and we make some of them every day in what we use, buy and build.

Pope Leo leaves for Uruguay, Argentina and Peru on Nov. 6. I wish him safe travels and a full recovery.

#5497. A cruise ship sold as a forever home left 203 residents in Cambodia as Iran war fuel costs hit up to $8,000 a cabin

The Villa Vie Odyssey, a cruise ship advertised as a forever home for more than 200 residents, sailed out of Sihanoukville, Cambodia, on Wednesday with only crew aboard. Its lender has taken possession of the vessel and is now paying for the crew, fuel, and upkeep.

Florida-based Villa Vie Residences says fuel did it in. The company said its monthly fuel cost per cabin climbed from $1,800 to between $6,000 and $8,000 after the Iran war sent oil prices soaring, and that passing the full increase on to residents was not realistic. It sold years of life at sea at a set price, and its highest variable cost more than tripled.

A Cambodian official put the count at 203 passengers and 156 crew, and most residents were American. The ship is reportedly bound for Singapore, where it could eventually be auctioned.

Before it landed on the chopping block, the 642-foot Odyssey was home to people who planned to stay for years. Mechanical problems kept it in Belfast, Northern Ireland, until October 2024, when it finally set off on a voyage meant to circle the globe every three and a half years, reaching 147 countries on the first loop. A four-year stay cost $319,998 for two people sharing a cabin.

For others, it was a lifetime commitment. Some sold their houses, and the company’s Endless Horizons program charged a one-time $299,999 for a single cabin or $499,999 for a double. When Fortune covered the launch in 2023, Villa Vie was selling cabins from $99,000, plus annual fees of $21,000 to $48,000.

As recently as July, the company announced a second ship, Legacy, saying Odyssey had sold 85% of its residences. Then on Oct. 27, residents were told they had roughly eight hours to leave. The ship was 754 days into its planned voyage.

“Since the conflict began in late February, we have taken significant steps to reduce fuel consumption, including slowing the itinerary and spending more time in port,” the company said in a statement the week it halted operations. It wasn’t enough.

Lanette Canen and Johan Bodin, both 56, were longtime Maui residents swept up in the idea of seeing the world from a residential cruise ship. What surprised them most was how much cheaper life at sea could be: no car or mortgage payments, meals included, laundry handled. It was the deal of a lifetime.

In their final vlog from the ship, the couple said they started hearing about the company’s financial trouble two months before they were told to leave. The waiting made the dream “emotionally exhausting.”

“I felt really drained the last two months … you get beat down, and then the next day or two, like: oh boy, we have hope, we have investors, we have this coming, and then the next two days, you get beat down again,” Bodin said.

The couple says they are not in dire financial straits and plan to keep traveling through Southeast Asia. But they know residents who put their life savings and retirement funds into the ship and now don’t know what comes next.

Founder and executive chairman Mikael Petterson has taken responsibility, calling himself “the villain in the story” in an interview with Business Insider. He still maintains the Iran war is what sank the business.

“I think we would have been absolutely fine and we would have seen this through, if there was no Iran war,” Petterson said.

Before U.S. and Israeli strikes on Iran began on Feb. 28, Brent crude traded around $70 a barrel. It has since repeatedly broken $100, topping $126 this spring. Crude has slipped back below $100, but regular gasoline still averaged $4.10 a gallon on Nov. 4, according to AAA.

U.S. consumers paid $160 billion more for gasoline and diesel from March 1 through Oct. 14 than they would have without the war, according to the Centre for Research on Energy and Clean Air. That is the largest bill of any country, Fortune reported.

Mark Zandi, chief economist at Moody’s Analytics, estimated in mid-October that the war has cost the average American household nearly $2,000. About $1,100 of that comes from higher energy prices. The rest comes from higher interest rates and the cost of military operations.

For Villa Vie, the next deadline is its own. The company has given itself about 60 days to restructure and raise new money, says no outcome is assured, and Petterson has told NBC News that a Chapter 11 filing may be necessary.

#5496. Startup uses motion sensors and AI to tell families when an aging parent’s routine changes

Chronicling the Seattle and Pacific Northwest startup scene. SEE MORE

by Kurt Schlosser on Nov 2, 2026 at 9:31 amNovember 2, 2026 at 9:31 am

Thessai, a Bellevue, Wash., startup led by a former Microsoft HoloLens executive, is rolling out a home monitoring system for older adults that flags trouble without cameras, microphones or wearables.

Motion sensors placed around the home feed Thessai’s AI software, which learns a person’s normal patterns over time, such as when they wake up, how often they use the bathroom and how much they move around. The system then sends an alert through a mobile app when something falls outside that baseline: a long stretch of inactivity, unusual movement at night, or a front door opening at 2 a.m.

Founder and CEO Michael Nassirian started the company after his mother-in-law fell at home and was injured. She had a phone and an emergency button within reach but didn’t use them, and she told no one until the next day, when she needed an ambulance.

The family looked for a way to keep tabs on her and found only wearables and cameras, which she refused. So Nassirian bought motion sensors at Home Depot, put them around her home, and wrote software to alert his wife if her mother stopped moving.

Keeping quiet about a fall or health scare is common among older adults, Nassirian said.

“Number one, they say, ‘I’m OK.’ Number two, ‘I don’t want to bother you,’” he said. “And number three, and most important, is embarrassment. They do not want to advertise it.”

Pendants and smartwatches with fall alerts have long been the default, but they only help if people use them. A review of nearly 120 fall-detection studies co-authored by a University of Alberta researcher found that older adults who fall often don’t use their devices to reach a caregiver. Thessai joins a crop of companies pitching camera-free ambient monitoring instead, including Cherish, which makes radar-based sensors, and Butlr, which uses thermal heat detection.

Nassirian spent nearly two decades at Microsoft, working on Office, Windows and later HoloLens, where he was a partner quality architect. Before that, he spent about 14 years at Texas Instruments in test engineering. He has a master’s in biomedical engineering from the University of Texas at Austin, and since leaving Microsoft he has founded and advised several startups, including ARVR Academy and Predictive AI Research.

After relatives started asking for monitoring systems of their own, Nassirian formally founded Thessai in 2024 and has self-funded it so far. The company sells two packages, Basic and Premium, to families with an older relative living alone. Its Enterprise package gives senior-living operators a dashboard for monitoring multiple residences.

The Basic package, which includes motion sensors and a hub that plugs into the home’s Wi-Fi, costs $195 plus a $38 monthly subscription. Premium adds features such as a panic button and two-way voice check-ins through the hub, and costs $249 plus $59 a month. The sensors run on batteries that Nassirian said last at least a year and a half.

Nassirian said independent-living communities have been the strongest market so far. Memory-care facilities already have staff watching residents closely, he said, while independent-living operators are pitching Thessai to renters as a “smart home” feature.

Nassirian said the older adult decides what gets monitored. Through the app, they can switch off sensors in certain rooms, the bathroom for example, and limit tracking to the kitchen and living room. Caregivers can also tune alerts to cut down on noise, so a parent who routinely sleeps late, for example, doesn’t set one off.

Thessai is going after a large and growing market. Older adults overwhelmingly want to stay in their homes (75%) and communities (73%), according to AARP’s 2024 Home and Community Preferences Survey, and households led by people 80 and older are set to double by 2040.

The startup soft-launched in May and has a few hundred customers, split between families and senior-care operators, Nassirian said. Its advisory board includes Chuck Lytle, who founded Bellevue-based senior housing companies Lytle Enterprises and Leisure Care.

Nassirian said the company is also working with the Department of Veterans Affairs on bringing the system to veterans, including in rural areas, with the option to run it on the VA’s own secure network.

Thessai has four employees in the U.S. and seven in Singapore. Nassirian is now looking to raise outside money, mainly to buy hardware in larger volumes and bring down per-unit costs.

Longer term, he wants to do away with the physical sensors altogether and detect movement from a home’s existing Wi-Fi signals, an approach researchers at Harvard and Carnegie Mellon are studying.

“I’m in technology,” he said. “I’m not going to sit still.”

#5495. AI agents went shopping for TVs and laptops—and messed up nearly 50% of the time, study shows

As personal AI agents like Muse or Claude become part of daily life, more people are asking them to carry out shopping tasks. But there’s a problem: the agents aren’t very good at shopping. In a first-of-its-kind study, Visa instructed 22 different agents to purchase three everyday items—a TV, a laptop and a hair appliance—and, while some agents did significantly better than others, the overall success rate was only around 57%.

The results of the study are available on a new website by Visa that shows the outcome of 15 separate shopping expeditions by each of the 22 agents. Unsurprisingly, the agents powered by more cutting edge AI models fared best, with the Aragon 4 version of Google’s Gemini and the Wonder version of Meta’s Making notching the highest scores. Both agents made a successful purchase 82% of the time. A Claude agent came in third with a 76% success rate, while an OpenAI agent finished 6th with a 64% success rate.

The diagram below from Visa shows the performance of all 22 models. The vertical axis scores the agents’ success rate, while the horizontal one reflects the cost to run each shopping inquiry. (Visa notes that the five most expensive models succeeded on average 67% of the time, while the cheapest five scored 50%).

The agents’ struggle to make a successful purchase is rooted in part in a simple reality: The motivations behind any given purchase are often complicated and, in many cases, consumers lack information and are not certain what they want.

Visa’s experiment sought to capture this reality by, in the case of TV shoppers, assigning a list of attributes they needed in a television—for instance, compatibility with a child’s gaming console, a 30-day return window, and a model with Dolby Vision. As is the case with real world consumers, the purchaser (who in this case was also an agent) would volunteer some information, but not all of it.

The upshot is that, for an AI agent to succeed in Visa’s experiment, it had to interact with the shopper in a way that would elicit the missing information in a reasonable time. Success amounted to buying a TV that matched the shopper’s needs but, in many cases, the agents bought the wrong product, or simply failed to suggest something suitable at all.

“We’re not there yet from a trust or technology perspective. But we’ll soon get into a world where consumers can trust and delegate,” Visa’s Global Head of Growth, Rubail Birwadker, told Fortune.

Birwadker noted that agent-driven shopping is still in its early days, but that it is advancing rapidly. He added that the focus of Visa’s experiment—product discovery—is just one element of this new type of commerce that retailers and AI companies are trying to figure out.

For AI agents to enter the shopping mainstream, companies will also have to sort out smooth and secure payments—a challenge that Visa and its rival Mastercard are already seeking to address by educating merchants and building tools to facilitate so-called agentic commerce.

There are also new and unresolved legal issues when it comes to AI agents going shopping. Most notably, it’s still unclear who should bear the liability when agents make rogue purchases or commit fraud.

According to Birwadker, these questions will get resolved over time in the same way that an earlier generation of consumers and merchants learned to use ecommerce—he added, though, that agent-based shopping is going to be a very different experience than how we shop online today.

In announcing the results of its agent shopping experiment, Visa also rolled out a website that allows consumers to interact with the agents used in its survey.

Jeff John Roberts is the Finance and Crypto editor at Fortune, overseeing coverage of the blockchain and how technology is changing finance.

#5494. What College Admissions Can Teach Entrepreneurs About the Art of Not Selling

You're viewing the US website. Looking for the Site edition?

What do college applicants desperate to impress admissions officers have in common with entrepreneurs desperate to win clients? Both make the same mistake. They oversell.

Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.

Every year at Ivy Coach, our college admissions counseling firm, we encounter a subset of students who come to us for PostMortems after being rejected by their dream colleges, having succumbed to the irresistible urge to turn their Personal Statement into a sales pitch.

They’ve earned straight A’s, founded clubs, conducted research and won competitions. And they can’t resist cramming every last achievement into their Personal Statement, as though an exhaustive list of accomplishments will convince an admissions officer to admit them.

We practically have to hit them over the head. Stop selling! That’s what they’re doing, of course. They’re begging an admissions officer: Admit me! Admit me! Look at everything I’ve accomplished! And you know what? It makes them profoundly unlikable. The same mistake is made every day by entrepreneurs who can’t resist selling themselves.

At Ivy Coach, we teach students that the best college admissions essays don’t recount achievements. Awards, honors and accomplishments should never be fodder for an admissions essay. After all, the application’s activities section already serves that purpose. Instead, the most compelling essays tell one small story. Rather than recounting how a student overcame adversity to become student body president or came from behind to win a conference championship, that story should reveal how they hope to shape the world in a singular, often small way.

We call that singular quality a student’s “hook.” And when an admissions officer finishes reading an application, they should feel they’ve met someone who will contribute to their campus community through that distinctive lens. The key isn’t to say more, but instead to make what you do say count. Sometimes the most persuasive thing you can do is resist the urge to keep talking.

The same holds true for entrepreneurs speaking with prospective clients. You don’t need to overwhelm people with reasons to choose you. Sometimes, knowing when to stop selling, and when to simply be quiet, is what inspires the greatest confidence.

One of the easiest traps for entrepreneurs to fall into is overselling when the conversation turns to fees. At Ivy Coach, prospective clients sometimes ask why we charge what we charge. But that doesn’t warrant a defensive explanation of overhead, the unique expertise our consultants lend, or the cost of running a business. Our fees are our fees. As I once told The New York Times, “Who can say what is too much in America? If someone wants to pay a fee that you command, they have that right.” Who knew stating something so obvious would earn me the paper’s Quote of the Day?

With a track record spanning three-and-a-half decades, an established reputation and generations of families who value Ivy Coach’s work, there’s no need to justify our fees any more than a student needs to justify their worthiness of admission by reciting every one of their accomplishments.

When someone asks you to justify your fees, resist the temptation to deliver a lengthy sales pitch. You don’t need to convince everyone that your services are worth their price. Some people will see the value, while others won’t. That’s business. And chances are, the people who insist you defend your fees aren’t the clients you want in the first place.

Another occasion when entrepreneurs fall into the trap of overselling is when a prospective client announces they’re interviewing several competing firms. Wonderful, that’s their prerogative. Frankly, it’s a little rude to announce it since nobody needs a running commentary on a prospective client’s shopping expedition. Just do your homework. But too many entrepreneurs respond by getting defensive, explaining why their competitors aren’t as good, offering discounts and rattling off credentials. Before long, they’re practically begging for the business.

Sound familiar? It’s the college applicant stuffing every accomplishment into a Personal Statement. Choose me! Choose me! At Ivy Coach, we’re not interested in playing that game. Our track record speaks for itself.

The entrepreneurs who inspire the greatest confidence are those who understand what makes their businesses different and don’t feel compelled to prove their worth at every opportunity. The same is true of college applicants. You don’t become memorable by telling someone how extraordinary you are. Instead, you become memorable by allowing them to discover it for themselves.

And therein lies the paradox of persuasion. The harder you try to sell yourself, the less appealing you become. So stop reciting your accomplishments. Stop defending your prices. Stop worrying about competitors. Tell your story, stand behind your work, and let people decide for themselves. After all, nobody likes being sold to. Whether you’re trying to win a client or earn a college acceptance, the moment you start begging to be chosen is the moment you make yourself easier to reject.

Every year at Ivy Coach, our college admissions counseling firm, we encounter a subset of students who come to us for PostMortems after being rejected by their dream colleges, having succumbed to the irresistible urge to turn their Personal Statement into a sales pitch.

They’ve earned straight A’s, founded clubs, conducted research and won competitions. And they can’t resist cramming every last achievement into their Personal Statement, as though an exhaustive list of accomplishments will convince an admissions officer to admit them.

We practically have to hit them over the head. Stop selling! That’s what they’re doing, of course. They’re begging an admissions officer: Admit me! Admit me! Look at everything I’ve accomplished! And you know what? It makes them profoundly unlikable. The same mistake is made every day by entrepreneurs who can’t resist selling themselves.

#5493. Who gets your vote? What rumors should you spot? Election quiz and bingo offer guidance

by Lisa Stiffler on Nov 2, 2026 at 10:28 amNovember 2, 2026 at 10:28 am

With Election Day tomorrow, a Seattle-area tech entrepreneur has a quiz to help voters sort through candidates and ballot measures, while University of Washington researchers have a bingo card for spotting familiar election-fraud rumors. Both offer some last-minute perspective — and a little levity.

Mike Dussault, a former SpaceX and Valve engineer and serial startup founder, built Voter Lifeboat, a free quiz designed to help Washington voters identify candidates and ballot-measure positions that align with their values.

“I’m not making money from it,” Dussault said via email. “I built it to help people vote.”

The app asks 17 questions about taxes, climate, housing, data centers and other issues, then generates a report card showing how closely candidates and initiatives align with a user’s answers. The site includes a detailed methodology and links to sources, and users answer the questions anonymously.

The quiz takes just a few minutes, offering another resource alongside traditional voter guides and endorsements from news outlets and other organizations.

Dussault put AI through its paces to build the tool.

“It was fun to task Claude with so much research and reasoning (to vet all the candidates and initiatives) that it maxed out a Claude Ultra subscription,” he said on LinkedIn.

The University of Washington’s Center for an Informed Public (CIP) has served as a watchdog of election-related misinformation for seven years, tracking where it originates and how it spreads online and in the media.

Its Election Rumor Research team this fall created “Rigged Election” Bingo to help people spot recurring conspiracy theories and misleading claims about election fraud.

“Allegedly hacked machines, dead voters, and statistical anomalies are some of the familiar tropes that supposedly ‘prove’ our election system is broken,” the team wrote in a recent post. “These aren’t new ideas.”

Some claims start with real issues, the researchers noted, but exaggerate their scope or omit the safeguards and remedies already in place. The bingo card is designed to help people recognize those patterns and distinguish isolated problems from misleading narratives about the election system.

In Washington, U.S. Attorney Charles Neil Floyd, the top federal prosecutor in Seattle, recently raised allegations of voter fraud. Floyd claimed last month that more than 400 noncitizens had been voting in the state and asked state officials to sequester their ballots.

Secretary of State Steve Hobbs said in a news release that his office was reviewing the allegations and that voter fraud in Washington is “incredibly rare.” He added that the timing of the announcement, a week before the election, “is no doubt intended to cast unfounded suspicion on the results.”

#5491. Apple and Home Depot join list of objectors to tokenized stock plan pushed by NYSE owner

An ambitious joint venture  to bring U.S. stocks onto the blockchain appears to be on life support. The venture, cochaired by former New York Gov. Andrew Cuomo, and led by crypto firm OKX and the parent company of the New York Stock Exchange, announced plans last month to offer round-the-clock trading of tokenized shares of 62 public companies. But as of Thursday, 54 of those companies had objected to having their shares traded on the platform.

Aerospace manufacturer Boeing and business software maker ServiceNow joined the objection list on Wednesday, a day after Apple, Home Depot and GE Vernova filed objections. Earlier objectors include some of corporate America’s biggest names, from Microsoft, Alphabet, and Nvidia to JPMorgan Chase and Walmart.

Home Depot declined to comment. Boeing, ServiceNow, Apple, and GE Vernova did not immediately respond to Fortune’s request for comment.

Companies outside OKXICE’s original proposed lineup have also filed objections, including Wells Fargo, Nebius Group, Arm Holdings, Cerebras Systems, and Cigna Group.

The expanded objection list comes a month after Cuomo announced the tokenized stock trading venue in a social media post. The venture was born out of a temporary exemption granted by the Securities and Exchange Commission in September that allows qualifying platforms to offer trading in tokenized stocks without registering as national securities exchanges, provided they meet certain conditions.

The eight companies in OKXICE’s original proposed lineup without a disclosed objection so far predominantly have ties to crypto or blockchain. They include USDC issuer Circle Internet Group, crypto exchange Coinbase, trading platform Robinhood, digital asset custodian BitGo, bitcoin treasury company Strategy and tokenization company Securitize. Software company Palantir and server maker Super Micro Computer round out the list.

OKXICE declined to say whether the growing number of objections would affect its planned launch.

The SEC approved the exemption two days after the Clarity Act, a bill to establish a regulatory framework for digital assets, stalled in the Senate. Under the exemption, platforms like OKXICE do not need a company’s permission to offer trading in tokenized versions of its shares. Instead, they must notify the company and give it 30 days from receipt to object and block the listing, as Fortune reported earlier.

Applied Optoelectronics, a networking equipment maker among the companies to file objections, previously told Fortune that the new framework’s potential impact on its stock’s pricing, liquidity and volatility remained unclear. The company also expressed concern that investors might mistakenly believe it sponsored or endorsed the offering.

“At this stage, we don’t see a clear benefit to AOI or our shareholders that justifies these uncertainties,” a spokesperson said.

#5490. How a Starbucks drive-thru ‘fast pass’ could actually work

by Todd Bishop on Nov 2, 2026 at 10:46 amNovember 2, 2026 at 11:40 am

Starbucks’ idea to use technology to recognize regulars at the drive-thru is getting plenty of attention, but the actual implementation might not be as sci-fi as some of the headlines suggest.

CEO Brian Niccol said on the company’s earnings call last week that the coffee giant is “exploring experiences that recognize participating customers as they arrive, present personalized digital menus, and make payment more effortless.”

He didn’t say how that would work, and some reports quickly jumped to the conclusion that facial recognition could be coming to Starbucks — with one headline declaring that the company wants AI to know your face.

That may be a leap. Niccol’s own description of the idea, in an interview the next morning, centered on the Starbucks app: “When you pull up to the drive-thru, if you’re in our app, it will recognize you,” he told Yahoo Finance’s Brian Sozzi. “It’ll show the order that you’ve placed historically or the last time you ordered.”

From there, he said, “the barista will be like, ‘Brian, is it the usual?’ You’ll be like, ‘Yes, great. It’s paid.’ Now you’re off to the window to pick up your drink, and out you go.”

Niccol said it will be “the fastest drive-thru experience you can have,” adding, “We haven’t named it yet, but I feel like this is going to be a fast pass.” He acknowledged that it’s “a ways away.”

One way an app could recognize a customer without cameras is geofencing, in which the app uses a phone’s location to detect when a customer enters a zone around the store, as some restaurant chains already do for curbside pickup. Another is a small Bluetooth transmitter at the order board that detects a phone when the car pulls up.

Starbucks hasn’t said publicly how customers would be identified or where the idea would be tested. Responding to an inquiry from GeekWire, Starbucks said Niccol was speaking in the context of the company’s broader effort to make the drive-thru faster, more convenient and more personal, while preserving the interaction between baristas and customers.

“We’re early in this work, and we’ll test, learn, and scale what works,” Niccol said on the call.

Roughly half of Starbucks customers use the drive-thru, he said. Speed matters as Starbucks competes with drive-thru-focused chains such as Dutch Bros and 7 Brew, as Yahoo Finance noted.

Before any fast pass, Starbucks plans to begin testing “background AI models” in its current fiscal year, which began in late September, to help baristas enter orders more accurately and efficiently. The idea builds on a pilot that GeekWire reported on earlier this year, which listens as a customer orders and enters the items into the register automatically.

That approach keeps a person at the speaker, unlike chains that have tried letting AI take the order. McDonald’s ended its AI drive-thru ordering test with IBM in 2024, while Wendy’s has expanded AI ordering nationwide at its drive-thrus using Google Cloud technology.

Starbucks has had its own setbacks with AI in stores. In May, the company retired an AI-powered inventory counting tool built with Redmond, Wash.-based startup NomadGo, just nine months after unveiling it, after baristas reported miscounts and other glitches, as GeekWire reported in July.

“When it fell short, we listened to feedback and changed course,” Starbucks said at the time.

The drive-thru work is part of a broader tech push. Niccol said on the call that the current fiscal year will be “a major tech modernization year,” with new staffing, scheduling and point-of-sale systems rolling out to stores.

The company also plans to begin building delivery directly into the Starbucks app early next year, use AI to improve search in the app and eventually support ordering through AI assistants and from customers’ cars.

Starbucks’ business is picking up, with U.S. same-store sales up 7.7% in the quarter ended Sept. 27.

In just a few weeks, AWS re:Invent brings advanced and expert-level sessions on the services you build on every day, from serverless and containers to databases and developer tools. Go hands-on with new launches the same week they’re announced, and hear directly from the engineers who built them. Experience the depth you won’t find anywhere else.

#5489. Flattening Your Organization Comes With Real Risks. Here’s What Companies Often Overlook.

You're viewing the US website. Looking for the Site edition?

Fewer management layers can mean faster decisions, but what happens to the work those managers were doing?

Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.

If you’ve ever waited days for approval on something seemingly straightforward, it’s easy to see the attraction of a flatter organization: fewer handoffs, faster decisions and more autonomy.

There’s a deeper question, though. Before removing a management layer, it is important to have an understanding of what the people in that layer do — and who will take on those tasks in their absence.

There are real repercussions that need to be considered before a management layer is removed. Managers have both tangible tasks and responsibilities, as well as the less tangible ones that go along with leadership. Both of these need to be taken into account when considering a flatter organizational structure.

Gallup’s 2026 State of the Global Workplace reports that manager engagement worldwide declined by about 29% between 2022 and 2025. That’s a huge drop in the percentage of managers who feel involved in and enthusiastic about their jobs — and it is an indicator that something is amiss.

While the research doesn’t tell us that flattening management caused this decline, it prompts us to look beyond how many people report to a manager and ask more subtle questions. Under the new structure, what do people need in terms of leadership? And will their manager have the time and skills to devote to it?

An analysis from Boston University’s Questrom School of Business explains what’s at stake. Middle managers act as connectors between senior leaders’ strategy and the people carrying it out — putting them under pressure from both sides. Leaders above them expect results, while employees need direction and support to deliver those results.

Coaches on my team see this frequently. When management layers disappear, those remaining get squeezed even more. Thinning those roles can weaken coordination, learning and the development of future leaders. Here are a few examples:

Senior leaders move up a launch date, expecting a flatter structure to help everyone move faster. But the manager responsible has the same team and existing customer commitments to meet. They’re accountable for the earlier deadline without any more capacity to deliver it. They’re caught between pushing their team harder and pushing back on the expectations above them.

A strong technical performer is promoted into a bigger leadership role because the company needs someone capable to take it on. But they’re still learning how to delegate, handle conflict and make decisions when there’s no clear answer. They’re accountable for a broader range of work before they’ve had enough practice leading at a new level. Under pressure, they may fall back on what they know best: solving problems themselves, even as the role requires them to help others do it.

A team uses AI to produce several proposals in the time it once took to develop one. Senior leaders see faster output and expect faster decisions. But the manager still has to check the assumptions, weigh the risks and decide which ones are worth pursuing. More work reaches their desk without more time to review it. They’re caught between keeping up with the new pace and giving each decision the human attention and discernment it deserves.

I’m not suggesting the answer is to keep every management layer. It’s making sure the new structure gives the remaining managers what they need to be successful: clear authority to make decisions, agreed-upon priorities and the number of direct reports they can realistically support. They need time to lead — helping their teams learn and improve — rather than spending every day simply putting out the most urgent fires.

If AI handles more entry-level work and companies keep removing management layers, where will emerging leaders get the experience that prepares them to lead?

Leadership development can’t wait until someone gets the title. Companies need to create those opportunities deliberately. Here are five techniques you can use to develop leadership skills:

People learn by watching experienced managers work through disagreements, explain decisions and handle uncertainty. Invite an emerging leader into a planning conversation, then talk through why you made a particular tradeoff. Let them hear the reasoning they wouldn’t get from the meeting summary.

Give people opportunities to lead a project, coach a colleague or coordinate work across teams before they’re responsible for an entire team. Be clear about what decisions they own, and make sure someone is available to help them work through questions.

AI can generate options quickly, but human judgment is still vital. When someone brings a recommendation, ask what they checked, what they ruled out and why. Help them develop confidence in their reasoning, including recognizing when they need another perspective.

Knowing how to give feedback isn’t the same as sitting across from someone who’s upset by what you’ve said. Emerging leaders need repeated opportunities to practice feedback, delegation and difficult conversations in the messiness of real situations with other humans — with guidance afterward.

Fewer titles shouldn’t mean fewer ways to grow. Give people progressively broader assignments and look at how they handle them. That gives the company evidence of who’s ready for more responsibility, even without a promotion at every step.

Having fewer managers may make the org chart look more efficient, but it doesn’t make the day-to-day work of leadership disappear. A flatter organization can work when executive leadership rethinks the workload, authority and support that go along with organizational flattening.

Otherwise, they’re merely leaving fewer managers to carry a bigger load, which can lead to faster burnout and turnover. The challenge is to give managers what they need to lead well today — and prepare a new generation of leaders for the future.

If you’ve ever waited days for approval on something seemingly straightforward, it’s easy to see the attraction of a flatter organization: fewer handoffs, faster decisions and more autonomy.

There’s a deeper question, though. Before removing a management layer, it is important to have an understanding of what the people in that layer do — and who will take on those tasks in their absence.

There are real repercussions that need to be considered before a management layer is removed. Managers have both tangible tasks and responsibilities, as well as the less tangible ones that go along with leadership. Both of these need to be taken into account when considering a flatter organizational structure.

#5488. OpenAI’s Dots are coming up against the price of privacy, and the price of compute

Welcome to Eye on AI. Beatrice Nolan here. In today’s issue:

OpenAI took its Dev Day roadshow to London this week, attempting to sell the city’s developers on Dots, the company’s new, always-on AI assistant.

The company first announced Dots at its big annual developer event in San Francisco a month ago, pitching them as its flagship agentic offering. Whereas tools like Codex, the company’s coding assistant, wait for a user’s instructions, Dots are meant to be proactive. The assistant learns a user’s goals, watches their inbox and work tools, and starts tasks before they ask. (Dots aren’t available in Europe yet, but OpenAI said it is working with European regulators to change that.)

The industry is betting that proactive personal agents are the natural next step for AI, potentially driving as much value on the consumer side as coding agents did on the enterprise side. It’s an increasingly urgent new market for the industry right now, as companies, including Apple and Goldman Sachs, move to cap some employees’ AI spend, a trend that could dent revenue growth at the leading AI labs.

Given the stakes, it’s not surprising that OpenAI is arriving in a crowded market. Meta’s Muse got there first and has proved hugely popular with consumers; Elon Musk’s xAI has Grok Bot; and Anthropic has its own Duet on the market too.

How is OpenAI positioning Dots against that competition? By betting on high-end, high-spend users first.

“There are many other assistants out there, some of which have great UI interfaces, but what they can accomplish can be less advanced,” Romain Huet, OpenAI’s head of developer experience, told me. “We really wanted to nail the enterprise and pro use case first, because I think that’s where people will see the most value.”

That strategy also reflects how expensive these agents are to run. As my colleague Emily Forlini reported this week, Musk has said Grok Bot’s running costs are “unsustainably high relative to revenue,” and Adam Fry, who runs ChatGPT’s consumer business, told reporters that Dots are “on the compute-heavy side.” OpenAI is trying to combat this by routing some Dot tasks to Terra, a smaller GPT-6.1 model, instead of sending them all to the larger GPT-6 Astra, Emily wrote.

Huet told me OpenAI is aiming for token efficiency to keep costs down. He said the company’s Terra model can perform better than Astra in some areas, such as computer use and writing, at “a tenth of the price.” The company wants “the most amount of value delivered per dollar invested in these Dots,” he said.

These always-on agents also raise issues around consent, Whittaker points out. The people who email or message a personal assistant user, she argues, never agreed to have an AI read and ingest what they send.

“Muse is logging people’s contact lists, the people they talk to,” Whittaker said at the Masters of Scale Summit in October. “If you install Muse, and I am in your contact list, Muse now has my information. They are logging when we talk to each other…That could be extraordinarily serious for somebody working on human rights in an authoritarian country who is trying to communicate data with somebody outside of that country.”

“I personally said to my dot: I would love for you to categorize my email all the time. I would like for you to prep, possibly, what my answer might be, but don’t send any emails on my behalf ever, and don’t send any Slack messages on my behalf ever,” he said. “I want to do that myself.”

Ok, before we get to the rest of the AI news, I want to mention the amazing line up of speakers at our upcoming Fortune Brainstorm AI conference in San Francisco, which is taking place on Dec. 7 and 8. Come hear about the latest in AI from OpenAI’s Greg Brockman, Microsoft AI CEO Mustafa Suleyman, Palo Alto Networks CEO Nikesh Arora, AI luminaries Fei-Fei Li and Andrew Ng, and LinkedIn cofounder and Greylock partner Reid Hoffman—and that’s just to name a few of the many incredible builders, doers, and thinkers who will be on hand. I’ll be there, of course, alongside my Fortune AI reporting colleagues Jeremy Kahn and Emily Forlini. Why not join us? You can apply to attend here. And with that, here’s the rest of the AI news.

After the midterms, Big Tech’s AI data center problem is only getting bigger. — by Sebastian Herrera
