#5415. Readwise takes on Amazon’s Kindle and Goodreads with its new app for book lovers

Buy One Founder Summit Ticket, Get a Second for Free. Register now.

Founder Summit begins Nov. 4, 9:00 a.m. ET. Get your pass savings & deals before it starts. REGISTER HERE.

Readwise, the maker of a read-it-later app and digital reading companion that keeps track of your highlights across services, is now taking on Amazon’s e-book empire with its latest app, Readwise Books. The app is an e-book store and helps you track what you’ve read, similar to Amazon’s Goodreads.

The bootstrapped startup described the new app as “a cross between Kindle and the Goodreads apps,” as it offers a single place to buy, read, and track books. However, Readwise Books aims to offer more detailed reading stats than the dates you read a book and whether you finished it. It lets readers visualize richer reading data like words read, pace, depth, immersion, and sessions.

Meanwhile, its new store offers “millions” of e-books from the big five publishers and others, initially in the U.S., with more countries to come. Print books (fulfilled by Bookshop.org’s distributor) and some audiobooks are available as well, the company notes.

The launch comes at a time when there’s been an explosion of new reading apps and book trackers, all hoping to challenge Goodreads by introducing new features like book clubs, widgets, improved discovery features, goal-setting, better lists and organizational tools, habit-tracking, and more. However, few indie developers have gone so far as to launch an alternative to Amazon’s Kindle e-books store, which remains the industry leader, with an 83% share of the market when Kindle+ (formerly Kindle Unlimited) is included in the stats.

One of Kindle’s bigger advantages is that it offers an end-to-end solution for everything related to reading e-books, from the hardware devices to the book-tracking log. Readwise isn’t selling its own e-readers, but it is attempting to create its own community around reading, complete with tools for reading purchased and uploaded e-books, tracking them (like on Goodreads), sharing your reading progress with friends, and more.

It also offers a number of ways to track books outside its ecosystem. This includes a way to track reading sessions by using Kindle’s browser-based Cloud Reader and a feature that lets you snap photos of physical books to mark your progress. Plus, you can upload any DRM-free EPUBs (a common e-book file format without copy protection). The app can read your e-books aloud via text-to-speech.

Readwise believes its more in-depth metrics could be a big selling point, too, likening them to a “Strava for reading” — a reference to the metrics-heavy exercise app.

“The desire to read books, like exercising and eating well, is laden with guilt,” the company explained in a blog post penned by co-founders Daniel Doyon and Tristan Homsi. “Many people feel like they should be reading more, but feeling bad about it tends to change nothing. The session tracking taps into a different psychological mechanism. It makes the reading you’re doing legible and, as the adage goes, that which is measured is improved.”

The company adds that the most consistent feedback from users is that the app has led them to read more without willpower tricks like goal-setting, streaks, or scheduling.

With publishers’ permission, the app will support AI-powered features as well, like session recaps, definitions and term lookups, word and phrase translations, and a location-aware ability to ask questions about the part you’re reading. (So far, only HarperCollins has opted in, though.)

Unlike Goodreads’ locked-down ecosystem, Readwise is embracing open technology. This includes a public API and an MCP server. The latter supports AI agents that could be used to research book recommendations on your behalf, use your Readwise data to create a books page on your personal website, or even wire up your hackable e-reader to log your sessions automatically, depending on how involved your AI use cases may be.

The new Readwise Books app will remain free, with some AI features later going behind a paywall. Its prior apps for reading and tracking highlights are either $7.99 per month each or $9.99 per month for both.

Polygon is approaching a critical price level as a proposed crypto hard fork puts the network back trending. POL recently recovered toward $0.10, while Binance and Polymarket are seeking to recover millions in stolen tokens through a controversial governance proposal.

The plan could strengthen confidence in Polygon’s ability to protect users, but it also raises questions about decentralization. Can the recovery effort help POL extend its rebound or trigger another round of selling?

Polygon Labs Member Proposes Hard Fork to Recover Approximately 70.49 Million POL Stolen from Polymarket and BinanceA member of the Polygon Labs Validator Support Team has published a Polygon Improvement Proposal (PIP) suggesting a hard fork on the Polygon PoS mainnet to… pic.twitter.com/n8hoCCsYms

The proposed hard fork would zero the balances of four addresses linked to the Polymarket incident and one tied to Binance. Polymarket accounts for 23.86 million POL, while Binance’s address holds 46.63 million POL. The proposal would credit the equivalent balances to recovery wallets verified by the affected platforms.

Polygon block producers have already restricted transfers from the identified addresses. However, the current blacklist prevents movement without returning the assets to their owners.

The proposal would make the recovery permanent through a coordinated network upgrade. It would not create new POL or alter the token’s total supply. Governance discussion is scheduled for today. Approval would still require client development, testing on Polygon’s Amoy testnet, and coordination with validators.

The proposal describes the intervention as an exceptional measure tied to publicly acknowledged thefts and traceable funds. It warns that the action should not become a routine mechanism for reversing transactions.

#5413. Trajectory raises $45M to make AI model training accessible to nontechnical experts

Buy One Founder Summit Ticket, Get a Second for Free. Register now.

Founder Summit begins Nov. 4, 9:00 a.m. ET. Get your pass savings & deals before it starts. REGISTER HERE.

Whether developed by OpenAI or Anthropic or built on open source alternatives, current AI models share a critical limitation: They don’t learn from their mistakes without further training.

Businesses adapting these models for specialized fields, such as law and finance, typically get around this by fine-tuning general models. However, that often requires hiring internal research teams or relying on expensive consultants, commonly known as forward-deployed engineers (FDEs).

Trajectory, a startup founded about a year ago by three Stanford classmates with experience at Google DeepMind and Apple, wants to automate that process, allowing AI models to learn from feedback and continuously improve at specialized tasks.

The 18-person company just announced that it raised $45 million in a Series A round at a $300 million valuation, led by Sequoia, with participation from Nvidia, Bessemer Venture Partners, and Bain Capital Ventures.

Trajectory co-founder Ronak Malde compared foundational models to a very smart PhD student who’s always starting a new job. “But what the economy values is someone who worked on the job for 30 years,” he told TechCrunch.

The startup aims to solve this problem through an approach known as continual learning. Businesses using Trajectory can start with an open source AI model and connect the platform to their applications, allowing it to collect feedback on how the model performs. Trajectory then uses that information to retrain the model, helping it improve at specialized tasks over time.

With Trajectory, lawyers, doctors, and other specialists can improve the models near automatically themselves, Malde said. That capability could make deploying specialized AI faster and cheaper.

Companies like Harvey and Rogo are already using Trajectory’s platform to post-train open source models, helping them perform more like experienced lawyers or financial analysts by learning from previous tasks, such as reviewing a particular type of legal contract or valuing a company using a specific methodology. Trajectory’s other customers include Decagon, Mercor, and Nvidia. The startup is now making its post-training platform publicly available.

The people using Trajectory decide “what good looks like for their organization and can turn that into improvements for their model,” Malde said.

Trajectory’s approach to continual learning shares some similarities with recursive self-improvement (RSI), the idea that AI systems can improve their own capabilities. But co-founder Michael Elabd argues that keeping humans involved in the training process makes Trajectory’s approach safer, since autonomous self-improvement could lead to unintended or even dangerous outcomes.

Trajectory isn’t the only startup trying to automate post-training. Other companies going after this market include Thinking Machines Lab, founded by former OpenAI CTO Mira Murati and the company behind the fine-tuning platform Tinker, Applied Compute, which was valued at $3.25 billion last month, and Prime Intellect, a platform that helps companies build and train their own AI agents.

Malde believes the startup’s biggest advantage is its team. He was among the handful of researchers Google DeepMind acqui-hired from Windsurf. Elabd also worked at DeepMind, while Trajectory’s third co-founder, Arjun Karanam, previously worked on generative foundation models at Apple. The startup has also recruited researchers and product designers from OpenAI, Stripe, and Netflix.

Why does design matter so much to a company focused on AI training? Karanam says the startup has developed an interface that makes post-training more accessible to its nontechnical customers.

#5412. “I’m Still Very, Very Bullish”: Charles Hoskinson Predicts Bitcoin Will Hit $250,000 in 24 Months

Cardano (ADA) founder Charles Hoskinson has predicted that Bitcoin (BTC) will reach $250,000 within 24 months, maintaining a bullish outlook despite ongoing questions about cryptocurrency adoption and market volatility.

Speaking during a fireside chat with Ana Tutova, founder of AI Crypto Minds, at TOKEN2049 in Singapore, Hoskinson said he expects the crypto asset to climb substantially over the coming two years. He also argued that artificial intelligence could create new demand for cryptocurrencies as autonomous agents increasingly conduct economic activity.

“Yeah, I’m still very very bullish. You know, the next 24 months that Bitcoin will reach $250,000,” Hoskinson stated.

His forecast comes as Bitcoin faces questions about its near-term direction, with traders watching key price levels for signs of a recovery or a deeper correction.

Beyond Bitcoin’s price outlook, Hoskinson pointed to the growing relationship between artificial intelligence and blockchain technology as a potential source of demand across the crypto market. He argued that AI agents will need digital assets to transact, pay for services and participate in online marketplaces. Cryptocurrencies, particularly stablecoins, could provide the financial infrastructure for these activities.

“For agents to have agency and for agents to have economic identity has to be crypto,” he said.

Hoskinson believes AI-driven commerce could expand the practical uses of blockchain networks beyond speculative trading. He also suggested that combining crypto with AI could significantly increase transaction volumes across several digital assets.

“If we can get AI into crypto in just the right way, uh it’ll 10x or 100x the volume of a lot of these cryptocurrencies, and it’s going to be very good for our prices,” he said.

The Cardano founder added that the industry needs to prioritize real-world applications rather than relying primarily on price speculation.

“We have to move beyond speculation to utility,” he stated, identifying AI and real-world asset tokenization as areas with potential to deliver more practical blockchain use cases.

Despite his optimism, Hoskinson acknowledged that cryptocurrencies have yet to become part of everyday life for most consumers. He said the industry has made considerable progress in user numbers and market value, but the experience of using digital assets remains too complicated for widespread adoption.

Meanwhile, market indicators offer mixed signals about Bitcoin’s near-term trajectory. Santiment reported Tuesday that Bitcoin had lost approximately 30,000 non-empty wallets since October 16, bringing the total to around 59.95 million. The analytics platform suggested that smaller holders may be exiting after an extended period of stagnant price action, potentially creating conditions for a local market bottom.

The firm further identified $80,000 as a key level, with a recovery above roughly $82,500 strengthening its potential bottom scenario.

“Retail capitulation has historically been more constructive for price than a sudden flood of new buyers chasing rallies. Crypto typically moves opposite crowd expectations at emotional extremes, so shrinking participation while BTC struggles near $80K strengthens the case that a local bottom may be forming shortly.” It wrote.

CryptoQuant analyst ‘Trader Gemini’ also identified Bitcoin’s Trader Realized Price, then in the mid-$70,000 range, as a level to watch if prices fall. The metric reflects the average acquisition price of Bitcoin last moved between one and three months earlier. However, the analyst cautioned that the level is not a guaranteed floor, although it has historically acted as support during some bullish periods.

At press time, Bitcoin was trading at $80,550, reflecting a 4.14% surge in the past 24 hours.

#5411. Y Combinator’s Garry Tan uses AI agents so much, he spends up to $200K a year on tokens

Buy One Founder Summit Ticket, Get a Second for Free. Register now.

Founder Summit begins Nov. 4, 9:00 a.m. ET. Get your pass savings & deals before it starts. REGISTER HERE.

Y Combinator CEO Garry Tan has, in the past, jokingly admitted that he’s suffered from “cyber psychosis” and sometimes barely sleeps because he’s so excited to be working with his AI agents. On a new episode of Walter Isaacson’s podcast The Builders, set to publish on Tuesday, Tan put a price tag on his passion.

“I spend about maybe $100[,000] to $200,000 a year on tokens,” he told Isaacson. He uses agents for countless work projects and coding tasks and has freely shared his set of 23 Claude Code skills, called gstack, on GitHub — an effort to help teach others what agents can do, he said.

On the one hand, he uses his agent the way many people use AI: to help him research Isaacson’s podcast and prep for the kinds of questions he might be asked. On the other, his agent also helps him run his life.

“It’s read all of my email and all of my Dropbox. It’s read, like, all of my Apple Notes, even my therapy notes going back 20 years,” he said.

He describes using AI agents as getting help with “almost anything that you do in your day-to-day life, and for it to do it somewhat more autonomously. Think of it as a Jiminy Cricket on your shoulder at all times. Like, almost anything you want to do, it knows you, and it’s there to help. And it will actually sort of run ahead and say, ‘What about this?’ Or it’ll help you see around corners.”

As an early OpenClaw adopter who is now a power user, Tan says one thing he’s learned is not to treat AI agents like traditional software. Some people are so worried about “repeatability and safety that they actually trade off all of the beautiful parts of working with an AI agent, which basically can be so similar to a human,” he said.

For instance, Y Combinator is also using an agent that is “rebuilding the way we operate at YC,” he said. “We now have an internal AI agent, for instance, named Stray Light that kind of has a personality, and then it has a company brain. Like it actually has the total context of every founder we’ve ever backed, anyone who’s ever emailed us, like all the applications.”

Tan, who is, naturally, an avid lover of technology (as anyone running Silicon Valley’s famed startup accelerator would be), believes personal AI agents will eventually become mainstream, if one major problem is solved: Costs have got to come down.

“It’s too expensive right now,” he said, adding that he knows the amount of money he spends on AI agents is “a crazy privilege that not everyone can do.”

But freebie agents controlled by Big Tech maybe aren’t the answer, either. When discussing the future he’d like tech to build, and how Meta as a social media company has impacted us, he said, “This is a huge company that controls the algorithm, and we all wish that they didn’t at some level,” he said. “So you could imagine a personal AI that you control, that you program.”

#5410. Ukraine’s new pocket-sized gadget turns Russian drones’ cameras against them

Buy One Founder Summit Ticket, Get a Second for Free. Register now.

Founder Summit begins Nov. 4, 9:00 a.m. ET. Get your pass savings & deals before it starts. REGISTER HERE.

Ukrainian drone teams have a new way to spy on the drones that spy on them. A Kyiv equipment startup called CODE380 has been gaining attention for a pocket-sized receiver, the D·Vision SDR, that picks up live camera video from many Russian drones and shows it on a screen.

Those drones send their video over the air without any scrambling, so anyone with the right receiver can watch along. A Ukrainian unit can see where a drone is heading and what its pilot is aiming at before it hits.

According to Defense News, the device is light, at about 10 ounces, which is less than half the weight of competing Ukrainian models, one of which weighs a couple of pounds.

It also listens on the radio channels Russia’s newer Molniya drones started using for video in June. Serhii “Flash” Beskrestnov, a radio specialist who advises Ukraine’s president, said in a June Facebook post cited by Defense News that “most detectors don’t see these frequencies, or see them poorly.” He warned that putting too much trust in a detector could prove fatal.

Beskrestnov has also warned that digital video could one day replace analog, which would blind receivers like this one. The New York Times reported in August that some Molniyas are AI-guided, using Nvidia chips and emitting no signals.

Something potentially enormous could be approaching for Tesla (TSLA) by January 1, 2027. Mark Zuckerberg’s Meta AI predicts that TSLA stock could be a standout performer through Q4 and into 2027, based on a hypothetical landmark catalyst that isn’t impossible.

The concept focuses on Tesla obtaining widespread regulatory approval for unsupervised full self-driving robotaxi operations in several major markets, while also scaling up the production and deployment of Optimus humanoid robots beyond current expectations.

In this scenario, Tesla would quickly shift from primarily an electric vehicle manufacturer to a high-margin platform company centered on autonomy and robotics. This transformation could open up multi-trillion-dollar markets and significantly increase the company’s stock valuation.

On the higher timeframes, TSLA has been consolidating in the $390–$415 region after a recovery from lower levels earlier in the year. Price continues to hold above key intermediate supports while facing resistance around the $420–$450 zone.

In a standard bull market for growth and technology stocks, a sustained breakout above $480–$520 would confirm intermediate strength and open the path to higher-cycle targets.

Under the extreme robotaxi approval and Optimus scaling scenario outlined above, clearing significant resistance levels would likely trigger powerful measured-move extensions and multi-cycle projections from the longer-term base.

Momentum indicators currently sit in neutral-to-constructive territory with substantial room to run into the strong overbought readings typical of high-beta technology rallies.

Key nearer-term supports sit near $380–$390 and $350–$360; holding those levels would keep the broader recovery structure intact.

More importantly, Tesla confirmed that production of Optimus humanoid robots has begun on high-volume lines in Fremont, marking a shift from prototypes to early manufacturing.

On the autonomy side, the Cybercab robotaxi service continues to expand, with the Austin fleet growing rapidly, plans to launch in Dallas, and an ambition to deliver the first Cybercabs to customers by the end of 2026.

Unsupervised robotaxi miles have increased sharply, while Full Self-Driving subscriptions remain on a strong upward trajectory. Tesla has also entered volume production of the Semi.

While near-term profits remain under pressure from heavy investment, these operational milestones reinforce the narrative of Tesla evolving beyond vehicles into high-margin autonomy and robotics platforms.

Under this highly speculative scenario, and assuming supportive market conditions return, Tesla (TSLA) could reach between $1,800 and $3,000, with a stretch target toward $4,500+ by January 1, 2027.

This remains pure speculation and entertainment, not a realistic base-case outlook. The catalyst would require extraordinary regulatory progress and execution on robotaxi and Optimus at a scale that is currently highly unlikely.

#5408. Reconciling the OCC’s Final Stablecoin Reserve Floors Against the Fed’s Proposal

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

The OCC's final GENIUS Act rule sets a 5% cash floor and a 40% cap on any one counterparty. The Fed's open proposal uses neither figure, and its comment window runs until November 30.

Issuers now face two sets of reserve rules that share a redemption deadline and differ on almost everything else.

Ask a stablecoin issuer what its reserves must look like in 2027, and the honest answer is now: it depends which regulator you ask.

The Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC) gave its answer on October 21, the final rule implementing the GENIUS Act. Our October 19 piece on staggered agency filings expected that rule "before the end of October," and it came two days later. The rule sets specific numbers: at least 5% of reserves in demand deposits or similar instant-access funds, and no more than 40% of reserves with a single counterparty.

The Federal Reserve's answer is still a proposal. Its GENIUS Act rulemaking remains open for comment until November 30, and it contains neither of those numbers. Until the Fed finalizes its rule, any company planning to issue under both agencies' rules, or deciding which one to apply to, is working with one fixed set of numbers and one open-ended set of principles.

The OCC's final rule was published in the Federal Register on October 23 and takes effect on January 18, 2027, the same day as the GENIUS Act itself. Comptroller Jonathan V. Gould called it "a clear, practical framework for payment stablecoin innovation, with strong standards for reserve backing, redemption, and risk management."

The reserve rules are looser than the March proposal in several places:

The OCC also removed the rebuttable presumption that some affiliate yield arrangements break the GENIUS Act's ban on paying interest, though it kept its broader anti-evasion powers. The agency received about 328 comments.

For existing issuers, the timeline is short. Under OCC Bulletin 2026-51, firms already operating in the United States that file a "substantially complete" application by January 18 can generally expect a waiver of the prior-approval requirement.

The Fed released its two proposals on September 24. They were published in the Federal Register on September 29 under Docket No. R-1899, and comments are due November 30.

The main requirements proposal would require Board-supervised issuers to "fully back their stablecoins with certain permissible reserve assets". The reserves' fair value would have to equal or exceed the stablecoins' outstanding value at all times. Permissible assets include:

On diversification, however, the Fed sets no numbers. Reserves must be "sufficiently diverse" to keep one-to-one backing at all times, and issuers must manage concentration in uninsured deposits and repo counterparties. The Board says it generally expects reserves to be mostly Treasuries, but it sets no cash floor and no counterparty percentage.

Redemption is where the two agencies agree most closely. Both define timely redemption as no later than two business days after a request. The difference lies in what happens under stress.

The FDIC, in its own proposal, uses a third approach: issuers would report on their own when redemption requests exceed 10% of issuance within 24 hours.

The clearest conflict is not about how much cash an issuer must hold, but how each agency treats bank deposits.

Under the OCC rule, at least 5% of reserves must be held in demand deposits or similar balances. That is a direct requirement to hold bank money.

The Fed proposal has no deposit floor. Instead, it would charge 2% capital against reserves held as uninsured deposits at an insured bank, and the same charge applies to undercollateralized reverse repo. One agency requires a minimum amount in deposits, and the other makes issuers hold extra capital against the deposits they choose to keep.

Concentration works the same way. An issuer with 60% of its deposit reserves at one bank would breach the OCC's 40% cap, unless one of the custodian or government exemptions applies. Under the Fed's current text, that issuer would face only a judgment by its supervisor about whether it has managed concentration risk properly.

The rules for a reserve shortfall also differ:

The difference is largest on capital. The OCC sets an individualized capital requirement measured in GAAP tangible equity. It has a $5 million floor that now lasts for the issuer's whole life, plus an operational backstop equal to 12 months of total expenses, up to half of which can be funded with qualifying subordinated debt.

The Fed proposes a fixed formula. On top of the 2% charges on deposits and repo, it adds an operational-risk charge on outstanding issuance:

It also adds 25% of three-year average revenue from sources other than reserves, adjusted by a loss scalar.

For an issuer with $50 billion in circulation, the issuance charge alone works out to $850 million under the Fed's proposal, before the revenue add-on. The OCC rule has no comparable fixed figure. Its capital depends on the issuer's own risk profile, with the $5 million floor as the only set minimum.

For now, the OCC's figures are final and the Fed's are not. Issuers and banks that hold reserves can still argue for changes until the Fed's comment period closes on November 30, and the Fed has asked 277 questions.

The decisions that matter most are clear from the comparison above:

Both sets of rules apply from the same date, January 18, 2027. If the Fed's final rule keeps its current approach, the United States will begin regulating stablecoins with a common redemption deadline and two different reserve rulebooks, decided by which agency charters the issuer.

#5405. Rivian spinout Also was working on an e-moto project in Kenya — until it walked away

Buy One Founder Summit Ticket, Get a Second for Free. Register now.

Founder Summit begins Nov. 4, 9:00 a.m. ET. Get your pass savings & deals before it starts. REGISTER HERE.

Also, the micromobility startup spun out of Rivian in 2025, quietly started and then walked away from an electric two-wheeler pilot project in Kenya earlier this year, as it sought to focus its resources on its consumer e-bike and autonomous vehicle ambitions, TechCrunch has learned.

The project received grant funding from the Shell Foundation, an independent charity established by the British oil and gas giant Shell plc. A section of the Shell Foundation’s website that has since been removed said the project’s goal was to “enable and de-risk global OEM entry into Africa’s EV market by piloting a locally integrated electric two-wheeler platform in Kenya, with potential to scale across East Africa.”

According to the deleted section, Also was expected to work on modular battery designs and distributed EV charging, and planned on “developing a purpose-built electric motorcycle for African riders.”

The opportunity for electric motorcycles seems ripe on the continent, which has a massive two-wheeler market. African mobility company Spiro recently said it has more than 130,000 electric motorcycles operating across seven countries, along with 2,500 battery-swapping stations. This boom has drawn interest from Chinese mobility companies and investors, which are pouring resources into the space.

In a September email, Also told TechCrunch that it had “explored this project” with an unnamed partner, but ultimately “decided to focus on its core roadmap” after completing only “some early-stage work.” Also said the grant funding it received from the Shell Foundation “will follow the project to support its ongoing development,” but declined to offer specifics.

The Shell Foundation told TechCrunch in an email that the project was “intended to generate evidence on driver income uplift potential, operational performance and commercial viability to deepen the company’s understanding of the market opportunity.” But when TechCrunch asked for more specifics, the Shell Foundation declined, citing a nondisclosure agreement with Also. Days later, the project disappeared from the Shell Foundation’s website.

During an interview last month at TechCrunch Disrupt, Also co-founder and president Chris Yu said the Kenya pilot project initially made sense given Also’s mission to build small, purpose-built vehicles that are “first and foremost cost-optimized to do the job that needs to be done in a particular market.”

But other projects took precedence, Yu said, especially the development of small autonomous vehicles — which Also is working on as part of a partnership with DoorDash.

“We piloted and ultimately decided, largely because of just urgency and pace around autonomy, frankly, that our attention would be best, in the near term, served fully focused” on that, he said, adding that he thinks there’s a “high chance that autonomy will show up first, and at a broader scale in these types of purpose-built smaller vehicles than at scale in passenger vehicles.”

Also walked away from the Africa project during a somewhat rocky first year of independence.

Supply chain problems forced the company to repeatedly delay deliveries of its first product, a premium e-bike called the TM-B, frustrating customers who had reserved one. What made matters worse was Also’s relative silence. The company said little for much of 2026 about when the bikes would arrive — a communication failure its leadership now acknowledges was a mistake.

“I think we did a pretty poor job communicating to our reservation holders through the summer when they were all waiting, and we got called out for that,” Yu said in the interview. “But I think it’s actually great. It’s really hard to earn the opportunity for people to care, and to tell us what they think, and to help us improve.”

Getting its first product launch back on track is crucial for Also, which has ambitions far beyond e-bikes. The company plans to sell commercial cargo bikes to companies like Amazon, including four-wheeled models, and has the partnership with DoorDash. These products are next in the company’s pipeline, Yu said, and represent bigger revenue opportunities.

But the TM-B comes first. It’s Also’s most visible product to consumers, and its striking design has drawn plenty of curiosity.

Yu said no single problem was responsible for delaying the bikes, which finally started shipping to customers in early October. Instead, Also spent much of the year playing supply chain Whac-A-Mole, a particularly difficult challenge given the TM-B’s complexity. Yu described the bike as “kind of a computer on wheels.”

At one point, Also found itself competing for the same raw materials used to make printed circuit boards for AI data centers. At other times, the company struggled to navigate certification requirements with different government agencies.

Yu said the scope of these problems, and the pace at which new ones popped up — almost weekly — made it difficult to give customers reliable updates about why their bikes were delayed.

“The entire team is like running at a million miles an hour to get these things produced and shipped to customers, and then it’s also really dynamic as well,” he said. “I think what we could have done better is just [say], straight up: ‘We’re chasing down these things, we’ll have an update shortly.’”

That didn’t happen at first, but Also has steadily improved its communication, earning some goodwill from customers on Reddit. The company will need it as it works through the inevitable kinks that come with a first product. Early customers have already reported problems, including delivery damage and noticeable battery drain.

Fal, a San Francisco-based startup that hosts and runs AI video, image, and audio models, has raised $1.3 billion in its latest funding round led by Bessemer Venture Partners, with participation from Nvidia, Sound Ventures, and T. Rowe Price. The deal values Fal at $16 billion, double its $8 billion valuation in April, Bloomberg reported.

The startup announced its Series E and F rounds at the same time, noting that a combined $1.65 billion was raised across both. (Sequoia led the earlier round.)

The latest round (Series F) comes amid soaring demand for inference services, the process of running an AI model that’s already been trained to generate outputs, particularly from customers relying on open source models. Fal surpassed $800 million in annualized revenue earlier this year, Bloomberg’s report noted.

Companies providing inference services, including Baseten, Fireworks AI, and Modal, have also been growing rapidly and raising large funding rounds at higher valuations. But their gross margins remain thin because of the high cost of buying or leasing compute, according to several people familiar with inference companies’ financials.

Fal was co-founded in 2021 by Burkay Gur, a former Coinbase machine learning leader and Oracle engineer, and Gorkem Yurtseven, who was previously a developer at Amazon.

#5402. Crypto Stocks Edge Up Before the Bell as 50 Companies Now Block Tokenized Shares: What Is Happening in the Market?

All reviews, research, news and assessments of any kind on The Tokenist are compiled using a strict editorial review process by our editorial team. Neither our writers nor our editors receive direct compensation of any kind to publish information on tokenist.com. Our company, Tokenist Media LLC, is community supported and may receive a small commission when you purchase products or services through links on our website. Click here for a full list of our partners and an in-depth explanation on how we get paid.

Crypto stocks edged higher before Tuesday’s open, November 3, even as Nvidia, Costco and Nike joined the companies blocking tokenized versions of their shares on OKXICE, taking the count to 50, and an AI chip sell-off sent Seoul’s Kospi down 3.6%.

The bounce is small, and it follows a bad month. Coinbase traded at $138.74 at 13:00 UTC, up 0.7% from Monday’s close of $137.83, its lowest finish since February 2024. Robinhood, Strategy and Circle rose between 0.5% and 1.1%, and Galaxy led with 2.8% after losing 8.8% on Monday.

The bigger story for the sector is the pushback against tokenization. Objectors to OKXICE, the 24/7 venue for tokenized US stocks that OKX is building with NYSE owner ICE, went from 16 to 50 in 11 days. Today is the deadline for companies notified on October 4, so the list could still grow, while Coinbase, Robinhood and the other crypto names on it have yet to say no.

Asia offered no lift. After a 1.1% drop in the Nasdaq on Monday, Samsung and SK hynix dragged the Kospi to 5,648.79, Shanghai slipped 0.8%, and Tokyo was shut for a holiday. Only Hong Kong closed higher, and Bitcoin held steady through the session at $77,326.

Investors are DUMPING US tech stocks at a rapid pace:The Nasdaq 100 index has dropped -6.1% over the last 3 trading sessions, its biggest 3-day decline since the April 2025 Liberation Day selloff. $QQQ This also marks the 3rd-largest 3-day decline since the 2022 bear market.… pic.twitter.com/jNvmex3HZj

So why are so many companies saying no to tokenization, and why are markets red from Seoul to New York?

Because they would carry the risk and see little of the benefit. OKXICE, the venue OKX is building with NYSE owner Intercontinental Exchange, wants to offer round-the-clock trading of US stocks as tokens, paid for in stablecoins.

Under the SEC’s exemption, a company can keep its shares off such a venue if an outside firm does the tokenizing. It has 30 days from notice to object, and the objections have come fast:

The newest 12 are Nvidia, Costco, Micron, CrowdStrike, Corning, IREN, USA Rare Earth, Bloom Energy, Nike, Palo Alto Networks, Reddit and Hewlett Packard Enterprise. They join Microsoft, Alphabet, Goldman Sachs and JPMorgan, which runs its own blockchain unit and says it still likes the technology.

The fight is over shareholder rights, especially votes. “Right now companies like Goldman and Microsoft see all of the risk and none of the upside,” Injective’s COO Mirza Uddin told CNBC.

OKXICE co-chair Andrew Cuomo isn’t backing down. “We are at the very beginning of the rollout of fundamentally different market structure,” he said at the October 30 press conference.

Discover: JPMorgan and Coca-Cola Block Tokenized Stocks on OKXICE as Objectors Hit 33. Coinbase and Robinhood Stay Out of the List

Only the crypto names avoided objection to tokenisation, along with several major US stocks. Coinbase, Robinhood, Circle, Strategy, BitGo and Securitize remain outside the objection list, as do Apple, Amazon, Tesla, SpaceX and Netflix.

One crypto-born company did say no. IREN, the Bitcoin miner that now earns more from renting computers to AI firms than from mining, objected in the latest batch.

Silence isn’t a yes, though. Venues get up to five business days to publish objections, so companies that answered this week may not show up until next week’s notice, and staying off the list doesn’t guarantee a stock will trade at launch.

The AI trade is cracking again. Big Tech results last week showed Amazon, Alphabet, Meta and Microsoft will keep spending heavily on data centres and chips, and investors want to see faster returns first.

Monday’s selling on Wall Street, where the Nasdaq fell 1.1%, hit Asia’s chipmakers on Tuesday:

Seoul’s slide is the one to watch. The Kospi closed at a record 9,114.55 on June 22 and is now 38% lower, with 17% of that lost since the end of September.

Oil added to the strain. Brent climbed 1.7% to $106.58 after reports of limited US strikes on an Iranian island in the Strait of Hormuz, a day after it fell more than 7% on hopes of new talks.

Hong Kong’s crypto stocks split. Exchange operator OSL rose 0.4%, and Boyaa Interactive, which holds Bitcoin, fell 5.1%.

They have been sold off with tech, then sold again for crypto. Every big name is down at least 12% since the end of September, and the first trading day after the Binance hack was the worst of the run.

Coinbase’s daily chart shows how far the slide has gone. The stock is $34 under its 50-day average and more than $50 under its 200-day, and Monday’s close was the lowest since February 2024.

COIN 1D chart. Source: Yahoo Finance (Nasdaq).

Discover: Crypto Stocks Lost Up to 54% in October as Hedge Funds Erased Every AI Stock Purchase Since 2025: Why Did Bitcoin Miners Fall Hardest?

The tokenization fight won’t move share prices on its own. For crypto stocks, today’s pre-market bounce still has to survive Wall Street’s open and a long night of election results.

On Wednesday, CEO Carl Pei posted on X that the company’s first “AI-native product” ships in December. “It’s a tool, but one built with the personality and care that have come to define a Nothing product. It has no new screen, and it couldn’t have been an app,” Pei wrote.

#5397. Exchange Ledgers in the Middle as CFTC and SEC Diverge on What “Delivery” Means

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

A customer buys a token on a U.S. exchange and the app shows the balance. Under the CFTC's December 14 framework, nothing has been delivered yet.

Under the SEC's crypto proposal, delivery doesn't decide the question at all. An October 27 comment letter asks the two agencies to settle on one answer.

Open almost any crypto exchange app after a purchase and you'll see a clean number: 1.0000 ETH, available. To the customer, the asset is theirs. To the exchange's database, it's a row in an internal ledger. To federal regulators, that row is now being judged by two different tests that don't agree on what it means.

The Commodity Futures Trading Commission (CFTC) has opened an advance notice of proposed rulemaking on what it calls Regulation Crypto Asset Transactions (CTX) and Regulation Crypto Asset Markets (CAM). It sets out the agency's first formal view of "actual delivery" for crypto since it withdrew its 2020 guidance last December. Comments close on December 14.

The Securities and Exchange Commission's Regulation Crypto Assets proposal takes a different view of the same moment. Then, on October 27, a comment letter on the SEC's file raised the gap directly. It described the situation as "two conflicting definitions of the same physical facts" and asked the agencies to "please coordinate the definitions."

Delivery matters because it decides which rulebook applies.

For the CFTC, the answer comes from Section 2(c)(2)(D) of the Commodity Exchange Act. A leveraged, margined or financed retail commodity trade is treated like a futures contract unless "actual delivery" happens within 28 days. If delivery happens in time, the trade falls outside futures rules. If it doesn't, the exchange is effectively running a futures venue.

For the SEC, the question is whether a token is still part of an investment contract. Under the August proposal, a covered investment contract ends when the issuer has finished or permanently stopped its essential managerial efforts and files a Form TR transition report. Whether the buyer has received the token is not part of that test.

So one agency treats delivery as the deciding question, and the other barely considers it.

The CFTC's position is still preliminary, but it is detailed. Published in the Federal Register on October 13, the notice relies on the Monex case standard: actual delivery requires "the transfer of some meaningful degree of possession or control."

For crypto, the agency suggests that possession and control "may require possession of the credentials (e.g., private key(s))." It takes three positions that matter most to exchanges:

The agency is also asking whether control has to be exclusive, whether delivery can happen while a lien or security interest is outstanding, and how financing offered in an exchange's standard account documents affects whether a trade is covered at all.

The SEC's proposal, released on August 18, deals with a different question. It creates offering exemptions, including a $5 million startup exemption over four years, and a safe harbor for when a crypto asset's investment contract ends. Neither depends on where the token sits.

Under the proposal, a token held in a customer's self-custody wallet and a token recorded on an exchange's books are treated the same way. In both cases, the investment contract question depends on the issuer's managerial efforts and its filings.

That is the gap the October 27 letter tries to close. Its author, who describes themselves as a fintech founder designing a consumer platform, argues that "where the customer holds the private keys or execution is on-chain, with custody evidence, the asset should be treated as delivered and the covered-investment-contract analysis should end there."

Running four common exchange transactions through both frameworks shows where the tests split.

Trade one: a fully paid purchase left on the exchange.

Trade two: the same purchase withdrawn to a self-custody wallet on day three.

Trade three: a margined purchase kept on the exchange's ledger for 30 days.

Trade four: an on-chain swap that settles directly into the user's wallet.

The pattern is consistent. Self-custody is the only position that clearly counts as delivery under the CFTC's view and also ends the analysis under the letter's proposed SEC fix. Everything left on an exchange's internal ledger stays in an unclear position. The CFTC treats it as undelivered and the SEC's text doesn't address it.

The letter was filed on October 27, a week after the SEC's October 20 comment deadline. It is anonymous and brief, but its main concern is practical. If the definitions stay separate, it warns, founders will have to design products around whichever rule is stricter.

It is the only filing on either docket so far that sets the two definitions side by side.

The CFTC process is still at the advance-notice stage, so a formal proposal will follow. For U.S. platforms, though, the direction is clear. Under the CFTC's preliminary reading, an exchange that keeps customer assets in internal ledger accounts has not delivered them. If that exchange also offers margin or financing, it is on track to be treated as a futures venue.

The SEC's final rule could adopt the letter's custody-based approach or keep delivery out of its analysis entirely. Until one of those happens, the same ledger entry can be undelivered for one regulator and irrelevant for the other.

Exchanges and their customers have until December 14 to say which definition should prevail. The real decision is whether "delivered" ends up meaning the same thing at both agencies.

#5396. A YC startup is putting $1M behind 5 unsolved materials science problems for AI

Buy One Founder Summit Ticket, Get a Second for Free. Register now.

Founder Summit begins Nov. 4, 9:00 a.m. ET. Get your pass savings & deals before it starts. REGISTER HERE.

Discovered Materials, a months-old San Francisco startup using AI models to find new substances for building advanced chips, announced a million-dollar challenge for AI models to solve five critical problems in materials science.

While frontier AI models have solved a remarkable series of outstanding mathematics problems and made progress in the life sciences, they have yet to truly plumb the complex physics in advanced materials.

“It’s more difficult to specify problems clearly in materials science because it’s not like math, where you have a very specific definition and can get to a yes or no,” said Advaith Sridhar, a co-founder of Discovered Materials, which was part of Y Combinator’s spring 2026 batch. “We came to this discussion [wondering], what are the grand challenges in this field? How do we know AI is making progress?”

Though materials science doesn’t have an equivalent of the Millennium Prize Problems, Discovered Materials recruited an advisory group of academics at leading global universities to spell out five open problems. The company is offering a pool of prizes, worth $1 million in total, for solutions to the problems.

“Across materials science, there are phenomena we observe but cannot explain,” Felipe Jornada, a Stanford professor who helped develop the challenges, said in a statement. “Explaining these phenomena would improve our understanding of physics, and the answers would directly shape how we build electronics, store energy, and manufacture the materials of the future.”

Before announcing the challenges, Discovered Materials turned frontier lab models loose on them, giving AI agents internet access and other resources to work autonomously for days. The models spent several days on each problem without making much headway. Still, it’s easy to imagine OpenAI or Anthropic attempting to one-shot them with significantly more compute or a newer model.

“It’s not particularly a concern to us whether we find it, or someone else finds it, or a professor finds it, or the frontier labs find it,” Sridhar said. “The reason we’re putting out these challenges is because we want them to serve as the goalposts. If you go and solve these challenges, we are deepening our understanding of materials and how things around us behave.”

Tracking efforts to solve the problems will show “whether the models are climbing in this domain,” he added.

The challenge also reflects the changing nature of scientific inquiry as AI proves capable of uncovering insights and techniques human researchers didn’t anticipate. With solutions apparently easier to find than ever, the questions become more important.

“This is a new way of thinking about science, where we come up with the verification and the challenges first, and then we let somebody come up with the ideas that explain the problem,” Sridhar said. “Knowing what are the right questions to ask is not trivial and very difficult in this domain, so this is where the professors have really helped us shape what are the right questions we should be asking.”

Discovered Materials’ main focus is developing new materials for use in semiconductors; the startup partners with chip giants on research projects while also funding its own scientific efforts. When the company announced its seed round in August, Sridhar told TechCrunch that he hoped the company would generate a useful material within a year.

“Those timelines have accelerated a little bit,” he says today. “I’m more confident now that we will be able to find these industrially useful materials in a timeline shorter than a year.”

Dogecoin community member Mishaboar urged users who purchased a Trezor device from CryptoBilis in March this year or later to take immediate precautions, including moving their funds to a completely new wallet with a freshly generated recovery seed.

"If you bought a Trezor from CryptoBilis in March 2026 or later, move your funds to a completely new wallet, with a newly generated recovery seed, as soon as possible," Mishaboar wrote.

If you bought a Trezor from CryptoBilis in March 2026 or later, move your funds to a completely new wallet, with a newly generated recovery seed, as soon as possible. Use a device and wallet you trust to create the new wallet. If your wallet supports an additional passphrase, use it (and remember to write it down in your offline backups). An ELI5: I know this is obvious to many of you, but in my experience some people don't realize that hardware wallets don't actually "contain" their coins. Your coins "live" on the blockchain. #5392. Ripple CTO David Schwartz Explains Why XRP Could Gain Value as XRPL Adoption Grows

Ripple CTO emeritus David Schwartz has argued that rising adoption of the XRP Ledger (XRPL) could translate into stronger demand for XRP, pointing to the token’s role in liquidity, trading, and network transactions.

In an October 23 exchange on X, Schwartz challenged the idea that the ledger could become a major financial platform without its native asset gaining meaningful demand.

“The thesis is this: Low fees and reliable operation make XRPL a great place to move and hold value. That drives value flow to XRPL. XRP captures some of that value because of its unique advantages over other assets on XRPL,” Schwartz wrote.

He further noted that XRP has several advantages that could help it benefit as more financial activity moves onto the network. These include its role as a liquidity bridge between assets, its availability to accounts without counterparty risk, and its use to pay transaction fees.

“I think that’s one example of the mechanism I’m talking about. XRP has other advantages on XRPL too. It’s the only counterparty-free asset that any account can accept. People have to hold it to pay fees. All of those things can help drive value and demand,” he added.

Notably, the ledger’s built-in decentralized exchange can route trades through XRP when doing so offers a better exchange rate than trading two assets directly. If XRPL supports more markets and tokenized assets, XRP could therefore see greater use in connecting liquidity across those markets.

Schwartz said a scenario in which XRPL becomes highly successful in financial applications while XRP fails to attract strong demand is “very unlikely.” He acknowledged that a world dominated by a single settlement asset could produce a different outcome, but said he considers that possibility unlikely.

He also gave a hypothetical example involving Bitcoin. According to him, even if Bitcoin became the dominant settlement asset, wrapped or bridged versions of BTC could still trade on XRPL, creating opportunities for XRP to facilitate exchanges.

That said, on-chain data also offer another measure of adoption. Santiment reported last Thursday that the XRP Ledger had reached a record 8.24 million non-empty wallets, while daily wallet creation climbed to 4,772, its fifth-largest spike since March. This suggests that participation on XRPL has continued despite price volatility, which could generate sustained upward pressure on XRP.

Moreover, the firm identified $1.40 as an important level to watch, with a sustained move above it potentially opening the way toward $1.50 if wallet growth remains strong. Conversely, it warned that a drop below $1.30 alongside slower wallet creation would weaken the short-term adoption signal.

Some analysts have offered substantially more bullish price projections. Recently, Egrag Crypto said XRP appeared positioned to extend toward a macro target above $15, citing a chart pattern based on previous periods of price compression and breakout.

At press time, XRP was trading at $1.31, up 2.91% in the past 24 hours.

It's the 18th anniversary of the Bitcoin whitepaper. Today marks the historic date on which its pseudonymous creator Satoshi Nakamoto published the blueprint for the first digital cash.

On Oct. 31, 2008, a nine-page white paper called "Bitcoin: A Peer-to-Peer Electronic Cash System" was published, laying out a radical vision for transferring value electronically without the need for conventional financial intermediaries.

Bitcoin supporters, exchanges, and the rest of the crypto community are filling social media platform X with celebratory wishes on the 18th anniversary of Bitcoin's unveiling to the world.

Bitcoin proponent and Strategy Chairman Michael Saylor wrote on X: "Happy Bitcoin white paper day. 18 years."

One of the most salient features of the whitepaper is the fixed supply of Bitcoin at 21 million coins. The pre-determined issuance structure is what makes Bitcoin different from traditional monetary systems, where central authorities can inflate the money supply.

Major U.S. crypto exchange Coinbase highlighted this fact in its X post: "21,000,000. Never more. Happy Bitcoin Whitepaper Day."

21,000,000. Never more. Happy Bitcoin Whitepaper Day. https://t.co/JtKeHtCuSM

"Today marks 18 years since the release of the Bitcoin Whitepaper. A day that changed everything," Coinbase continued.

Stablecoin issuer Tether wrote: "On 31 October 2008, Satoshi published nine pages that explained Bitcoin to the world. Today we're explaining it to everyone else. Two pizzas, 10,000 BTC, 21 million coins, and one key you never share. Everything you need to know, in a comic. Happy 18th birthday, Bitcoin whitepaper."

Crypto platform Uphold wrote: "Nine pages that challenged the entire legacy financial system. Happy Bitcoin Whitepaper Day."

The Bitcoin whitepaper laid the groundwork for the network's launch in January 2009, when Satoshi Nakamoto mined Bitcoin's genesis block and introduced the first units of the cryptocurrency.

When Bitcoin launched on January 3, 2009, it had no market value or official exchange price. Over the years, Bitcoin has evolved from a niche technological experiment into a globally recognized digital asset. Its emergence has influenced the development of thousands of cryptocurrencies, blockchain applications, and decentralized financial systems.

The cryptocurrency now trades at $77,310 and is worth $1.55 trillion, according to CoinMarketCap data.

#5387. Clock Ticking on Zcash’s Sprout Pool: 22,263 ZEC Unmoved Ahead of NU7 Lock

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

Daily pool data shows Sprout holders moved more than 300 ZEC out in a September rush, then almost stopped. The last withdrawal was on October 19.

Unless someone acts in the next few days, nearly all of what remains will be unspendable at block 3,543,405.

Most coverage of Zcash's upcoming Sprout freeze quotes the same figure, about 22,000 ZEC. That number is accurate, but it is a single snapshot. It doesn't show whether the people who own those coins are doing anything about the deadline.

We checked the pool every day, and the answer so far is no.

According to ZecStats' daily value-pool records, Sprout has held exactly 22,263.34162335 ZEC since October 19. That is 11 straight days, and more than 12,000 blocks, without a single zatoshi leaving the pool. Our October 25 piece recorded the drop from 22,309 ZEC to 22,263 ZEC. Since then the balance hasn't moved.

ZecStats publishes a daily CSV of every Zcash value pool, using the last block of each UTC day. Its figures follow the valuePools field that a full node returns through the getblockchaininfo call. The archive starts on July 30, 2026, and gives a 92-day picture of the Sprout pool.

Across those 92 days, about 374 ZEC, or 1.65% of the pool, left Sprout. That is an average of roughly 4 ZEC a day. The average hides the real pattern, though: the pool moved on only 15 of the 92 days.

Most of the withdrawals came in a few large transfers in September:

Together with smaller moves on August 31, September 17 and September 19, the 30 days to September 29 saw 310.5 ZEC leave Sprout. That is about 10 ZEC a day.

October was much quieter. Apart from one withdrawal of 46.05 ZEC on October 19, the month's activity was small change:

Since October 19, there has been no movement at all.

At September's pace, about 70 ZEC more would leave before activation. At October's pace, it would be well under 15 ZEC. On the last 11 days' pace, the answer is zero.

The deadline is set in ZIP 259, which defines how the NU7 network upgrade is deployed. It sets the mainnet activation height at 3,543,405.

NU7 does not introduce a new transaction format. Instead, after activation, version 4 transactions become invalid, while versions 5 and 6 remain valid. Sprout's design is the problem. As ZIP 259 puts it: "Because Sprout transfers can only be represented by version 4 transactions, funds remaining in the Sprout pool become unspendable."

The coins would not be destroyed, and NU7 does not change Zcash's supply cap. They would simply be stuck in a pool that no valid transaction can spend from. Today the stranded amount would be 22,263 ZEC, about 0.13% of the roughly 17.01 million ZEC in circulation.

ZIP 259 also skips Zcash's usual three-month gap between the first supporting software release and activation. Operators running unsupported software could stay online and follow a pre-NU7 chain.

As of ZecStats' latest update on October 30 at 13:09 UTC, the chain was at block 3,535,877. That leaves 7,528 blocks until activation.

In October, the network averaged about 1,147 blocks a day, or one roughly every 75.3 seconds. At that rate, block 3,543,405 arrives around 02:00–03:00 UTC on November 6. That is the evening of November 5 in the Americas and the early hours of November 6 in Europe and Africa.

Small changes in block times could move that window by a few hours. Holders who plan to move funds on the final day risk missing the cutoff.

In practice, getting funds out of Sprout means sending a version 4 transaction that moves them into a newer pool before activation. Users need software that can still build Sprout transactions and a synced node or wallet that recognizes their old notes.

The September withdrawals show that some holders are still paying attention. Several were round amounts, such as 99.998 ZEC, which is consistent with someone moving 100 ZEC and paying a fee. The 11-day pause since October 19 suggests something else: most of the remaining 22,263 ZEC may belong to keys that are lost, forgotten or no longer used.

That has been part of the debate about Sprout for years. A pool that has been shrinking slowly since Zcash's early days is now on a fixed timetable. The daily data indicates that most of its remaining balance is not being moved.

Every report that cites "about 22,000 ZEC at risk" is technically correct. The more useful figure for anyone tracking the upgrade is the rate of change, and right now that rate is zero.

The useful thing to watch over the next week is whether the Sprout line in ZecStats' daily data moves again before block 3,543,405. If it doesn't, Zcash will activate NU7 with about 22,263 ZEC permanently locked in its first shielded pool. That would be one of the largest deliberate freezes of user funds by any major blockchain upgrade, and nearly all of it would be coins whose owners did not move them in time.

#5385. Binance to Resume XRP, Bitcoin, Ethereum and Other Crypto Withdrawals

Cryptocurrency exchange Binance will allow withdrawals for major cryptocurrencies such as XRP, Bitcoin (BTC), Ethereum (ETH), and Solana (SOL), among others, after suspending withdrawals because of a massive security breach involving $6.3 billion.

Binance announced on Nov. 1 that the exchange would begin resuming withdrawal services between 06:00 and 09:00 UTC.

Binance emphasized that the withdrawal resumption process will be carried out progressively as the exchange conducts security and infrastructure readiness checks.

"We aim to restore withdrawals progressively as we complete security and readiness checks," said Binance.

Binance continued to offer deposit services during the security breach.

The first phase of withdrawal resumption will include a total of 15 blockchain networks.

This list includes popular networks such as Bitcoin, Ethereum, XRP Ledger, BNB Smart Chain, Solana, Tron, and Dogecoin.

Other cryptocurrencies that will be available for withdrawals include Zcash (ZEC), Avalanche (AVAX), Sui (SUI), Polygon (POL) and Arbitrum (ARB).

Withdrawals of major stablecoins such as Tether (USDT) and USD Coin (USDC) will also be enabled on multiple networks.

The exchange noted that it selected the assets based on user withdrawal demand over the past week.

The exchange also warned that not all listed cryptocurrencies and networks may be enabled at the same time.

The withdrawal resumption comes only days after Binance suffered a massive security breach.

The breach led to the theft of around $6.3 billion worth of cryptocurrencies from the exchange's hot wallets.

The exchange temporarily paused withdrawals in order to contain the damage, conduct an investigation into the security breach and avoid additional losses.

Binance has now disclosed that it has recovered around 95% of affected assets.

This is up from 90% when Binance last provided an update on the recovery process.

The exchange said that it has fully backed the balances of cryptocurrencies like Bitcoin, Ethereum, XRP, Solana, BNB, USDT, USDC, Zcash, USD1, and Ripple USD (RLUSD).

The remaining 5% includes cryptocurrencies that are less liquid and harder to buy in large amounts.

Binance said on Tuesday, November 3, that the Binance hack started with a fake job interview, in which North Korean hackers gave one of its engineers a coding test laced with malware, but many traders still doubt that is the whole story.

The October 29 theft took $6.34 billion from Binance’s hot wallets, the largest crypto heist on record. Binance’s incident report describes a campaign that ran for months: a tampered download in June, the fake interview in September and an internal AI tool that led the attackers to the engineers who ran its wallets.

Not everyone is buying it. Since the hack, traders on X have called it an inside job. They point to how fast the money left, across ten blockchains in about 20 minutes, and to how often Binance’s account has changed.

BREAKING: Binance says hackers used a fake job interview to infect an employee's computer.The malware let them hijack Binance's internal AI tool, take over more engineers' accounts, and drain $6.34 billion from its hot wallets.

No one has offered proof. The FBI has tied the theft to North Korea’s TraderTraitor group, and blockchain analytics firm TRM Labs agrees with high confidence.

BNB hasn’t recovered either. It trades at $703.33, up 0.7% today but still 7.4% below its $759.85 close the day before the hack.

So what exactly does Binance say happened, and why are traders still unconvinced?

Slowly, through three engineers. Binance co-CEO Richard Teng told CNBC the attackers “spent months building their way in” and rejected the idea that a single laptop was the weak point.

“This wasn’t one mistake or one breach – it was a months-long campaign,” Teng wrote on X.

Binance says users won’t lose anything. It has replaced 98% of the stolen assets with its own funds, and about $2.85 billion has been frozen or intercepted with the help of Tether, Circle and others.

The skeptics keep coming back to five points:

The proof of reserves didn’t help. Binance’s November 2 proof used an October 31 snapshot, taken after it had already bought back most of the stolen coins, so critics say it can’t show how big the hole was.

A hack of this scale means serious security failures occurred. No platform is unhackable, but that cannot be an excuse. Every incident exposes weaknesses that should have been prevented.Some details are embarrassing. Public explanations also simplify what appears to have been a… https://t.co/ZMAjZt2hF8

Some of the louder claims have already fallen apart. A viral post blaming a North Korean “honey trap” passed 800,000 views before co-founder Yi He called it untrue and said ZachXBT, the investigator it quoted, never said it.

An employee’s laptop being the way in doesn’t make it an inside job. Fake job offers with booby-trapped coding tests are TraderTraitor’s best-known trick, the same group behind the $1.5 billion Bybit hack in February 2025.

Less than half of it has been stopped. Of the $6.34 billion taken, Binance says $2.85 billion has been frozen or intercepted, much of it stablecoins that Tether and Circle could lock.

The rest is on the move. Blockchain analytics firm Elliptic counts about $3.24 billion still in addresses linked to the attackers, and Chainalysis has found the stolen funds mixed with money from September’s Bitget exploit.

One pile hasn’t moved at all. The 233.46 million XRP taken from Binance, worth about $299 million, has sat in six wallets since November 2, untouched as of Wednesday morning.

Not yet. BNB fell 8.1% on October 29, from $759.85 to $698.46, on $414 million in volume, more than four times what it traded the day before.

It has leaned on its 200-day EMA ever since. BNB dipped to $680.74 earlier today, close to the $680 hack low, and bounced back to $703.33.

Binance has told its version of the Binance hack in detail. Until the independent review backs it up, traders will keep reading BNB’s chart as a vote of confidence.

#5382. Do Not Use Your iPhone as Hardware Wallet, OneKey Founder

Disclaimer: The opinions expressed by our writers are their own and do not represent the views of U.Today. The financial and market information provided on U.Today is intended for informational purposes only. U.Today is not liable for any financial losses incurred while trading cryptocurrencies. Conduct your own research by contacting financial experts before making any investment decisions. We believe that all content is accurate as of the date of publication, but certain offers mentioned may no longer be available.

Using an old iPhone as a crypto cold wallet may be less safe than it looks, OneKey founder Yishi Wang has warned. The practice is popular with self-custody fans: wipe a spare phone, take it offline, and keep your wallet recovery information on it.

Wang's worry is that an offline phone can still be attacked by someone who has it in their hands. He has pointed to flaws in several generations of iPhone. These include the publicly documented checkm8 issue on older models and, more recently reported, low-level weaknesses in certain later devices. They sit in the early stages of the boot process. A malicious app isn't involved.

An iOS update may not fix a weakness built into immutable boot code. Switching off Wi-Fi and cellular does nothing about someone who gets physical access to the phone. A vulnerability still doesn't automatically mean an attacker can recover a seed phrase, though. Device encryption, passcode strength and secure key handling remain real barriers.

Wang advises against trusting iPhone 11-generation and older devices with recovery phrases. If you think a phrase may have been exposed, create a completely new one using a trusted setup and move your funds to that wallet. Generating another address from the same seed won't help, because the underlying exposure stays.

He also stresses updated operating systems, long alphanumeric passcodes and careful control of USB connections. Earlier, he suggested that even newer iPhones shouldn't be treated as equivalent to purpose-built signing devices when the holdings are substantial and long-term.

Dedicated hardware wallets are built to isolate signing keys and let you check transaction details on the device itself. They carry risk too. Counterfeit hardware, compromised distribution channels and sloppy recovery-phrase handling can all undermine their security.

The argument is about threat models, not brand loyalty. An offline phone cuts remote exposure, but that doesn't turn it into a secure hardware wallet.

#5379. Hong Kong Passes Its Crypto Tax Reporting Law: Exchanges Must Collect User Data From 2027 and Share It Abroad From 2028

All reviews, research, news and assessments of any kind on The Tokenist are compiled using a strict editorial review process by our editorial team. Neither our writers nor our editors receive direct compensation of any kind to publish information on tokenist.com. Our company, Tokenist Media LLC, is community supported and may receive a small commission when you purchase products or services through links on our website. Hong Kong lawmakers passed a crypto tax reporting law on Wednesday, November 4, requiring crypto platforms tied to the city to collect their users’ tax details from 2027, so tax officials can share them with other countries from 2028.

The law brings in the OECD’s Crypto-Asset Reporting Framework, or CARF, the global standard for tracing crypto gains across borders. The government said Hong Kong’s Inland Revenue Department will start exchanging the data with partner jurisdictions in 2028.

The same bill updates the Common Reporting Standard, the system banks already use to report foreign accounts. Its new version, which also covers digital financial products, takes effect in 2028.

Hong Kong isn’t moving alone. It is one of 27 jurisdictions, including Singapore, the UAE and Switzerland, that have committed to first exchanges by 2028, the OECD’s latest list shows. Another 46, including the UK, the EU and Japan, start a year earlier.

So what does the new law ask of crypto platforms, and what changes for traders who use them?

It turns crypto platforms into tax reporters. The Inland Revenue Department’s CARF guide calls them reporting crypto-asset service providers: any business that carries out crypto trades for customers, whether as an exchange, a broker, a dealer or a crypto ATM operator.

A platform falls under Hong Kong’s rules if it is tax resident in the city, incorporated there, managed from there, or runs a branch or regular place of business there. Every platform that meets one of those tests has to register with the department, even if it has nothing to report.

Existing customers aren’t exempt. Platforms get 12 months after the rules take effect to collect self-certifications from users who already have accounts.

The law also sets offences for failing to register, skipping due diligence or filing wrong returns. Users can be prosecuted too, for knowingly or recklessly giving false information in a self-certification.

“Hong Kong has been supporting international efforts in enhancing tax transparency and combatting cross-border tax evasion,” said Christopher Hui, Hong Kong’s Secretary for Financial Services and the Treasury.

Discover: Franklin Templeton Readies Two ETFs That Turn Stock Dividends Into Bitcoin as Washington Writes Crypto Rules Without Congress

On January 1, 2027, less than two months away. The bill moved quickly: a public consultation ran from December 2025 to February 2026, and the government published the bill on May 22.

Platforms that first fall under the rules in 2027 have until January 31, 2028, to register. The department hasn’t yet published the details of its online portal or the data format it wants.

Hong Kong is in the second wave. The OECD’s commitments list, last updated on September 14, splits the world like this:

Hong Kong’s rivals for crypto business are on the same schedule. Singapore and the UAE have also committed to their first exchanges by 2028.

Existing users will get the same request within a year. Lying on it is an offence under the new law, so ticking the wrong country isn’t a way around it.

That is usually enough for a tax office to spot crypto gains that never showed up on a return. Transfers to outside wallets are covered too, so moving coins off the exchange still leaves a record.

Platforms carry the heavier load. They have under two months to build the forms, the checks and the records, and the department has yet to publish its portal details.

For traders, Hong Kong’s crypto tax law closes one of the last big Asian gaps in the OECD’s reporting net. By 2028, a crypto account in Hong Kong, Singapore or Dubai will be about as visible to a home tax office as a bank account.

#5378. Laurent Correia on the Crucial Difference Between Earning Wealth and Holding Onto It

Laurent Correia treats making money and keeping it as two separate skills. After years in business and Dubai property, he says the second one took him much longer to learn.

A good month in business feels like a turning point. Invoices get paid, sales pick up, and plans that looked a bit fanciful a quarter ago start to seem doable. Then a few months pass, and you’re under the same pressure to keep earning as before.

Often the issue isn’t how much came in. Each rise in income tends to bring a new commitment, whether that’s a bigger team or higher personal spending, and by the end there’s little left to show for the good stretch.

Laurent Correia describes making money and keeping it as two different skills. Having worked across business ventures and property investment, he says the second took him longer to learn.

Revenue is the number most business owners watch because it’s right there. A completed sale proves a customer was willing to pay, and a few strong months make it tempting to decide the idea has found its audience.

It leaves a lot out, though. Operating expenses, commitments you’ve already made, and the cost of simply keeping the business running all come out of that figure before anything is left over. You can run a growing operation and still have very little room to move.

Correia’s distinction gives you a second question to ask after a sale: what has this income made possible beyond the sale itself? You don’t need a complicated model to answer it. Could the business get through a quiet month? Could it handle an unexpected bill without panic? Can the owner make a decision without waiting for the next payment to land?

None of that shows up in turnover, but it tells you a lot more about whether things are getting better. Plenty of owners earn more every year and still feel just as stretched because the extra money goes out as fast as it comes in.

Property became central to Correia’s longer-term thinking, with Dubai at the center of that activity. He describes the move toward owning assets as a major stage in going from entrepreneur to investor.

What stands out to me is the change in timescale. Running a business mostly means reacting to what’s in front of you this week. Deciding what the proceeds should pay for over the next several years is a different kind of thinking, and it raises questions that day-to-day trading never does.

The answers depend on the person. The SEC’s guide to asset allocation says your choices should depend on how long you have before you need the money and how much risk you can stomach. Both of those are personal.

Correia’s path shows how one person worked it out, but your situation isn’t his, so it won’t copy across cleanly. What you can take from it is a habit: let the future shape what you do now. Words like freedom or security don’t mean much until you pin them to something.

For instance, how many months of bills you’d want covered, or what you’d like to do without worrying about it. Write that down, and you’ve got something to plan around.

Correia says becoming a father changed what success means to him. These days his ambition is tied up with freedom, security and what he can leave his children.

That makes earning versus keeping money feel personal. A target carries more weight when it’s attached to something you want your work to pay for, and a bare number usually isn’t.

Try it on your own last good stretch. Set the income figure aside and ask what actually got better. You might have more breathing room, or rely less on one large customer, or find you can plan further out than before.

If nothing comes to mind, that tells you something as well, and it’s a decent starting point for your next goal. Instead of just aiming higher, ask what a good year ought to leave you with.

The next sale will always need attention, and so will whatever you do with the money after it.
